#6316. Uranus and Neptune look alike, but their chemistry hints at different pasts

Models of the deep chemistry of Uranus and Neptune find far more oxygen inside Neptune, a sign the two grew from different parts of the disk.

Uranus and Neptune are similar in size and are both known as ice giants. But new model estimates suggest Neptune’s deep atmosphere contains a much higher proportion of oxygen than Uranus’s.

The researchers calculate that the two planets’ carbon-to-oxygen ratios differ enough that each may have grown from a different part of the disk that built the solar system.

Tom Briand of Aix-Marseille Université in France led the work.

His co-authors include Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colorado, who served as a co-advisor on Briand’s doctorate.

“Uranus and Neptune may resemble twins today, but their chemistry is telling us that they are more like cousins with very different histories,” Mousis said.

Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, and no spacecraft has been back. Telescopes see only the top of each atmosphere.

Most of the oxygen on both ice giants is in water, and water condenses into clouds at pressures hundreds of times higher than sea level on Earth.

Even the probe NASA is planning for Uranus would likely sample the atmosphere down to about ten times sea-level pressure.

So the team used a stand-in. Carbon monoxide forms in the hot depths, where it stays in balance with water, and rising gas carries it upward faster than chemistry can destroy it.

The amount near the top is therefore a record of how much oxygen there is far below, a method also used on Jupiter.

On Neptune, that carbon monoxide has been known since the 1990s and measured at about 0.2 parts per million.

On Uranus, the ALMA telescope array in Chile only confirmed it in the lower atmosphere in observations from 2022 and 2024.

The team’s own reading of the 2022 data gives about 5.6 parts per billion, roughly 35 times less than Neptune.

Briand’s team extended a model of the deep chemistry so that it changes with latitude, because a fast-spinning planet mixes its atmosphere more vigorously at the equator than near the poles.

They then asked how much oxygen each planet needs down deep to produce the carbon monoxide seen at the top.

For Uranus, the answer came out at roughly 60 to 180 times the Sun’s proportion of oxygen, depending on latitude. For Neptune it was about 220 to 340 times.

Uncertainty in the chemical reaction rates shifted those ranges by about a tenth at most.

Both figures are estimates from a model, and the biggest unknown is how vigorously each atmosphere mixes.

The team wrote that the equator, where mixing is strongest, is probably the best guide to the planet as a whole.

Carbon is easier to estimate. Methane carries most of it, and methane has been measured in the upper atmosphere of both planets.

Divide carbon by oxygen, and Uranus’s ratio runs from 0.06 to 0.52, while Neptune’s runs from 0.02 to 0.12.

At the top of its range, Uranus’s ratio is close to the Sun’s. Neptune’s falls well below the Sun’s at every latitude.

The two ranges overlap between 0.06 and 0.12, so the team can’t rule out that both planets share one value.

Uranus and Neptune probably never grew into gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, the authors wrote.

So the heavy elements each planet is made of came mostly from icy pebbles rather than from gas. That makes the ice’s carbon-to-oxygen ratio the number to match.

Mousis’s disk model follows gas and ice through the first million years of the solar system.

As the disk cooled, each compound froze at its own distance from the young Sun: carbon dioxide first, then methane, then carbon monoxide farthest out.

Where each one froze set how much carbon the local ice carried compared with water.

Both planets now orbit at about 20 to 30 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, and in the model the ice out there has close to the Sun’s carbon-to-oxygen ratio. That fits Uranus. It doesn’t fit Neptune.

Neptune’s low ratio does fit ice that formed much closer in, near the distance where water froze but carbon stayed as gas.

The authors suggest Neptune grew there and migrated outward.

“Neptune’s chemistry is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it formed where we see it today, pulling from the same reservoir of cosmic materials as Uranus,” Mousis said.

The disk model carries assumptions of its own, including how carbon was split among its molecules at the start and how turbulent the disk was. Either one moves the freezing lines. It also assumes that nothing after formation changed the planets’ carbon relative to oxygen.

The result depends on the equator being the right guide, too. If Uranus mixes less than Neptune, its ratio drops toward the shared range, and the two planets could have formed from similar material after all.

Further atmospheric measurements could help narrow the possibilities. Briand’s team wrote that its latitude maps could help choose where a Uranus probe should enter the atmosphere.

NASA’s Uranus Orbiter and Probe is a mission concept that the 2023 to 2032 planetary science decadal survey ranked as a high priority.

Mousis said it is expected to launch sometime in the next decade. Even then, estimating the oxygen hidden far below the clouds would still require models.

The full study was published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

#6314. Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by turning into giants

Cancer cells that survive chemo swell into giant senescent cells that summon immune repair, and drugs that block their IAP proteins kill them.

Chemotherapy can kill a cancer cell, but some survivors enter an unusual state. After a near-lethal dose, they stop dividing and swell to many times their normal size.

Then they start pumping out the chemical signals a wound uses to call in the immune system’s repair crew. These surviving cells may help tumors return.

A team in Dublin has identified a mechanism that keeps them alive after the damage, along with experimental drugs that kill them in laboratory tests.

Seamus Martin, the Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics at Trinity College Dublin, led the work from his lab with postdoctoral fellow Gokhan Gunay at the university’s Smurfit Institute of Genetics.

Collaborators at the University of Cologne and the Olivia Newton-John Cancer Research Institute in Melbourne took part.

Nearly all of it was done in human cancer cells grown in the lab, with some experiments in mice, and none of it involved patients.

In an interview with Earth.com, Martin was asked what surprised him most. He pointed to the cells themselves.

“These are really bizarre-looking cells,” he said.

“They are truly gigantic when compared with normal cells (approx. 10X normal size) and this is highly unusual behavior for cells, even cancer cells.”

The team gave cervical, bowel and lung cancer cells a three-hour pulse of cisplatin or etoposide, two common chemotherapy drugs that work by damaging DNA.

The dose killed about 40% of the cells within two days. The rest stopped dividing and were still alive a week later, flattened and enormous.

Biologists call this state senescence, and cells in it are often nicknamed zombie cells. They stop dividing but remain alive, secreting a stream of inflammatory proteins.

In a tumor, those signals can attract immune cells that promote new blood vessel growth and help create conditions that support tumor growth.

Martin’s lab studies the machinery that makes cells self-destruct, and the team wanted to know why these cells hadn’t.

The chemotherapy had switched on the cells’ own self-destruct receptors.

Two of them, known as Fas and DR5, rose sharply on the surface of the damaged cells, in every cell type tested and in mouse tumors treated with cisplatin.

Inside the cells, those receptors had assembled the protein complex that normally triggers death. It was fully assembled, and something was holding it back.

One of the restraints turned out to be a family of proteins called inhibitors of apoptosis, or IAPs. The senescent cells were making more of one of them than untreated cells do.

“IAPs act as the antidote to the killing effects of Death Receptors that enable the senescent cells to survive,” Martin told Earth.com.

“However, this now leaves the senescent cells in a state of addiction to the IAPs for their continued survival, which now makes them extremely vulnerable to IAP antagonists.”

Drugs that destroy IAPs already exist, and several have entered clinical trials. The team tested two of them, BV6 and birinapant, which wiped out the IAP proteins inside cells within eight hours.

Given alongside chemotherapy, the drugs killed more cancer cells outright and left far fewer survivors to enter the zombie state.

Given afterward, to cells that had already turned senescent, they killed those cells at doses that did little to normal cells.

Cells engineered to lack the self-destruct receptors, or the enzyme they activate, were largely protected from the drugs, which is how the team knew the receptors were doing the killing.

A widely studied senolytic drug, navitoclax, kills senescent cells by a different route, and it worked just as well without those receptors.

The team also went the other way. Mice bred without caspase-8, the enzyme the receptors activate, built up senescent cells in the lining of the small intestine and showed more inflammatory signaling in the liver.

In cells, deleting the same enzyme let more survivors enter senescence and kept them alive longer.

Old mice told a similar story. In lung, kidney and heart tissue from 24-month-old animals, the two death receptors were higher than in three-month-olds.

There was one living test of the drugs. Mice with an inherited retinal disease, which produces leaky new blood vessels and senescent cells in the retina, got injections of BV6 into the eye.

Their lesions shrank, and the count of senescent cells in the retina fell.

Professor Martin described the strategy as a one-two punch.

The first punch is a standard DNA-damaging drug such as cisplatin, and the second, delivered days later, is a drug that kills the senescent cells the first punch created.

In the paper, the team suggested giving an IAP-blocking drug 5 to 7 days after each round of chemotherapy.

Given ahead of chemotherapy instead, it would push more cells toward death in the first place.

The timing is the hard part, Martin noted. The second punch has to land while the tumor is vulnerable, and he said several trials of IAP-blocking drugs have been run or are under way.

The one-two punch has not been tested against a tumor in an animal in this study.

The chemotherapy-plus-drug experiments were in dishes, and the tumor experiments in mice measured the receptors rather than survival.

The one animal test of the drugs’ zombie-killing power was in a diseased eye, not a cancer.

Whether a human tumor’s survivors depend on IAPs the way these lab cells did is the open question.

Answering it means the trial the team proposes: chemotherapy paired with an IAP-blocking drug, timed to the days when the giant cells appear.

Martin said getting that timing right may decide whether the second punch connects.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6313. Nov. 12, 2014: The Philae lander touches down on a comet

The European Space Agency’s Rosetta mission launched March 2, 2004, on a 4-billion-mile (6.4 billion kilometers) path to Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The mission consisted of the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander, both designed for in-depth study of the comet. The spacecraft arrived at 67P/C-G on Aug. 6, 2014, and began orbiting the body a month later; on Nov. 12, 2014, the Philae lander descended to the comet surface. Both the spacecraft orbiting a comet and the landing on the comet’s surface were firsts in space exploration history.

Unfortunately, there were some complications with the landing: The harpoon system that was designed to hold the lander in place didn’t work, causing Philae to bounce and to float and drift above the surface. When it finally came to rest, it was in a shadowy location now known as Abydos, limiting to the sunlight its solar panels received.

Despite these challenges, Philae was able to operate for three days on battery power, and still sent back photos and data about the composition of the comet’s dust and its analysis of the body’s magnetism. (In short, the comet didn’t have a magnetic field.) Additionally, the orbiter transmitted data about water and oxygen in the tail that led to new understanding of such comets’ makeup.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6312. Anker’s New Power Station Is the Most Efficient I’ve Tested, Capable of Running My Fridge for 2 Days

My capacity test showed the Solix S5000 is nearly 97 percent efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

How long a power station lasts has the most impact on your experience when using one, whether you’re experiencing a blackout or enjoying a weekend off the grid. This year, Anker has upped its game with the S-series stations. Advanced algorithms have improved how its inverters deliver power and extend battery life. Not long ago, I reviewed this technology in the small but powerful S2000 and was impressed. Now, I’ve put the newer and larger S5000 power station through its paces, and it didn’t disappoint.

For context, I also compared the S5000 to Anker's other large power station, the F3800 Plus (now only available as a bundle with other home power accessories), which has been on our list of the best portable power stations. Each model offers both 120- and 240-volt output, but the S5000 has a much larger battery capacity of 5,024 watt-hours (compared with 3,840 watt-hours with the F3800 Plus), and the S5000 is much smaller in size. While it offers less total power output (4,500 watts versus 6,000 watts for the F3800 Plus), I think the S5000 represents an overall improvement for those looking to buy a home backup station that’s more powerful than a typical portable power station.

This is what I cared about the most because better inverter efficiency is the primary feature Anker touts with the S5000. To evaluate its efficiency, I ran two tests. The first was to turn on the AC output and let it run overnight with nothing plugged into it, making sure to deactivate any auto-off features. I did this because, even when idling, most power station batteries lose some stored energy. But after 18 hours, the S5000’s battery capacity was still at 100 percent—that’s impressive. To make a comparison for context, I ran the F3800 alongside it for the same amount of time, and its battery capacity dipped to 81 percent.

For the second test, I plugged a watt meter into the station and plugged a space heater into the meter. I then ran the heater at full power, drawing around 1,500 watts, until it drained the battery fully. Using a resistive load like this (a device that turns energy to heat) can drain a battery pretty quickly, but this also gives you a good read on a power station's performance. It lasted just over three hours, and my meter measured just under 4,900 watt-hours. Compared with its official spec of 5,024 watt-hours of capacity, I determined that this station is around 97 percent efficient. Many stations hover around 89 percent on average, so this was a big win for the S5000.

The technology behind this ability enables the inverter to throttle itself up and down to meet the demands of the devices plugged into it. This is especially significant for lower-powered devices and cyclical appliances with fluctuating power needs, like refrigerators, because the inverter maintains its efficiency, regardless of what’s plugged into it. That means longer run times across the board. This station could easily power my full-size refrigerator for more than 48 hours.

The size of this station in relation to the battery capacity is its second most striking feature. It’s two-thirds smaller than the F3800 but offers 1,184 more watt-hours. At 99 pounds, I wouldn’t call it light, but with two wheels and a telescoping handle, it’s easy enough to roll around, and it’s not too hard to lift in and out of a vehicle. It would be easy to transport this to and from a second home or a job site.

There are a few other enhancements, as well. The 30-amp, 240-volt connection (great for powering an electric dryer or other 240-volt appliance) has its own on/off button, so it won’t create any unwanted drain when all you need is 120-volt AC power. It also accepts both low- and high-powered DC input, which means you get up to 3,000 watts of solar power if you have enough panels to achieve that.

There’s also a port connection for adding up to five expansion batteries, potentially increasing the total battery capacity to as much as 30,000 watt-hours. That same port can be used to connect to Anker’s Solix 5000 Smart Tri-Fuel Generator for direct DC recharging, which is three times faster than standard AC charging. I had this very generator on hand and was able to test this out. I observed around 4,000 watts of input while the generator was running on gasoline. In an emergency where the power has gone out for several days, you could use this method to fully recharge the S5000 in less than two hours.

The only downside is the maximum total output of 4,500 watts. While that’s perfectly fine for very basic home backup and RV use, it’s not going to power a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, let alone a full bank of circuits on a manual transfer switch, no matter how many expansion batteries are attached (they only add capacity, not output). True whole-home backup would require a larger station.

Sometimes, newer power station models are just more of the same, with only minor tweaks to power output, capacity, or outlet configuration. But the Anker S5000’s inverter efficiency technology is a notable upgrade that delivers on its promise of longer runtime than comparable models with the same capacity.

It’s not a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that) and doesn’t have as much output power as the F3800, but it can bring substantial power during an emergency to several appliances or a couple of critical circuits, and it’s much more portable. And if you’re an RV owner looking for a compact yet powerful station, this should definitely be on your list for consideration.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. #6311. The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak

Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M. local time is M33, the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum. This lovely spiral glows at 6th magnitude and is technically visible from a dark site with sharp eyes — just wait until after moonset if you want to give it a try. You’ll find it in far western Triangulum, about 4.3° west-northwest of 3rd-magnitude Alpha (α) Trianguli.

Any telescope will show M33, but larger ones are better because its considerable size — some 70’ across along its longer axis — spreads its light out and makes its surface brightness quite low. Instruments 10 inches or larger will show some detail along the spiral arms, including brighter knots of star formation.

Located some 2.7 million light-years away, M33 is the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and our own Milky Way. This cosmic neighbor is a classic spiral with no central bar and a round, bright nucleus wrapped by its dusty arms. Oriented more closely to face-on than Andromeda, M33 is a popular target for visual observers as well as astrophotographers.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 14Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M. Sunset: 4:44 P.M. Moonrise: 11:33 A.M. Moonset: 8:56 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)

Sunday, November 15Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Sunrise: 6:45 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:05 P.M. Moonset: 9:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (38%)

Monday, November 16It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

Sunrise: 6:46 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:32 P.M. Moonset: 11:00 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (47%)

Tuesday, November 17First Quarter Moon occurs at 6:48 A.M. EST, floating among the stars of Aquarius.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Check out tomorrow’s entry for more detail.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M. Sunset: 4:42 P.M. Moonrise: 12:56 P.M. Moonset: — Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)

Wednesday, November 18The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early this morning after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Sunrise: 6:49 A.M. Sunset: 4:41 P.M. Moonrise: 1:19 P.M. Moonset: 12:03 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)

Thursday, November 19The solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky today to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

Compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

Pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

Sunrise: 6:50 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 1:41 P.M. Moonset: 1:07 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST. We’ll check out the planet in the predawn sky in next week’s column.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

#6310. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

P. Michel et al. The ESA Hera Mission: Detailed characterization of the DART impact outcome and of the binary asteroid (65803) Didymos. 2022. doi: 10.3847/PSJ/ac6f52

#6309. Tourists carved their names in a Spanish cave for 60 years before someone noticed 280 Ice Age drawings hiding on the walls

A Catalan cave open since 1957 holds 280 engravings, 55 of them animals, probably from the Ice Age and found among modern graffiti in 2019.

On Oct. 30, 2019, during the first excavation campaign of a new project, one of the study’s authors, visiting the Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia, noticed what looked like Ice Age engravings among the modern graffiti on a passage wall.

The find was a surprise to the team. The cave had been open since January 1957, and that passage had been part of a tourist route since 1993.

Researchers have now counted 280 motifs there, including 55 animal figures. The authors attribute them to the Ice Age, but no engraving has been dated directly, so that age rests on archaeological context and drawing style.

The cave lies under the village of L’Espluga de Francolí, in the Conca de Barberà district of Tarragona province. It belongs to a limestone system with 11,780 feet (3,590 meters) of mapped galleries, where the Francolí River rises.

Its entrance probably collapsed in Roman times. In 1853 people got in through the Pou del Palletes, a private well in the courtyard of a town house, and members of the Centre Excursionista Pirinenc surveyed the cave in 1956.

The town council cleared the blocked entrance in January 1957, using machinery and no archaeological supervision. Those works destroyed a large part of the deposit at the entrance. A hoard of bronze objects then drew visitors, cavers and treasure hunters.

In 1993 the cave became a museum, and the passage known as the Gatoneres de Cal Palletes joined a tourist circuit called the Adventure Route.

The Coves de l’Espluga website now lists that route as a caving-style visit along the underground river, running from April or May 2027.

For more than six decades, thousands of people walked past the engraved panels, and some cut names and dates over them.

They did so “without the Palaeolithic origin of the figures being recognised,” wrote Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès, of the IPHES-CERCA institute in Tarragona and Rovira i Virgili University.

The engravings sit about 820 feet (250 meters) from the entrance, in an enclosed space next to the underground river. Three narrow passages connect these small galleries to the main gallery.

Ceilings there run from under 3 feet (1 meter) to about 10 feet (3 meters). The galleries average about 6.5 feet (2 meters) across.

Most of the cave’s walls are conglomerate, a lumpy rock generally considered a poor surface for prehistoric art. The engravers worked only on layers of marl, a soft limy mudstone, set between the conglomerate beds.

Any reasonably hard tool could cut a line in that marl. High-resolution 3D models show that most grooves measure 0.1 to 0.3 inches (3 to 7 millimeters) wide and are shallow. About 80 percent of the figures run 6 to 18 inches (150 to 450 millimeters) long.

The same softness left the panels exposed to fingers, modern graffiti and accidental knocks. Every sector except the last stretch of sector 5 shows that damage, and the authors suspect the original total was higher than 280.

Ramon Viñas helped the two authors prospect and record the walls, with logistical support from the cave’s guides and the L’Espluga tourism office. Most of what they logged is not figurative, mainly parallel lines in groups of two, three or four, and sets of 15 to 40 strokes.

Sector 5 has 33 of the 55 animals. The list includes horses, caprines, female deer, bovids and one bear, with its ears drawn from the front and its mouth slightly open.

The authors could not name a species group for 30 percent of the animals, and they list another 15 percent as one of two options, such as caprine or deer. Eyes, nostrils and hooves are mostly missing from the outlines, and a few bellies look pregnant.

A horse in sector 5 has its feet on the boundary between conglomerate and marl. In sector 3, a deer’s muzzle touches a horizontal fissure, and the paper proposes it as ground or water, while saying that intent cannot be demonstrated.

Panel 2 of sector 2 holds hundreds of loop-shaped marks that have no clear parallels at other Paleolithic sites. An inscription dated 1199 sits on top of them, and a piece of charcoal from one groove gave a date no later than the 17th century, so the authors leave their origin open.

Radiocarbon dates from the inner galleries fall into two groups. One spans roughly 41,000 to 26,000 years ago, and the other runs from the eighth to the second century BCE.

Most of the older dates come from charcoal found near the Sala del Llac and downstream, with an apparent gap from 35,400 to 26,300 years ago.

A layer dated to about 26,000 years ago in the Galeria del Pessebre also yielded a flint backed bladelet. None of this charcoal comes from the engravings, so the dates show that people were in the galleries, not when the walls were cut.

The later group belongs to an Iron Age sanctuary in the Sala del Llac, where people left hundreds of ceramic vessels, metal objects, goat or sheep limbs and grain. One vessel held wine residue.

The drawings give a second clue. Hind legs shaped like a double Y and heads made of three lines also turn up at Mediterranean sites of the pre-Magdalenian phases, about 43,000 to 19,000 years ago.

Recent digs at sites such as Cova Foradada have also filled in the early Upper Paleolithic of southern Catalonia, a territory once treated as marginal for that period.

Until this find, only two wall images from the Upper Paleolithic were known in all of Catalonia. A black bovid at Cova del Tendo was stolen shortly after its discovery and survives in photographs and a tracing, while a possible deer at Cova de la Taverna has an uncertain human origin.

About 75 percent of known sites along Iberia’s Mediterranean side hold five animal figures or fewer, and more than 90 percent hold no more than 20. With 55, Font Major ranks third on that coast, behind Ardales and La Pileta in the far south.

The find sent researchers to check other caves, and a survey at Cova Simanya also turned up Paleolithic marks. Elsewhere in Spain, the cave of Cova Dones has yielded at least 120 Latin inscriptions in a single chamber.

The authors concluded that “no cave should be dismissed a priori,” whatever the quality of its walls or the number of its visitors.

At least one animal lies under a calcite crust that could allow uranium-series dating, which the team plans for a later stage.

Similar crusts were used to argue that Neanderthals made paintings in three Spanish caves more than 64,000 years ago, a reading other specialists rejected, and a natural varnish on the horse paintings at Chauvet Cave was recently detected under ultraviolet light.

The authors caution that one date would not fix the age of the whole collection. They also say it is too early to rule out engravings from the Magdalenian or later periods, and a full study of the panels is under way.

More than 62 years passed between the day the town council cleared the entrance and the day a member of the research team stopped at those walls.

The full study was published in the journal Antiquity.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6307. The 7 Best Electric Stoves to Upgrade Your Kitchen

These expert-picked models cook cleaner than gas, and offer features like convection and air fry.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Electric stoves burn cleaner and more efficiently than gas—in fact, per the Department of Energy, they’re about three times more energy-efficient than their gas counterparts. They’re also more straightforward to install—no gas line needed—and often feature flat, easy-to-clean, glass-ceramic cooktops. Plus, their ovens preheat quickly and provide even and consistent heat, which is ideal for anyone who loves to bake. No wonder electric stoves have become the go-to for the majority of households in the U.S.

Electric stoves and ranges come in a wide range of sizes and styles, and many models even have high-tech features such as convection baking, air frying with more room for food than countertop models, and Wi-Fi connectivity. These stoves make a great addition to any kitchen as they’re versatile, reliable, and often quite affordable, too. Plus, some even qualify for a tax rebate.

We rounded up the best of the best, so when you're ready to replace your existing electric stove—or switch from gas—you’ll know just what you need.

Frigidaire makes several lines of well-regarded electric stoves. This 30-inch freestanding model strikes a balance between affordability and modern features like air fry, standard convection, and a user-friendly mix of four stove-top control knobs and an oven touch screen. It’s also available as a slide-in version.

The spacious oven ensures even baking and roasting, with ample room between pans. It also lets you switch between standard baking and convection, making it ideal for those new to convection cooking. The built-in air fry function delivers crisp results without excess oil, and many customers report the fan is surprisingly quiet.

There are a few minor drawbacks: While the storage drawer is roomier than some, it feels quite flimsy. And you’ll need to purchase the air fry tray separately. Still, for the price, it’s hard to beat. For a step up, the brand’s Gallery range has a fifth knob, synchronized burner, and European convection at a slightly higher price point.

Outfit your kitchen on a budget with this freestanding electric range from GE. The no-frills 30-inch model has coil burners and limited features, but it still performs reliably, earning high praise from reviewers.

The stove delivers the power you want and offers decent oven capacity with 5 cubic feet of space. Dual bake elements in the oven provide more-even cooking. There’s also a full-width storage drawer at the bottom. If you just need your electric stove to handle the essentials at a low price point, look no further. It's also available in a white finish.

This LG range is a smart, energy-efficient pick that pairs a two-speed fan with a powerful rear heating element to preheat faster and bake more evenly across multiple racks. A built-in air fry feature can crisp up wings, fries, and veggies with no preheating, and the roomy 6.3-cubic-foot oven can easily accommodate large dishes, including a 20-pound turkey and the sides.

The five-burner cooktop has a 3,200-watt element that take dishes from a rapid boil to a simmer, with flexible 2-in-1 elements to fit everything from a small saucepan to your largest sauté pan. Wi-Fi and the LG ThinQ app let you preheat, adjust, and monitor the oven from your phone, or run it hands-free though Alexa or Google. For instance, you can turn a burner off from the other side of your house. It’s also Energy Star-certified, while cleanup is simple thanks to a 10-minute EasyClean cycle and a coating that helps repel spills and stains.

There is no steam-clean option, and the cooktop lacks a control lockout, so it’s not completely kid-proof. Otherwise, LG’s electric range is a solid smart option that makes cooking (and cleaning) easier.

This GE profile range is a top choice for tech-savvy home cooks looking for a sleek, high-performance stove with cutting-edge features. The slide-in model includes no-preheat air-fry mode and built-in Wi-Fi that lets you control oven functions remotely via the SmartHQ app, compatible with Alexa, Google Assistant, iOS, and Android.

The five-burner cooktop offers versatile heating, and includes a 12-inch/9-inch/6-inch power boil element for rapid heating, plus synchronized burners for large cookware and griddles. Inside, European convection ensures even baking and roasting. The fingerprint-resistant stainless-steel finish keeps it looking pristine outside; a 30-minute steam-clean cycle handles messes inside.

All of these bells and whistles make it a pricier option. And, its glide touch controls, which contribute to the stove’s ultra-modern aesthetic, means that every function is operated via touch—much like swiping on an iPad. If you prefer to use physical knobs, this will not be the best fit.

Built for speed and convenience, this freestanding double oven is a great choice for busy kitchens and home chefs who need flexibility, extra cooking space, and power.

Its five burners include a triple-radiant element that adapts to different cookware sizes while the extra-large European convection double oven—at 6.3 cubic feet, one of the largest in this size—ensures faster, even cooking.

A no-preheat setting lets you cook frozen favorites like pizza and lasagna straight from the freezer, saving time on weeknight meals, and a 50-minute steam-cleaning cycle tackles grime. The only downsides? No Wi-Fi or app support, and surprisingly, no air fry.

While most electric stoves on the market span 30 inches, this sleek freestanding GE model maxes out at just 24 inches across—making it a perfect fit for smaller kitchens. Despite its compact size, it doesn’t skimp on functionality: The front controls are easy to reach, the smooth ceramic glass cooktop wipes clean in seconds, and, thanks to its modular backguard, you can choose to install it with a traditional backguard or flip it down to create a slide-in look.

While there are only four burners, no timer, and a smallish standard (not convection) oven, it’s a stylish, efficient choice for studio apartments, small homes, or anyone cooking for one. It also has a 30-minute steam-clean cycle and a built-in storage drawer that’s deeper than many other stoves on the market. (And if your kitchen can handle a standard-sized stove, GE’s 30-inch free-standing range is a solid, very affordable, choice.)

If you need a stove that’s even more compact than the 24-inch GE, the freestanding 19.5-inch Avanti stove offers serious space efficiency and decent functionality at a very low price. Available in stainless or white, it easily tucks into small kitchens, RVs, and tiny homes. Plus, its retro aesthetic adds a vintage touch.

The four old-school coil burners—three 6-inch and one 8-inch—feature chrome reflector bowls and temperature safety sensors for efficient cooking. While they lack the modern sleekness of a glass cooktop, users report they heat up fast. Inside, the 2.1 cubic feet of oven capacity is roomy enough for one-pan baking and roasting and comes with a broiling pan.

That said, this stove is as basic as it gets. It’s perfect for simple fry-ups and one-pan roasts, but serious home cooks will definitely want more precision and features. If size is your limiting factor, Avanti also makes a more-expensive 19.5-inch glass-top electric stove, which some users say is worth the extra cost, as it provides more even contact with cookware for better heat distribution.

Size can be a significant limiting factor, so measure your stove space first. The standard width for ranges is 30 inches, but if you’re outfitting an apartment kitchen, tiny home, or RV, you’ll want to focus on the few narrower models available.

Next, choose your style: Freestanding stoves have finished sides and back guards, allowing them to stand alone. Slide-in models are designed to sit between cabinets for a seamless look; their stovetops typically sit flush to the back wall, which may require a backsplash update. Drop-in ranges need a custom cabinet base for installation.

Most electric cooktops feature smooth surfaces with heating elements housed beneath tempered glass or ceramic, though traditional coil-style options still exist and tend to be much cheaper. Smooth-top stoves are easier to clean, while coil burners are simpler to replace if one fails.

Standard electric ranges typically come with five burners (four on narrower models). One is often a warming burner, useful for timing multiple dishes. Some models also offer bridge elements—also referred to as "synchronized burners"—which link two burners, handy for griddles or oversized pots. If you frequently boil water, look for one with an express boil burner, designed to heat up faster.

Conventional ovens rely on stationary heating elements—one at the bottom for baking, one at the top for broiling—leading to natural heat rise and possible temperature variations. Standard convection improves on this by adding a fan to circulate hot air for more even cooking. European convection (also called “true” convection) goes a step further, with a third heating element behind the fan for uniform heat distribution across multiple racks.

For everyday cooking, conventional or standard convection works fine. But if you want more precise, even baking and roasting, true convection is worth considering. Be prepared for a slight learning curve if switching to convection, as most recipes are designed for conventional ovens. A good rule of thumb: reduce the temperature by 25°F (e.g., 450°F to 425°F, or 375°F to 350°F), or keep the same temperature but cut the cooking time by about 25 percent. Either way, start checking for doneness earlier than the recipe suggests. A meat thermometer can also help ensure accuracy.

Control panel placement affects both aesthetics and functionality. Backguard controls, found on most freestanding stoves, keep buttons and knobs safely out of reach of children but may be less visually streamlined. Front-control stoves, common in slide-in models, offer a sleek, built-in look and easier access to settings but can be a hazard if you have small kids or frequently lean against the stove while cooking. Many models now include touchscreen controls, which allow for precise adjustments and smart features but may require more care to keep clean.

Many newer electric stoves come with high-tech features designed to make cooking more efficient and hands-free. Wi-Fi-enabled models let you monitor and control your oven remotely via an app—preheating, adjusting temperatures, and setting timers from anywhere. Some even integrate with voice assistants like Alexa or Google Assistant for hands-free commands.

Touchscreen controls and digital displays offer a sleek, modern look, but keep in mind that they can be more finicky than traditional knobs, especially when wet or smudged. If you prefer a more tactile experience, look for models with physical dials or a hybrid control panel.

Some ovens now include built-in air fry functions, which circulate superheated air for crispy, fried-like results without the oil. It’s a great feature for quickly roasting veggies, crisping up frozen snacks, or making healthier versions of fried favorites—no extra countertop appliance needed.

Beyond the sticker price, you’ll want to factor in some extra costs. For one, power cords aren’t usually included in the price, and you can’t reuse your old one. Lowe’s, for example, charges $39.98 to install—which includes a new power cord. Some retailers also charge a separate delivery fee. And, if you’re replacing an existing stove, you should expect to pay around $50 to have your old one hauled away and disposed of. Finally, while most stoves come with a one-year limited warranty (which typically covers manufacturing defects and basic repairs), some retailers offer extended protection plans (for an additional fee) at checkout.

When the glass top of my ancient JennAir electric stove cracked—thanks to a DIY mishap (we stood on it to paint a high part of the kitchen; lesson learned)—I had to find an unplanned replacement. Fortunately, the stovetop still worked, giving me time to explore my options. I visited my local Lowe’s and other reputable retailers to assess everything in person and quickly noticed a difference in selection. Suburban stores only carried standard 30-inch ranges, while city retailers stocked a wider variety, including smaller 24-inch models—something to keep in mind if you’re shopping for a compact space.

I assessed everything: control placement (knobs vs. touchscreen and ease of use), oven heating methods, aesthetics, and extra features like voice control (we’re a household that regularly asks Alexa for help in the kitchen). The models I selected come from trusted brands like GE, Samsung, and Frigidaire, with thousands of positive reviews attesting to their reliability and efficiency. Many are top-sellers across multiple retailers, and some incorporate the latest technology to make cooking faster and more enjoyable. I also chose options across various sizes and price points to fit different spaces and budgets—and included a few solid upgrade picks from the same brands for a slight price increase.

Arabella can often be found immersed in DIY projects at her mid-century modern house in upstate New York—a hands-on pursuit that inspires many trips to Lowe’s.

#6304. The Sky Today on Friday, November 13: Spot Mirach’s Ghost

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6302. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#6300. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.
