#6264. 12 Airline Booking Traps That Could Cost You Money in 2026

Airline websites are not necessarily badly designed, even though they often feel that way. In many cases, the booking process is doing exactly what it was designed to do: get you focused on the lowest advertised fare before revealing the cost of everything else.

You start with a flight that looks like it costs $400. By the time you add a carry-on bag, choose a seat, and work through the final checkout screens, the total is suddenly $650.

After more than 18 years of travel to over 130 countries, we still catch ourselves slowing down to double-check airline bookings. The difference now is that we know where the expensive mistakes are usually hiding. We also use flight-search and tracking tools to compare routes and monitor changes. See our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

The lowest price on the first screen is rarely enough information to tell you which flight is actually cheapest. You need to compare the complete journey, including baggage, seats, fare restrictions, connections, operating airlines, and the risk involved if something goes wrong.

To avoid costly airline booking mistakes, compare the total price of the journey rather than the advertised base fare. Check the conditions of the exact fare, baggage allowances, operating airline, cabin on every segment, connection times, and whether the flights are issued on one protected ticket.Before paying, compare the flight as a round trip, two one-way tickets, and a multi-city itinerary. Before leaving home, verify your passport, visas or travel authorizations, transit requirements, check-in deadline, and gate-closing time.

These airline booking traps—also common flight-booking mistakes—can turn an apparently cheap ticket into the most expensive option.

One of the first mistakes travellers make is comparing flights by airline logo.

You see the airline you normally use, remember the points sitting in your account, and stop comparing. But loyalty should not convince you to pay hundreds of dollars more for a worse schedule, a more restrictive ticket, or a fare that excludes everything you need.

Airline points can still be valuable, especially when you are close to earning useful status or have benefits such as complimentary baggage. But loyalty should be one part of the calculation, not the starting point.

The days of automatically paying more because “this is our airline” are over. Loyalty should follow value, not the other way around.

Basic Economy can be a perfectly reasonable fare. The trap is buying it without understanding what has been removed.

It may work well when you are taking a short flight, travelling with only a small personal item, do not care where you sit, and are confident your plans will not change.

The problem is that airline websites normally display the lowest available fare first. Once you are in booking mode, it is easy to select that number and move forward without reading the restrictions.

You may save $40 on the ticket and then spend $85 adding the carry-on bag you needed from the beginning.

Before booking Basic Economy, price the next fare category. A Standard Economy ticket may cost more initially but include a carry-on bag, checked luggage, seat selection, or greater flexibility.

Also consider whether seat selection genuinely matters. Travellers with children, mobility considerations, medical needs, or a strong need for an aisle or window seat should include that cost when comparing fares.

Do not buy the lowest number. Buy the fare that includes what you actually need.

Airlines do not necessarily sell every Economy Class seat at the same price. Seats are divided into fare classes or pricing tiers, often called fare buckets.

When the cheapest tier sells out, the price can jump even when the aircraft still has many empty seats.

That is one reason a flight might appear at $480 in the morning and $620 later that day. It does not always mean the plane suddenly filled up. It may mean the least expensive fare class is no longer available.

When you see a noticeable price increase, do not assume you must either pay it immediately or lose the trip.

A competitor may now be cheaper. In other cases, the next fare level may include baggage, seat selection, or flexibility that makes it better value than the stripped-down ticket you were originally considering. A fare jump is a signal to widen the search, not automatically accept the new price.

For the tools we use to compare dates, airports, and fare changes, see our guide to the best travel apps for finding flights.

The standard airline search box encourages travellers to enter a departure city, destination, outbound date, and return date.

That does not mean a traditional round trip is always the cheapest or most efficient way to book.

Before purchasing an expensive international itinerary, compare it three ways:

An open-jaw ticket means flying into one city and returning home from another.

For example, if you are travelling through Europe, you might fly into Paris and return from Rome. Even if the airfare is similar to a return ticket from Paris, you could avoid paying for a train or flight back to your starting point. You may also save a hotel night and an entire day of backtracking.

Different airlines can also be used in each direction. One carrier may offer the best outbound flight, while another has a much better return schedule.

When comparing separate tickets, check baggage fees, fare restrictions, connection risks, and cancellation policies. The goal is not to find the cleverest itinerary. It is to determine which option gives you the best total trip.

With a codeshare flight, the airline selling the ticket may not be the airline flying the plane.

You might purchase the journey through one airline’s website and then arrive at the airport to discover that a partner carrier operates the flight.

Before buying, look for the words “operated by” in the flight details.

Then check the itinerary on both airline websites. Confirm the aircraft, seat map, baggage allowance, terminal, and check-in instructions.

After booking, make sure you have the operating carrier’s reservation number. The confirmation number issued by the airline selling the ticket may not work on the partner airline’s website.

Codeshares are not automatically bad. They can provide more destinations and useful connections. The problem is that they create a handoff between companies, and that handoff can become confusing when you need assistance.

As we have learned, one of the most expensive sentences in travel can be: “You need to contact the other airline.”

Mixed-cabin fares are one of the easiest airline traps to miss.

The search result may display a large Premium Economy or Business Class label, making it appear that the entire journey is in the upgraded cabin.

Then you expand the flight details and discover that the 40-minute connection is in Premium Economy while the eight-hour overnight flight is in regular Economy.

We have come close to booking this type of itinerary several times.

Before paying, check the cabin listed beside every individual segment. Make sure the premium seat is on the flight where you will actually benefit from it.

Do not assume one premium segment provides premium benefits throughout the trip.

Screenshot the cabin shown for each flight and confirm that it appears correctly in the final reservation. A mixed-cabin fare is only a deal when the upgraded cabin is on the part of the journey that matters.

There is rarely one simple baggage policy that applies to every passenger flying with an airline.

Do not check only the airline’s general baggage page. Open the conditions attached to the specific fare and route you are considering.

This is especially important when connecting from a transatlantic flight to a smaller airline or low-cost carrier within Europe. A bag accepted on the first flight may be too large, too heavy, or not included on the next one.

A bag fitting inside the overhead compartment does not automatically mean it meets the airline’s rules. Wheels, handles, and outside pockets are normally included when the bag is measured.

Price your luggage before buying the flight. A ticket that appears $30 cheaper can quickly become more expensive once the necessary baggage is added.

Paying for bags online in advance is also frequently less expensive than waiting until the airport, although the difference varies by airline.

Finally, weigh your suitcase at home using a real scale. Picking it up and declaring that it “feels about 20 kilos” is not a reliable baggage strategy.

Once you know your allowance, follow our two-minute checked-bag routine before handing your suitcase over at the airport.

A self-transfer may be the most expensive mistake in this guide.

Some search and booking sites combine two separate tickets and display them as one journey. Look for warnings such as:

The critical detail is that the airlines may not recognize the flights as one protected itinerary.

If the first flight is delayed and you miss the second one, the second airline may consider you a no-show. You could lose the remaining flights on that reservation and be forced to purchase a new last-minute ticket.

The first airline may not be responsible for helping because it transported you to the destination shown on its ticket.

Leaving the international transit area can also trigger entry or transit requirements that would not apply during a normal airside connection.

Self-transfers can work when you have a long buffer, carry-on luggage, an airport you understand, and enough flexibility to absorb a disruption.

We would not use one when connecting to a cruise, wedding, organized tour, or once-daily long-haul flight.

Always compare the self-transfer price with a protected itinerary. The higher fare may not simply be buying convenience. It may be buying the airline’s responsibility to get you to your final destination.

Airlines can sell a connection that technically meets the airport’s minimum requirements.

That does not necessarily mean it is comfortable, sensible, or suitable for you.

A 45-minute connection at a large international airport might involve:

If a connection makes you nervous while sitting at home, it will not feel better when you are waiting for the aircraft door to open. Choose connection time based on the consequences of missing the next flight.

A long layover can be inconvenient. A missed connection can cost a full day or derail the entire trip.

We use third-party flight sites for research. They are useful for comparing airlines, dates, and routing options.

Buying through one is a separate decision.

A third-party fare may be genuinely cheaper, but make sure you are comparing the same product. It could involve:

The biggest issue normally appears when the schedule changes or the flight is cancelled.

The airline may tell you to contact the company that issued the ticket. The booking company may then tell you that only the airline can resolve the flight.

Before buying, find the itinerary through the search site and compare it directly with the airline. When the price difference is small, booking with the airline may be worth it for easier communication during disruptions.

Also check the payment currency. Some booking sites offer to convert the total into your home currency. This feels convenient but may include a less favourable exchange rate.

When your credit card does not charge a foreign transaction fee, paying in the original currency may be less expensive. Compare the final converted amount and check your card’s fees rather than choosing a currency based on familiarity.

Some of the most expensive travel problems do not happen during booking. They happen at the airport after your hotel, tour, rental car, or cruise has already been paid for.

A valid passport may not be enough to enter your destination or transit through a connecting country.

Depending on your nationality, route, and destination, you may need:

A passport can be valid on your departure date and still fail to meet the destination’s entry requirements. Complicated connections are also a good reason to review our international travel safety tips before departure.

Names matter too. The name on your airline ticket should match your passport and any visa or travel authorization. Do not assume that a nickname or commonly used name will be accepted.

Before an international trip, take five minutes to verify:

Canadian travellers should verify current destination-specific requirements using official government travel advisories and the relevant embassy or immigration authority, since entry and transit rules can change.

Five minutes at home can save the entire trip at the airport. For our complete pre-departure routine, read our travel safety checklist for 2026.

Departure time is when the aircraft is scheduled to leave. It is not the time you should arrive at the gate.

Boarding begins earlier, and the gate closes before departure. The exact cutoff depends on the airport, airline, route, and destination.

Once the gate is closed, seeing the aircraft through the terminal window will not save your seat.

If you miss the flight, the cost may extend far beyond a replacement ticket. You might also lose:

Build your airport schedule backward from the airline’s check-in, baggage-drop, boarding, and gate-closing deadlines.

Check current security conditions using the airport’s official app or website, but do not treat an estimated wait time as a guarantee. Add time for airport parking, shuttle transportation, baggage drop, security, passport control, terminal changes, and finding the gate.

It is better to have extra time near the gate than to spend the start of your trip running through an airport while your name is being called over the loudspeaker. Arriving early does not help much if your carry-on slows you down at screening. Read our airport security tips and common mistakes before packing.

Before confirming a flight, we recommend checking the entire itinerary one final time.

The best defence against airline booking traps is not a secret search setting or complicated flight hack. It is slowing down long enough to compare the complete journey.

All 12 of these traps work best when travellers are rushing.

We see a low fare, get excited about the trip, and want to finish before the number changes. The booking process then reveals the bags, seats, restrictions, connections, and other costs after we have already become emotionally committed to the flight.

The cheapest flight is not necessarily the one with the lowest number on the first screen. It is the flight that gets you to your destination without surprise charges, unrealistic connections, or an expensive problem at the airport.

After more than 18 years of travelling, experience has not made us immune to booking mistakes. It has simply taught us when to stop, reopen the details, and check everything one more time.

Take five minutes before pressing confirm. Those five minutes could save hundreds of dollars—or save the entire trip.

#6263. When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds

You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind. On a first visit, you want time to take in the massive scale of the Inca city on its forested ridge above the Urubamba River, and then to walk among its stone walls. That picture, of course, depends on the weather. Here, where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, a single bank of cloud can hide Waynapicchu, the peak behind the ruins, and with it the panorama you came to see.

The drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours. The weeks just after the rains offer greener slopes—and often thinner crowds—to anyone prepared to pack for showers. The best time to visit Machu Picchu comes down to matching the conditions to the type of visit you want, as well as confirming that your route is available before you commit to booking trains and rooms. Below are the questions that first-time visitors ask most, with advice from travel advisors and experts.

For a first visit, May and September—before and after the June-to-August rush, respectively—will have generally favorable walking weather, before the rains creep back in October. The two months aren’t interchangeable, especially if you hope to walk to the Sun Gate or the Inca Bridge. The 2026 route calendar opened those seasonal paths in September but not in May, so check the 2027 dates as soon as they’re published.

April brings greener slopes to anyone who can live with a little more water. “It’s also shoulder season so there aren’t many tourists yet,” says Alice Farkas, who leads marketing and communications at Aracari, a company based in Lima that plans private trips across South America. Kiernan Cochran, product manager at Andean, which plans trips throughout Peru, also favors April into early May. Even so, Cochran’s team books those weeks for travelers with much the same lead time as high season, since popular routes fill early.

When it comes to visiting Machu Picchu, daily timing might matter even more than which time of year you visit.

November through March offers significant savings on airfare and accommodations, though strategic planning remains essential. Permits for popular routes like Huayna Picchu still require three-month advance booking during these months (compared to six months of required lead time during peak season).

Mosquera makes a case for embracing the rainy season: "It's actually my favorite time. The site becomes magical with fewer crowds given that overtourism is one of Machu Picchu's greatest threats. The rain isn't nearly as disruptive as people imagine, as it mainly falls in the evenings, not all day. February is particularly special because the Inca Trail closes for maintenance, making the site even quieter." (Note: If you plan to arrive by trek, options will be more limited during these moments.)

The wet season transforms the landscape dramatically. Stone terraces flush vibrant green, hidden waterfalls emerge, and morning mist creates atmospheric reveals of the citadel. The timing also aligns perfectly with Peru's coastal summer. "More travelers are discovering this split-season strategy," says Mosquera. "You can explore misty ruins early in the trip, then travel down to Lima's world-class restaurants or Máncora's beaches where summer's in full swing." Temperatures at Machu Picchu remain moderate year-round, with rain typically following predictable afternoon patterns rather than all-day downpours.

The dry months from June through August draw the main crush of tourists, when the most desirable entry hours can sell out along with hotels and trains. Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun, culminates in Cusco on June 24, and Peru’s Independence Day on July 28 brings another surge. In 2026, the daily cap was 4,500 visitors on ordinary dates and 5,600 on specified days, including June 19 through November 2, though that calendar doesn’t automatically carry over to 2027. Those places are also divided by route and hour, so your preferred route and entry time may be full even when the site has space overall.

Once each year’s tickets are released, Andean suggests booking sought-after routes about six months ahead in high season and at least three months ahead in low season.

Allow four or five nights in the region, as Cochran recommends, and begin in the Sacred Valley if your itinerary allows. Its Inca towns and terraces also mean the citadel isn’t your first encounter with the culture that built it. Cusco, where flights land for now, sits at roughly 11,150 feet. Heading straight down to the valley gives you a gentler start, and you can return to explore the city afterward. Cusco’s long-delayed replacement airport, Chinchero International, is under construction on the plateau above the Sacred Valley at about 12,340 feet, higher than the city itself. Its opening is targeted for late 2027, so most 2027 trips will still begin at the old one.

Ollantaytambo, at about 9,160 feet, is halfway between Cusco and Machu Picchu, and where travelers board the train to the latter. The town of ‘Ollanta’ has Inca-era streets and archaeological sites to explore, and is well worth a stop either going to or coming from Machu Picchu (the lovely El Albergue hotel sits just beside the train station).

From there, travelers catch the train to Aguas Calientes, also known as Machu Picchu Pueblo, which is the small town at the base of the ancient citadel. Spend the night prior to your Machu Picchu visit in Aguas Calientes for an early start up the mountain. Some allow just one day at Machu Picchu; others who want to appreciate the landmark from a few perspectives should budget two. You may, for instance, want to experience an upper terrace or a mountain climb alongside Classic Circuit 2, which is the standard walk through the Inca city (more on these routes below). If so, book that second route for another day. Either way, you can usually spend a full day at Machu Picchu and still catch a late afternoon/early evening train out, or bed down for another night in Aguas Calientes and depart the next morning.

Before buying anything sold simply as “Machu Picchu admission,” take a look at the official route maps, since the three circuits divide the site by elevation and access. For a single visit, Andean favors Classic Circuit 2. Its routes 2-A and 2-B each pair a viewpoint with a walk among the Inca buildings of the urban sector. Route 2-B takes its view from the lower terrace, a distinction worth knowing if you have a particular camera angle in mind.

For the upper-terrace panorama, choose Circuit 1’s route 1-B, which keeps you above the main streets, while route 1-A adds the climb up Machu Picchu Mountain which offers the classic view down onto the site. The Sun Gate and Inca Bridge carry seasonal tickets of their own. Circuit 3 covers the lower royal sector, including the Temple of the Sun. Its route 3-A adds the steep ascent of Waynapicchu (often spelled Huayna Picchu), which is the distinctive peak in the background of most Machu Picchu photos, and 3-B stays below. If Circuit 2 sells out, Andean suggests booking Circuits 1 and 3 separately to combine the panorama with a closer look at the ruins. Choose wisely before you arrive, since a ticket cannot be switched to another route at the gate.

Hikers face their own paperwork. Permits for the classic Inca Trail are limited and booked through authorized operators, and the shorter one-day trail from kilometer 104 of the rail line needs a permit and an operator, too. That day hike is Cochran’s own favorite—the final leg of the historic Inca route to the Sun Gate, without the multiday inn-to-inn or camping journey required. Ask what your hike covers before buying a separate admission.

Under the September 2026 rules, trail arrivals enter on a designated Circuit 3-B ticket, which matters if you also want Circuit 2 or the upper panorama. Heavy rain can also shut the kilometer 104 path outside the usual February maintenance period, which is something to keep in mind for any rainy season travel.

Your train booking does not include admission (treks are on a case-by-case basis; ask!), so buy entry through the Ministry of Culture’s Tu Boleto portal, where you choose your route first and your entry hour second. Enter each visitor’s details carefully, matching names and information to the same identification document they’ll present at the gate. The ticket fixes the holder’s name, date, time, and route; current rules allow no changes to the name or date after purchase.

The purchase process changed in September 2026, when the ministry began a 30-day trial of direct paid checkout in place of the earlier unpaid hold. Under the portal’s current purchase manual, you have 15 minutes from the start of an order to enter everyone’s details and pay. Have documents and payment ready, and follow the instructions on screen. Rail and admission are also released on separate timelines. PeruRail opened 2027 train sales on September 22, but Yuriko Aquino of PROMPERÚ, Peru’s tourism promotion agency, says the Ministry of Culture has yet to announce when 2027 admission will go on sale or what the daily visitor cap will be. If you buy rail first, read the fare’s change terms before you pay.

Within the overall cap, up to 1,000 tickets a day are held for in-person sale in Machu Picchu Pueblo, valid for entry the following day. If you’re counting on that uncertain fallback, budget a night in town. Whichever way you buy, a guide is recommended for a standard citadel visit, while Inca Trail hikers follow their operator’s separate requirements. Guides can be booked through your hotel or at the entrance to the site.

From Cusco, most travelers cross the Sacred Valley by road to Ollantaytambo and board the train there for the ride along the Urubamba to Machu Picchu Pueblo. From town, a separate shuttle bus climbs to the entrance in roughly half an hour. Check boarding points and total travel time before choosing a fare, since PeruRail’s January-to-April departures from Cusco involve a bus-and-train transfer.

For a first visit, Cochran favors a morning train from the Sacred Valley and an afternoon Circuit 2 entry, when her team generally finds the site less crowded; three or four hours is usually enough to take it in. Among the premium trains, she points to Belmond’s Hiram Bingham, PeruRail’s Vistadome Observatory, and IncaRail’s First Class.

Whichever train you choose, leave a cushion between arrival and admission. Peru’s tourism authority advises reaching the shuttle station about an hour before your gate slot, or setting out about two hours ahead if you plan to walk uphill. A train that pulls in just before your entry time leaves little margin for the bus queue and the gate check.

Down in Machu Picchu Pueblo are two fantastic Peruvian-owned options—Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel, with scattered adobe casitas among orchids, and Sumaq Machu Picchu Hotel, which faces the Urubamba River. Both are close to the shuttle stop. Sanctuary Lodge, a Belmond Hotel, is the only property up on the mountain at the gates of Machu Picchu, which spares you the morning shuttle ascent, though hotel guests still enter on the same timed admission as everyone else.

If you typically fly with American Airlines and its partner airlines, earning elite status in the AAdvantage program can unlock many perks, from complimentary upgrades to priority boarding.

In 2022, American AAdvantage revamped the method for earning elite status to a system based on Loyalty Points.

Nowadays, members earn Loyalty Points through eligible flights, credit card spending and purchases with participating partners.

Here’s what you need to know about American Airlines elite status, including how to earn it and what benefits it brings.

American Airlines elite status gives perks to AAdvantage members who interact with the program and its partners. The program lets you earn Loyalty Points toward elite status through many activities unrelated to travel, including shopping, dining and spending on cobranded American Airlines credit cards.

You can earn each American Airlines elite status tier by accumulating a set amount of Loyalty Points during the elite-qualification year that runs for 12 months from March 1 through the end of February. Once you reach the threshold, your status takes effect immediately and remains valid through March 31 of the following full year.

Note: Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles are not the same thing (but more on that below).

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning American AAdvantage elite status

You’ll find four published tiers of American Airlines elite status that you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points during the 12 months starting each March 1:

In addition to these tiers, there’s also the exclusive, invite-only Concierge Key status. However, American AAdvantage doesn’t publish any specific requirements for this status.

You’ll also earn Loyalty Point Rewards as you reach specific Loyalty Point thresholds, including some that fall between elite status tiers. You’ll earn your first Loyalty Point Rewards choice after earning 15,000 Loyalty Points within the 12-month qualification period beginning March 1.

Related: Your guide to American Airlines Million Miler status

To qualify for American Airlines elite status, you must earn the required number of Loyalty Points during each 12-month qualification period following March 1. As discussed, you’ll need to earn 40,000 Loyalty Points for Gold status, 75,000 for Platinum, 125,000 for Platinum Pro and 200,000 for Executive Platinum each qualification period.

We have a full guide to earning Loyalty Points. But, in short, you'll earn two types of American Airlines miles: base and bonus. And while both base and bonus miles are redeemable, generally only base miles earn Loyalty Points. The exception is the elite status bonus on flights, which also counts (more on that below). So, each time you earn a base mile with AAdvantage, you'll also earn a Loyalty Point.

You can earn American AAdvantage base miles through many different activities. Here’s a noncomprehensive list of some ways you can earn base miles (and hence Loyalty Points):

There are many other ways to earn American Airlines miles. However, check whether you’re earning base or bonus miles before you get too excited about how many Loyalty Points you’ll earn. Bask Bank mileage accounts are one example of an activity earning only bonus miles — hence, no Loyalty Points. Basic Economy fares on American don't earn Loyalty Points either.

Note: American and Hyatt ended their enhanced loyalty partnership in 2026, so World of Hyatt status is no longer offered as a Loyalty Point Reward. You can still earn 500 AAdvantage miles per eligible Hyatt stay by giving your AAdvantage number at check-in.

Related: Be careful: 9 times you won’t earn American Airlines Loyalty Points, even if you earn miles

American Airlines elite status comes with some valuable benefits. Here’s a look at some of the most noteworthy benefits, including how they differ by status tier.

American Airlines elite members receive complimentary upgrades on eligible flights to select destinations within North America, the Caribbean and Central America, subject to availability. Depending on the aircraft, these upgrades can move members from Main Cabin to premium economy, from Premium Economy to business or domestic first class, or directly from Main Cabin to business or domestic first class (on aircraft without a Premium Economy cabin).

These upgrades are automatically requested and are available on paid tickets and award tickets. Members can also receive a complimentary upgrade for one companion traveling on the same flight. However, Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, aren't eligible for complimentary upgrades.

American will start processing these upgrades at different times depending on your American Airlines elite status tier. Executive Platinum members may have their upgrades confirmed as early as 100 hours before departure, Platinum Pro members as early as 72 hours, Platinum members as early as 48 hours and Gold members as early as 24 hours.

American Airlines prioritizes upgrades — including complimentary upgrades, mileage award upgrades and systemwide upgrades — in the following order:

Members with American Airlines elite status — and up to eight passengers traveling with you on the same reservation — can select Preferred seats without any extra fees during booking or anytime after booking (based on availability). Preferred seats have standard legroom but are located in more desirable locations throughout the economy cabin. This benefit does not apply to Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026.

Main Cabin Extra seats, which offer additional legroom, are also complimentary for AAdvantage elite members and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation (based on availability). Executive Platinum, Platinum Pro and Platinum members can select these seats at booking, while Gold members must wait until within 24 hours of departure. Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, are not eligible for complimentary Main Cabin Extra seats.

American Airlines elite members get a mileage bonus as follows when flying on eligible flights:

The status bonus is added to the base miles earned on eligible flights, and unlike most bonus miles, it counts toward Loyalty Points as well. For example, on flights marketed by American, a member without status earns 5 miles and Loyalty Points per dollar, while an Executive Platinum member earns 11. That makes it easier for higher-tier members to requalify through flying.

AAdvantage elite members enjoy priority access at check-in, security and boarding on eligible American Airlines flights. Specifically, Executive Platinum members board in Group 1, Platinum Pro in Group 2, Platinum in Group 3 and Gold in Group 4. Boarding with any of these groups might mean there’s still space in the overhead bin for your carry-on suitcase.

AAdvantage status members also get priority when standing by for a different American Airlines flight on the same day of travel (and can standby for a later flight the same day) on eligible flights within the U.S. and between the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Executive Platinum and Platinum Pro members — and up to eight companions traveling with them on the same reservation — can enjoy complimentary same-day confirmed flight changes on American when flying to or from the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

AAdvantage elite members also enjoy complimentary checked bags when flying American Airlines: Gold members get their first checked bag free, Platinum members get their first two checked bags free, and Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum members get their first three checked bags free. Best of all, this checked baggage allowance is also offered to guests traveling with the status member on the same reservation.

American Airlines elite status offers a variety of other perks, including the following:

Finally, American Airlines offers additional rewards at specific Loyalty Point milestones. Though these rewards are separate from AAdvantage elite status, you’ll inherently unlock them as you accumulate Loyalty Points toward the program's elite status tiers.

Here’s a look at the Loyalty Point Rewards you could choose as you progress toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required for Executive Platinum status:

Related: Why (and how) I'm earning AAdvantage Platinum Pro elite status and not going for AAdvantage Executive Platinum

Having a cobranded American Airlines credit card is extremely helpful if you want to earn American Airlines elite status. Although the sign-up and category bonuses provide bonus miles — which won’t give you Loyalty Points — you’ll earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent with all U.S.-issued AAdvantage credit cards. This means you can boost your Loyalty Point balance as you use your card for purchases and even qualify for American elite status from credit card spending alone.

If you value Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is an excellent choice. Meanwhile, existing cardholders who had the AAdvantage® Aviator® World Elite Silver Mastercard® and were transitioned to the (see rates and fees) can still earn up to 15,000 additional Loyalty Points by meeting specific spending thresholds during the qualification year ending Feb. 28, 2027. Unfortunately, this benefit is not available to new Globe card applicants.

The information for the Aviator Silver card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

American Airlines elite status is worth it for some travelers. I've held Platinum Pro or Executive Platinum status since 2016 because I value the domestic upgrades, waived checked bag fees, Priority check-in lines and Oneworld Emerald status these tiers provide.

But, after reconsidering what I value in American Airlines elite status, I've only strived to qualify for Platinum Pro in recent years. In short, I decided the incremental value of Executive Platinum over Platinum Pro didn’t justify the extra costs I’d incur to earn the higher status.

It’s important to consider how much you’ll use your AAdvantage perks and the cost of earning American Airlines status. If you’ll organically earn American Airlines status through flights, then it’s likely worth earning. But if you’ll have to earn a significant number of Loyalty Points through other means, such as using the AAdvantage eShopping portal or spending on an AAdvantage credit card, there’s an opportunity cost to doing so.

Finally, if you’ll only use your American Airlines elite status perks occasionally or only need a specific perk, consider whether you can get what you seek through booking premium-cabin fares or applying for a credit card that offers that particular benefit.

Related: Which credit card should you use for American Airlines flights?

American Airlines offers four elite status tiers you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points: Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum. These tiers offer perks including Preferred seats, complimentary space-available upgrades on eligible American Airlines flights, and Oneworld perks on select partner airlines.

#6260. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

#6259. These Music City Airbnbs Exude All of Nashville’s Southern Charm

In the two decades I’ve lived in Nashville, I’ve seen a lot of changes. When I first moved, my friends and family would ask why I lived here; now, they’re asking when they can come visit. And as the Music City grows, so does the number of gorgeous places to stay. Travelers can choose from vacation rentals in any neighborhood for any group size, whether that be large bachelorette parties looking to hang out near the honky-tonks, or solo music lovers who want to catch a show at the Grand Ole Opry. Houses with vast yards are good options for folks with kids, dogs, and songwriter friends who want to pull out the guitar, and some even boast private pools that let you keep the summer heat at bay. Nashville, of course, is known for its street of honky-tonks, and securing a modern condo downtown with a bird’s-eye view of all the action offers a one-of-a-kind experience that you won’t soon forget. No matter what type of stay you’re after, there’s an excellent Nashville vacation rental worth holing up in. Read on for some of my favorite vacation rentals in the city I call home.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, editor stays, ratings, amenities, location, decor, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Cozy fireplace, roomy layout, spacious yard, large dining table

Comfortable and quiet, this family-ready home in South Nashville will make you feel like a true local. With four bedrooms—three kings and a room with bunk beds for kids—all dressed in modern, neutral tones; two baths; and a dog-friendly policy, the whole family will enjoy a stay here. There’s even a dedicated workspace if you have to check in with the office while on the road. It’s an oasis slightly away from all the noise and activity that downtown brings, but just a short drive from any late-night action you desire.

Location: South NashvilleThings to do nearby: Geodis Park (the MLS stadium); the Nashville Fairgrounds; Adventure Science Center; Zanies’ comedy club; bars, restaurants, and shopping in Wedgewood-Houston

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Shou Sugi Ban traditional Japanese design, peaceful location, firepit

Just 16 miles away from downtown Nashville, this bed-and-breakfast tree house on 22 wooded acres can feel worlds away from Lower Broadway and the neon honky-tonk nightlife. But in half an hour, you could be back in the center of the action, should you want to be. It’s the perfect spot for those who like to balance their big-city trips with a bit of solitude and relaxation after a long day. At home, expect great views, a delicious breakfast, and the chance to truly disconnect—there’s no Wi-Fi or TV.

Location: Ashland CityThings to do nearby: Hiking trails on property, Beaman Park, Cumberland River kayaking

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Photogenic pink backdrop, free parking, wood-fired pizza oven, outdoor projector, guitar, local landlords

East Nashville’s self-named “Nashville Pinky” is bedecked in a paler pink than some other properties in the city, but it doesn’t scale back when it comes to making Music City fun. Spend the day at home watching movies on the outdoor projector and eating pizza from the wood-fired oven. There’s also a guitar if you want to pick your way through some songs, and vinyl records from the nearby record shop, The Groove. When you’re ready to head out, the neighborhood is full of bars, boutiques, and restaurants, and you’re a quick bus ride, bike ride, or Uber from Lower Broadway.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Five Points bars and restaurants, Shoppes on Fatherland, the Basement East music venue, Shelby Park

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private parking, stock tank tub, electric fireplace, cozy loft space

Finding a pet-friendly Airbnb isn't as easy as it seems, as many homes come with extensive rules regarding what Fido can and can't do, and high nightly fees in addition to the booking price. This two-bedroom guesthouse sits in a middle ground: There's a $75 fee per small or medium dog, who will have to hang out in a crate if you leave them home alone. There's a small backyard for your pup to explore (with a firepit for humans), and the neighborhood has wide sidewalks for safe, on-leash adventures. The tchotchke-filled home itself is best for families, since the primary bedroom lacks a true door, and the secondary bedroom has twin beds. Inside, there's also a kitchenette with an oven, mini-fridge, and coffee maker, and an indoor fireplace to curl up in front of.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Salt Ranch pool club, Cleveland Park shopping, bars and restaurants, Drkmttr music venue

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Relaxing atmosphere, private connected apartment for more space, big deck, private parking

The unofficial bachelorette capital of the world, Nashville is a hot spot for group trips—especially for women. And while the rowdier set may be found on Broadway driving past the honky-tonks in “party barges,” there's a more, well, sophisticated way to celebrate upcoming nuptials. To start, book this 1930s East Nashville cottage that's away from the crowds and has an explicit “no parties” rule. With two bedrooms in the main house plus a third in the connected apartment, and two queen-size sofa beds, there's plenty of room to spread out. Outside, the home has a backyard, two-level deck, grill, and firepit. Plus, you're only 10 minutes from downtown if you want to get in on the honky-tonk action.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Cumberland River kayaking; Shelby Park; Five Points restaurants, bars, and shopping; The Basement East music venue

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Chocolate-themed decor, location in a multi-use complex with a coffee shop and a chocolatier, blackout shades

You’ll definitely have sweet dreams when you stay in this chocolatier-owned apartment next door to her high-end chocolate shop. The rooms at Cocoa Casa are bright, colorful, and decorated with chocolate-themed decor, without being over-the-top or hokey. You can head next door to sample the goods from Poppy and Peep Chocolate (or take them home as souvenirs). The South Nashville location is within walking distance of coffee shops and more, but offers a little less hustle-and-bustle than the downtown scene.

Location: South NashvilleThings to do nearby: International food along Nolensville Pike; Wedgewood-Houston’s restaurants, bars, and luxury shops; Geodis Park (the MLS stadium); the Nashville Fairgrounds

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound porch, seasonal in-ground pool, piano, view of Shelby Park, bunk beds

This beautifully designed East Nashville farmhouse may come with a large price tag for a two-bedroom, two-bath home, but its location and heated pool (open April to October) are well worth it. Facing Shelby Park—and close to the greenway, which is packed with walking and jogging trails—the home is just 10 minutes from downtown Nashville. There's a wraparound porch to enjoy your morning coffee, plus hammocks and bikes to take in the fresh air. Inside, the bright white design gives the home a fresh, clean look. (If you have a big group, there are a few air mattresses available, and the hosts allow up to eight guests.)

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Kayaking; golfing; Shelby Park; Shelby Bottoms Nature Center; Five Points bars, restaurants, and shopping

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Location on a working organic farm, views of Tennessee hills, gourmet kitchen, farm animals

If you're a Nashville regular, it may be time to look outside of the city for your next vacation. About 30 minutes south of Nashville International Airport, this rental on Bloomsbury Farm is just far enough away to feel like a retreat, but not too far that you can't head into the city every day. It's also perfectly located for a visit to Franklin (a 20-minute drive), one of my favorite day trips from the city, and Arrington Vineyards for wine tasting. Set on over 400 acres of working farmland, the loft is kitted out with a full kitchen, living area, bathroom with a walk-in shower, and king-size bedroom, all overlooking the Tennessee hills. Bonus: The farm has turkeys, horses, and chickens—so if you're lucky, your host will pass on a few fresh eggs for your morning breakfast.

Location: SmyrnaThings to do nearby: Bloomsbury Farm tour, wooded paths, Smyrna Depot District, boat rentals at Fate Sanders Marina

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows; private balcony; access to laundry, pool, and gym in building; central location

A sleek, modern pied-à-terre, this apartment offers floor-to-ceiling windows with city views, complemented by leather and metal furnishings and a few scene-stealing art pieces, like the LED angel wings. It all adds up to a great photo op for the whole crew on a memorable Nashville vacation. Make use of the year-round heated pool and fitness center, and then walk a few blocks to Lower Broadway for the honky-tonk action. The home can sleep up to six across a king bedroom, queen bedroom, and pull-out sofa bed in the living room.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, Lower Broadway honky-tonks, Bridgestone Arena, Nashville Symphony Schermerhorn Symphony Center

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, laundry room, welcoming decor, large backyard, budget-friendly prices

The real perks of this serene East Nashville cottage are outside: The backyard offers space for kids to wear themselves out running around while you sit on the back patio, taking a breather. Inside, the two-bedroom home has a washer/dryer, room-darkening shades, and a bathtub. It's only about a 10-minute drive to downtown Nashville and 15 minutes from the Grand Ole Opry. And best of all, you can score it for under $200 a night.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: TopGolf; Salt Ranch pool club; Cleveland Park shopping, bars, and restaurants; Drkmttr music venue; Nissan Stadium

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Access to laundry, early luggage drop-off, elevator access, high ceilings

This industrial loft is among a variety of rentals in one of downtown Nashville's century-old buildings—and is run by local company Anchor Rentals, which also manages The Russell, a boutique hotel in a renovated East Nashville church. What that means for business travelers headed here is that they won't have to worry about the hosts canceling or not being in the area. This particular apartment, with its high ceilings, multiple workspaces, and well-equipped kitchen (which includes a microwave, coffee machine, and toaster oven for quick breakfasts), is a great spot for weekday visitors.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Ryman Auditorium, Lower Broadway, Frist Art Museum, Dolly Museum Nashville

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pack-and-play, toys for kids, minimalist design, groovy bar cart, French press coffee

Perfectly located 15 minutes away from both Vanderbilt and Belmont University on foot, this apartment in Music Row is an easy home base for parents visiting collegians or touring with high schoolers. With two bedrooms and one bathroom, it has enough space to comfortably fit four people. (If you're traveling with toddlers or infants, the home also offers a pack-and-play and children's books and toys.) There's also a full kitchen complete with a gorgeous Smeg fridge.

Location: Music RowThings to do nearby: Studio B; Vanderbilt University; Belmont University; restaurants, bars and shops in Hillsboro Village and Edgehill Village; Belcourt Theatre

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Nashville?

East Nashville and Wedgewood-Houston are two busy and buzzy neighborhoods with great dining scenes, music venues, and fun shopping. They’re also a quick Uber or bike ride to downtown, making it easy to experience it all. If you’re looking for something a bit quieter, check out the leafy Sylvan Park neighborhood. For something fit for families, head to Donelson, with easy access to parks and the Opryland attractions.

When is the best season to visit Nashville?

There’s no bad time to visit Nashville, but spring and fall offer more temperate weather, when it is easier to hike, bike, and paddle, or just stroll down Broadway without the steaminess of a southern summer collecting under your hat. Most people want to be in Music City during the warmer months to take advantage of outdoor concerts and street festivals, but if you come in winter, you’ll get to cheer on the NHL’s Nashville Predators and see the holiday magic of the five million lights at Gaylord Opryland.

In my opinion, a trip to Nashville should be about five days long, which offers you enough time to expand your vacation beyond Broadway and the honky-tonks. You’ll have enough time for a day or two in town—you can boot-scoot under the neon lights of Lower Broadway—and still have a few days for exploring the surrounding parks, greenways, museums, shops, and music venues away from the crowds.

#6258. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.
