#6234. The Best Ski Resorts in Europe: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

For our 39th annual Readers’ Choice Awards, survey voters weighed in on their favorite ski resorts in Europe. Swiss resorts earned four of the top five spots, with Verbier claiming the number one ranking for the second consecutive year. Italy’s Olympic spotlight helped it land an unprecedented five resorts on the list. The tiny ski resort of Gudauri in Georgia’s Caucasus Mountains made its debut in the rankings—proof that readers are venturing further afield for fresh tracks. Here are the ski resorts that you loved most, for both their diversity of terrain, excellent après ski scenes, and exceptional hotels.

The Caucasus Mountains may not have the cachet of the Alps or the Rockies, but there are plenty of reasons to make the journey to ski in Georgia. The ski passes are a bargain. The slopes are uncrowded. And the food rivals anything you’ll have in France or Italy. Gudauri, the country’s premier ski resort has just over 50 miles of groomed trails, plus freeriding opportunities. There’s a mom-and-pop vibe, with stalls at the base of the mountain selling wool-knit socks, and churchkhela, candle-like strings of nuts encased in a wax-like, grape juice. Travel Bar and La Suite are the main après ski spots (be warned, the local brandy, chacha, is like rocket fuel). Plan an early on-slope lunch at Cafe Vitamin, where you can dig into traditional dishes like khachapuri, molten cheese (often topped with an egg) baked into a shallow bread bowl.

Where to stay: Ski-in/ski-out Gudauri Lodge has 171 rooms across five categories and a sprawling open-air hot tub. Ati Ambavi is a boutique hotel with room decor inspired by cultural icons like Georgian-American ballet master George Balanchine and Georgian artist Niko Pirosmani. The Rooms Kazbegi hotel is a 40-minute drive from the ski resort but its mountain views, delicious Georgian restaurant, and hip vibe are worth the commute.

Stats: There are 14 lifts for nearly 50 miles of runs. One-day lift ticket from $27.

Located on the Italian side of the Matterhorn massif, the high-altitude ski resort of Cervinia is linked with the Swiss resort of Zermatt. The combined terrain is vast, making it possible to log serious mileage without repeating a run all day. The majority of slopes are geared toward beginners and intermediates and the on-piste dining options are exceptional. Many skiers cross the border just to lunch on pasta all'Amatriciana and sip Bombardinos (an Italian riff on eggnog). Cervino The One is a new cableway project connecting Breuil-Cervinia with Plateau Rosa/Testa Grigia in just over 15 minutes. The modern two-section 3S gondola by Leitner includes a mid-station at Plan Maison.

Where to stay: Stylish apartments at Saint Hubertus Resort have modern kitchens, marble bathrooms, and stone living rooms with fireplaces. The team at five-star Hermitage Hotel & Spa can arrange adventures ranging from snowshoeing to heliskiing.

Stats: There are 19 lifts for 72 runs. One-day lift ticket from $52; on the Ikon pass.

Located on the sunnier, Italian side of Mont Blanc, Courmayeur attracts both dedicated skiers and unapologetic sybarites who prefer to sip Aperol spritzes on terraces by day and dine on gourmet meals at night. The Skyway Monte Bianco cable car whisks skiers across the Italian-French border where they can test their mettle on 11-plus miles of spectacular off-piste slopes, including the bucket-list glacial run of the Vallée Blanche in Chamonix. The resort’s modernized snowmaking system guarantees snow on over 8o percent of the slopes, every day of the season. After the pistes close, the Courmayeur Cable Car continues running until midnight so you can dine at mountain-top restaurants like LaChaumière. You can also experience the adventure of a snowmobile climb to reach fancy alpine huts like Rifugio Monte Bianco.

Where to stay: Auberge de la Maison is the epitome of alpine romance. Most rooms have panoramic views of Mont Blanc and the spa features unique alpine therapies such as a hay bio-sauna.

Stats: One-day lift ticket from $83; there are 18 lifts for 33 trails.

When an Egyptian billionaire opened five-star The Chedi Andermatt hotel (more on that later) in 2013, it turned a relatively unknown ski area tucked between Zermatt and St. Moritz into an international ski destination. The largest ski area in the heart of Switzerland has such varied and vast terrain you never have to repeat a run. Gemsstock is a steep, free-riding playground while neighboring Nätschen is laced with cruise-y runs. And if you want something more mellow, you can easily link to the family-friendly slopes of Sedrun. When your legs get tired from all the skiing, the Matterhorn Gotthard railway (also included in the ticket) will take you back to Andermatt. This season, Andermatt-Sedrun will open two new chairlifts, the Val Val-Calmut and Val Val-Cuolm, doubling capacity to 2,400 skiers per hour. The culinary scene is more impressive than ever now that Swiss star chef Andres Caminada has opened an outpost of his IGNIV restaurant concept in Andermatt’s Reuss district.

Where to stay: The extravagant Chedi Andermatt has 123 spacious rooms and suites all boasting fireplaces, Hästens mattresses, and large balconies. Set aside plenty of time to soak in the spa’s hydrotherapy zone and indulge in the 16-foot-high, glass-walled, climate-controlled Cheese Tower or The Japanese, the hotel’s Michelin-star Japanese restaurant.|

Stats: Average price for a one-day lift ticket is $120; the Andermatt-Sedrun-Disentis ski region comprises 33 lifts for 93 marked pistes; on the Epic Pass.

Located on the ridge between Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, Abetone is Central Italy’s largest ski region. Many call it Florence’s secret ski resort as it’s just a 90-minute drive from the city. The family-friendly resort is made up of four interconnected valleys. Local ski champ Zeno Colò designed a handful of runs including the “Zeno” slopes in the Valley of Luce. There’s also a dedicated Nordic skiing area. The slopes are rarely crowded, especially in the afternoons, which are dedicated to long leisurely lunches at rifugios like La Selletta and Monte Gomito.

Where to stay: Val di Luce Spa Resort has spacious family suites that sleep four to six, many with well-equipped kitchens. The spa is a highlight with a pool housed in a Louvre-like glass pyramid so you can gaze at the starry night sky.

Stats: There are 17 lifts for just over 30 miles of runs. One-day lift ticket from $60.

Perched at 5,950 feet, this remote ski town in Lombardy is nicknamed “Little Tibet.” Its four, high-altitude snowparks served as the Winter Olympic stage for freestyle skiing and snowboarding. And its party scene is just as rowdy as its terrain. Set at the base of the Carosello 3000 cable car beneath a huge circus tent, Stalet is an après ski institution known for its crazy costumes, tabletop dancing, and DJ sets. On the Mottolino slopes, Camanel di Planon is an old-school mountain hut with a panoramic terrace and daily 1p.m. music-and-dance show. The best way to arrive at Milky’s Disco Club is via a copper slide at the entrance (stairs are also an option). Party nights are often themed and costumes are highly recommended.

Where to stay: Hotel Spöl is a five-star, adults-only property in Valtellina with a new longevity-focused spa that offers therapies like cryo and molecular hydrogen boosters.

Stats: There are 32 lifts for 78 runs. One-day lift ticket from $74.

Zermatt, surrounded by the Alps’ tallest peaks, has 223 miles of runs in four huge ski areas—some at an altitude of over 10,000 feet, so snow here lingers well beyond the winter season. This enchanting, alpine village lies at the foot of the Matterhorn, Switzerland's most famous mountain, and has plenty of modern touches, like its swanky après-ski diversions and state-of-the-art lift system, recently enhanced this season with the new 6-seater Patrullarve chairlift. Horse-drawn sleighs are the preferred choice of transportation in the car-free village. On the slopes, be sure to stop for the burger at Chez Vrony (reservations a must) and a glass of bubbles at the tiny Champagne bar at the end of the Sunnega run. The new Matterhorn Glacier Ride II now links the entire stretch between Zermatt and Cervinia by cable car, connecting the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise mountain station with the Testa Grigia valley station. Cervino The One is an ambitious new cableway project on the Italian side, connecting Breuil-Cervinia with Plateau Rosa/Testa Grigia in just over 15 minutes.

Where to stay: Grand dame Mont Cervin Palace and modern-luxe Schweizerhof Zermatt, both offer prime central locations and every imaginable amenity. Just above the village, slope-side CERVO Mountain Resort has an ashram-inspired spa with an expansive network of outdoor pools, saunas, and soaking tubs.Riffelalp Resort is another favorite located directly on the slopes, and the Omnia is beautifully nestled into the mountains just above the village.

Stats: There are 55 lifts for 147 runs. One-day lift ticket from $87; on the Ikon Pass.

Poised on a south-facing mountain plateau, Alpe d'Huez is aptly nicknamed “Island in the Sun,” averaging 300 days of sunshine per year. This vast ski area connects several charming villages—Huez, Vaujany, Oz-en-Oisans, Auris-en-Oisans, and Villard-Reculas—and contains terrain to satisfy every skier, from cruisey blues to 10-mile-long La Sarenne, the lengthiest black diamond run in France. Its high elevation—Pic Blanc summit reaches 10,925 feet—also makes it reliably snow sure. On-mountain restaurants, like L'Alpette Chez Passoud, served made-from-scratch regional dishes like tartiflette. And there’s a lively après ski scene anchored by iconic party spot La Folie Douce. Each March, electronic music festival Tomorrowland, takes over the slopes.

Where to stay: Club Med’s all-inclusive ski packages offer great value and the brand’s Alpe d'Huez location is perched at 6,100 feet, delivering ski-in/ski-out access and sensational views. The 5-star Daria-1 Nor hotel, part of the French Les Étincelles Collection, offers direct access to the Alpe Express gondola, and its spa is the ultimate sanctuary for recovery with a hammam, contrast therapy, and a Himalayan salt wall. Hotel Pic Blanc has cozy chalet vibes and a fantastic restaurant.

Stats: There are 84 lifts for 111 runs. One-day lift ticket from $65.

With three nearby airports—Munich, Salzburg, and Innsbruck—Kitzbühel is easily Austria’s most popular holiday resort. The legendary alpine sports town has it all: posh hotels, a picturesque 750-year-old town center, a lively après-ski scene along quaint, cobblestone streets, and unsurpassed skiing that includes 11 renowned ski schools and the most demanding course on the World Cup circuit. With more than 60 mountain huts and restaurants, there are plenty of delicious options to refuel, or lounge leisurely over lunch on the slopes. The resort also has a stellar line-up of winter events, including the Sound Escape music festival (December 11 -12, 2026) and the Bendura Bank Snow Polo World Cup (Jan. 15-17, 2027).

Where to stay: Hotel Schloss Lebenberg, a medieval hillside castle overlooking the village that earns high marks for its stellar service, dining room, and ornate, Gothic-style décor. For affordability and convenience, check out the Henri boutique hotel by the train station.

Stats: 58 lifts for 96 runs covering 145 miles. One-day lift tickets average $92; on the Ikon Pass.

Megève may not have the haute party scene of, say, St. Moritz, or the breadth of sporty-centric Courchevel, but it still has plenty to tout. Two ski areas are covered with nearly 250 miles of runs linked by state-of-the-art cable cars. Skiers can choose from 50-plus on-mountain restaurants, like the excellent La Ferme de Mon Père. A charming, car-free city center featuring an open-air ice rink, cobbled streets, horse-drawn sleighs, as well as a number of smart boutiques makes Megève a family favorite.

Where to stay: The resort's primary patrons—streams of well-heeled Parisians looking to escape the city—reserve rooms at Relais & Châteaux Flocons de Sel, or the Les Fermes de Marie, a tiny mountain chalet where the rooms have fur throws, wood-beamed ceilings, and stone accent walls. Four Seasons Hotel Megève and 12-room Le Chalet, from Zannier Hotels, both offer five-star service.

Stats: There are 112 lifts for nearly 250 runs for the Évasion Mont-Blanc ski area. One-day lift tickets from $60. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited Pass starts at $116 and includes 10 ski areas and nearly 450 miles of slopes across three countries; on the Mountain Collective Pass.

Val Thorens is a resort of superlatives. Europe’s highest ski resort offers one of the continent’s longest ski seasons, running from November 21, 2026, to May 2, 2027, and is part of Les 3 Vallées, the world’s largest linked ski area, with more than 370 miles of runs. This winter, the resort is expanding its appeal with new dining spots, thrilling off-slope activities and a fresh high-altitude experience. At Caron 3200, perched at 10,498 feet, visitors can embark on a virtual-reality ascent of Everest, immersing themselves in the journey to the world’s highest summit without leaving the Alps. For those seeking a different kind of adrenaline rush, the resort is introducing Mountain Kart Xperience, while the Cosmojet toboggan run offers three miles of exhilarating downhill fun. The Bee zipline adds another dose of adventure, soaring 5,905 feet above the slopes. The dining scene is also evolving: Le Bouchon Alpin brings a taste of Lyonnais and Savoyard classics, Le Neva serves contemporary French cuisine inspired by seasonal ingredients, and Zig Zag Café opens as the resort’s first dedicated coffee shop. Meanwhile, the international freeride spotlight returns to Val Thorens from January 25 to 30, 2027, when the Freeride World Tour brings the world’s best skiers and snowboarders to its dramatic high-mountain terrain. The après ski scene has long been legendary, known for party institutions like La Folie Douce and low-key gathering spots such as La Timbale, a tapas bar in the heart of the village.

Where to stay: Five-star Hótel Pashmina for the outdoor spa with stunning mountain views.

Stats: 25 lifts for 93 miles of pistes. One-day lift ticket for Val Thorens starting at $77. One-day lift ticket for the Three Valleys $98; on the Epic Pass.

The oldest winter holiday resort in the world is as elegant and exclusive as it gets. As if St. Moritz wasn't already blessed enough at nearly 6,000 feet above sea level, the sun shines 322 days a year, pairing with the dry air for what’s known as a “Champagne climate.” But it’s the world-class hotels and restaurants, chic shopping, and excellent skiing on- and off-piste that draw celebrities and royalty alike. The iconic alpine city is equally famous for its unique events on the frozen lake St. Moritz: the Snow Polo World Cup St. Moritz, the White Turf horse racing and the ICE car show. The restaurant scene has never been more varied, from cult Italian franchise Crazy Pizza and Greek hotspot Neora at the Grand Hotel des Bains Kempinski St. Moritz to Beefbar at Grace La Margna.

Where to stay: A room in the Serlas Wing at alpine grand dame Badrutt's Palace Hotel, which has been indulging A-listers since 1896, or at the Kulm Hotel—one of our Gold List favorites—can do no wrong.

Stats: There are 58 lifts for 88 runs. One-day lift tickets range from $45 to $100; on the Ikon Pass.

Lech Zürs may lack the bling of areas like St. Moritz and Cortina d’Ampezzo, but that’s part of its charm. Behind traditional farmhouse facades you’ll find chic, family-run boutiques, art galleries, and stylish hotels and chalets. The village of 1,600 may be tiny, but it boasts one of the highest density of award-winning restaurants in the world (Rote Wand Chef’s Table at Rote Wand Gourmet Hotel is a must). And of course there’s the draw of its excellent snowfall and the famed White Ring, a circuit of nearly 14 miles that links Lech, Zürs, Zug, and Oberlech. Two modern cable cars make the slopes even more accessible.

Where to stay: Five-star Hotel Almhof Schneider is the epitome of alpine elegance, with a serious art collection, serene spa, and a 25,000-bottle wine cellar. The family behind the property also recently opened two, design-centric chalets, Haus W and Chalet Sonnenhof. Boutique stay Hotel Kristiania was originally established by Olympic skier Othmar Schneider, and his family continues the hotel’s legacy of hospitality. The Yurt, a salon-inspired après bar within a Kyrgyz-style tent, takes up residency on the hotel grounds this season.

Stats: Part of the Arlberg, Austria’s largest inter-linked ski area, 85 lifts and cable cars can access more than 180 miles of marked slopes and 120-plus miles of backcountry runs. One-day lift ticket from $95; on the Epic Pass.

Chamonix-Mont Blanc’s expansive backcountry and gnarly terrain make it a bucket-list destination for serious skiers. Host to the first winter Olympics in 1924, the pedestrian-friendly town oozes alpine charm and, despite the mountain’s extreme reputation, there are plenty of beginner and intermediate runs. Riding the Aiguille du Midi, the highest cable car in Western Europe is a must simply for the views. From the top, experienced skiers can schuss down the legendary Vallée Blanche, 12.4-mile glacier descent in the heart of Mont-Blanc Massif. A guide is essential for the descent and Chamonix has the world’s oldest and largest guiding organization. The eclectic dining scene draws on flavors from around the world. Essential reservations include Mumma, which specializes in Asian and South American fusion cuisine, and Yumidori, a Japanese spot helmed by a sushi world champ. Restaurant Le 3842, one of the highest restaurants in Europe, serves a three-course lunch atop the Aiguille du Midi.

Where to stay: La Folie Douce Hotel has a hip vibe, a lively après scene and an unbeatable location in the heart of Chamonix, with a ski lift steps from the front door. For over-the-top luxury, book a stay at Hameau Albert 1er. The five-star hotel has 33 rooms, two suites and two stand-alone chalets and a Michelin-star restaurant. Le Collectionist’s portfolio of luxury chalets range from three to 12 bedrooms.

Stats: There are 82 lifts for 91 runs. One-day lift ticket from $55; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective Pass. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited Pass starts at $85 and includes 10 ski areas and nearly 450 miles of slopes across three countries.

#6233. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6232. Singapore Airlines CEO May Rethink New Business Class Colors, And He Should

Singapore Airlines has made a mistake with the colors of its new business class cabin. The gray and black surfaces with bright yellow accents look more like a cheap hybrid of Spirit Airlines and Scoot than the premium airline whose name is on the aircraft. Now CEO Goh Choon Phong has left the door open to changes. I hope Singapore Airlines takes that opportunity.

When I covered the new Singapore Airlines business class seat, I welcomed several functional improvements, particularly the redesigned footwell. Singapore has addressed complaints about sleeping comfort and added features passengers increasingly expect.

I keep looking at the photographs and wondering how this particular color scheme made it through the approval process. Singapore Airlines has spent decades cultivating an identity associated with understated luxury. Its warmer, muted cabin colors help communicate that identity before a “Singapore Girl” even shows up to offer a welcome drink.

The new business class looks disconnected from it. The yellow accents against the gray and dark surfaces suggest a budget airline or a gaming chair. Neither association strikes me as particularly useful for Singapore Airlines.

During the launch Q&A, executives defended the decision to move in a different visual direction.

A post shared by Brandon · The Points Wanderer (@thepointswanderer)

Vice President of Product Experience Ong Wah Li said customer research had identified a desire for a more contemporary appearance. She described the resulting palette as “modern and refreshed, yet elegant and refined.”

Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin emphasized that the Singapore Airlines experience extends beyond cabin colors. He defended the different palette, saying:

“We do not feel that a different colour palette creates any kind of inconsistency.”

Of course the Singapore Airlines experience involves more than colors. Service and comfort are far more consequential over a long flight. But the airline does not invest in cabin design because appearance is irrelevant. It understands that the surroundings help establish what passengers think they are buying.

Asking for something “modern” does not mean asking for this. Singapore Airlines could refresh its interiors while preserving the warmth and restraint that make them recognizable. I simply do not understand why contemporary design should require such a sharp departure from the brand. Plenty of modern interiors feel inviting and expensive without a bright yellow accent running through the seat.

At a November 11 employee town hall, Goh acknowledged the negative reaction. According to The Business Times, he said:

“We’ll look at it, we’ll see what is feasible.”

He also expressed confidence that passengers would appreciate the seats once they experienced their comfort and practical features.

They may well do so. I hope I do too. But enjoying the seat would not make the color choice better. I can appreciate a more comfortable bed while wishing the cabin looked like Singapore Airlines…and the fact that I say that underscores what a brand Singapore has built and should be careful not to fritter away over idiotic consultants who are out of touch with Singapore’s customer base.

Goh has not promised a redesign, and I would not describe this as a reversal. Still, his willingness to consider what can be changed is welcome. We all make mistakes. There is considerably more dignity in acknowledging one and correcting it than spending years defending it.

The contrast with the new Singapore Airlines first class suite makes the business class decision even stranger.

PriestmanGoode designed first class, while Designworks, a BMW Group company, designed business class. Factorydesign handled premium economy and economy.

First class looks like a natural evolution of Singapore Airlines. The warmer finishes and batik details give the new suite a connection to the airline without making it look old. It demonstrates that you can introduce a substantially different product while retaining a recognizable identity.

I worked closely with PriestmanGoode during my time at Star Alliance and have a great appreciation for its work. Looking at these two cabins, I would ask the firm to help bring the business class finishes into the same visual family.

Designworks does have aviation experience, including work with STARLUX and EVA Air. Nevertheless, I think it has badly misjudged this assignment. The BMW association does not automatically make the result luxurious, and this particular result does not look worthy of Singapore Airlines.

I am not particularly impressed with the new premium economy aesthetic either, though that is a different firm’s work. Ultimately, Singapore Airlines approved all these designs. The responsibility for how they fit together belongs to the airline.

There is nothing inherently wrong with yellow. It works for Scoot because Scoot has a different identity and sells a different proposition. It worked for Spirit Airlines (until it didn’t…).

But Singapore Airlines has little reason to make its premium cabin evoke its own budget subsidiary. Nor does the comparison with Spirit help communicate the experience it wants passengers to pay for, right?

That is particularly strange in Southeast Asia, where travelers have plenty of experience distinguishing a full-service premium carrier from a budget airline. Singapore Airlines should reinforce what makes it different.

The yellow stripe will not suddenly send loyal passengers to another carrier: I don’t think people will book away from Singapore because they don’t like the seat color. But why should that be even a consideration? Singapore Airlines has the resources to deliver both comfort and an interior that reflects its reputation.

The earthy, muted colors have worked because they convey quality. This new palette feels like a needless attempt to be different, with too little consideration for what is being lost.

I welcome the functional improvements in the new Singapore Airlines business class seat and look forward to trying it. But the color scheme is a mistake. Sorry, it is. To my eyes, it cheapens the appearance of a product intended to command a premium.

Goh has indicated that the airline will consider what is feasible. My suggestion is straightforward: retain the improvements to comfort, ask PriestmanGoode to help reconsider the finishes, and give business class an appearance consistent with the airline passengers have chosen. Dark brown would work well.

Singapore Airlines does not need to spend the next decade explaining why a cabin that reminds people of Scoot actually represents luxury. It has time to reconsider. I hope it does.

#6231. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

#6230. The Great Sea Reef Is Fiji’s Wildest Dive, and a New Frontier for Conservation

The bull shark appeared out of the blue in an instant. And it was … fat.

Floating 60 feet below the surface in the South Pacific Ocean, I gave a shout of excitement through my scuba regulator when I saw it. Flanked by two remora fish, like bodyguards, the nine-foot bull shark turned in the water with surprising speed given its bulk, swimming just above the sandy sea floor. Deep water beckoned to its left. To the right, a wall of coral stretched upward above me in a mosaic of neon green, milky orange, and soft pink. A fellow diver floated nearby, clad in a speckled cerulean camouflage wetsuit, with wild hair floating around his mask. He flattened the side of his hand and placed it to the top of his head, the universal symbol for one of the biggest-ticket sightings a diver can hope for: shark. We’d be logging the bull into our census for sure.

Author Samantha Falewée jumping in to dive the Great Sea Reef in Fiji.

I was scuba diving in the Great Sea Reef (traditionally named Cakaulevu in Fijian), a 280-mile-long underwater paradise in northeast Fiji. Relatively unknown, with only a single scuba diving lodge that has direct access to it, this place is the third-largest coral reef system in the world. More than three-quarters of all coral species known to science live and grow here, as do more than half of all recognized fish.

The Great Sea Reef, nicknamed the GSR, is also a growing hub of conservation research. In July 2026, a new partnership between the Professional Association of Diving Instructors (PADI), PADI AWARE (the affiliated NGO), and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) was launched to push community-backed ocean conservation. A key part of this is PADI AWARE’s new Global Shark & Ray Census, an ambitious project to collect data that PADI and WWF can use to inform governments, in Fiji and beyond, for the creation of new Marine Protected Areas. This recent collaboration made our morning shark sighting even more exciting—and meaningful.

“We are bringing together PADI’s 30-million-plus certified divers and 6,600 dive centers with WWF’s conservation work in over 100 countries,” says Ian Campbell, a driving force behind the collaboration and the programs director of PADI AWARE.

In visiting the GSR, I was experiencing firsthand how travelers can experience this ecosystem and be a part of an innovative approach to protecting coral reefs. When I saw the lone bull shark, I wrote “bull shark: 1” in my waterproof notebook. The scribble was below my other excited notes from that same dive that read: “leopard shark! Amazing: 1” and “white-tipped reef shark: 2”. This underwater note-taking is the first step of the shark and ray census; the logging would happen when we returned to land.

Nukubati Resort, the sole property located on the Great Sea Reef.

Awaiting us, past a sandy beach and the angled heights of coconut trees, was Nukubati resort (pronounced Noo-koom-bah-ti). As the sole property located on the Great Sea Reef, Nukubati is the labor of love of two Fijian generations: It was opened in 1992 by Fiji-born Jenny Leewai and her Australian husband, Peter Bourke; and is now helmed by their daughter, Lara, with her husband, Leone, who was born and raised on the nearby Mali Island. Set against the slow pulse of the waves, styled in classic, custom-ordered cane palm furniture atop gleaming wooden floors, this little haven delivered a peaceful welcome after every dive.

Following a hot shower in my private bure, or bungalow, I rejoined the others at the broad open-air lounge, nicknamed the pavilion, which serves as the heart of this intimate resort. Jenny was already there, barefoot in a caftan with Champagne-colored pearls at her ears and fingers. Lara was there too, a red hibiscus flower tucked behind her ear. Lara and Leone’s young son, Masei, pattered past on the shining wooden floor, followed by a russet, tail-wagging dog, Bēbē.

Fijian tatavu, aka a traditional Fijian barbecue, served at Nukubati Resort.

In this deeply relaxed atmosphere, alfresco lunches can last hours. But as soon as we finished the meal—spicy pawpaw soup, followed by skewers of whitefish, pineapple, onions, and peppers in a bed of peanut sauce—I gathered with the other divers around a coffee table, where a weatherbeaten copy of Tropical Pacific Fish lay.

There, PADI regional manager Robyn Vincent and Leone led us through a lecture on sharks and rays, which ranged in topics from biology (many sharks are late bloomers: the remarkable greenland shark, for example, doesn’t reach sexual maturity until it’s 100 years old) to shark tourism (each year, roughly 500,000 people dive specifically to see sharks around the world, creating an industry valued at $314 million USD).

Then, we logged the sharks we’d just seen on the PADI AWARE app. Tapping through the details took just me six minutes as I marked our location (a dive site called “Fish Market”), our activity (options include diving, snorkeling, boating, fishing, and others), our maximum underwater depth (60 feet), and the number and species of sharks I’d seen (one bull shark, two gray reef sharks, one whitetip reef shark, and one zebra shark).

Since the census launched in April 2026, more than 212,000 people have participated, submitting thousands of sightings from around the world. That data is vetted by employees at PADI AWARE, with scientific support from the James Cook University Centre for Sustainable Tropical Fisheries and Aquaculture in Australia. And what’s been logged so far is already being used: According to the university, some data has been implemented in a scientific paper currently under review, and verified images submitted to the app have helped confirm the presence of four shark and ray species in the neighboring country of Vanuatu. One of those four, the great hammerhead shark, is listed as ‘Critically Endangered’ on the IUCN Red List. These awe-inspiring animals can grow up to 20 feet long and engage in mysterious mating rituals, swimming in synchronous, ascending spirals. Their very existence off the reef-fringed, tropical shores of Vanuatu had been debated by scientists—until now.

During the author's five-day stay, she saw multiple species of sharks and rays on every single dive.

Thanks to PADI’s presence in remote natural places like these, the census’s fast-accumulating data could also have ramifications in PADI and WWF’s efforts to help reach the UN Convention on Biological Diversity’s 30x30, the goal to protect 30% of the world’s oceans by 2030.

“WWF brings the political clout,” says Cheryl Bowlin, the founder of Reef Stewardship Frameworks, a community-based conservation nonprofit in Fiji. “They help encourage policy to create Marine Protected Areas.” Those Marine Protected Areas keep reefs healthy and safe for locals and travelers alike, and can provide new forms of income to communities. (An academic paper published in 2025 found that turning unprotected dive sites into fully protected marine areas could generate more than $2 billion globally in direct tourism revenue—an income stream that largely incorporates dive centers owned and run by locals.)

Places like Nukubati Resort are a prime example of the reach and impact that travelers can have, even if they might not realize it at first. During my five-day stay there, I saw multiple species of sharks and rays—utterly wild, without human influence of feeding or baiting—on every single dive. Stats like that make scuba diehards and casual passersby alike take notice, especially since diving on the GSR is an option for all skill levels, from snorkelers to beginner divers (like me) to advanced. Visitors can experience top-notch diving and contribute helpful data at the same time.

“I’ve been working as a PADI scuba diving instructor since 2013, and I’ve traveled and dived extensively all over the world,” Vincent said as we motored out to a dive site the following day, where a gentle current carried us over seawalls coated with hard corals and neon fish. “The fact that we’ve seen sharks on every single dive, and we are the only boat here, is incredible. There could be 50 dive centers here, 50 other dive boats.”

The reef holds significance in local heritage, too. “The name of the Great Sea Reef in our northern dialect is Bainivualiku, which means the fence of the north,” said Leone. We sat at Nukubati, along with Leone’s wife and business partner, Lara, not far from the beach one afternoon, after another morning of glorious diving. “In the old days, the reef protected our community from sailing invaders who wanted to come in,” he said. The Great Sea Reef has been celebrated in songs and stories amongst regional communities for generations. Today, Leone and other locals are recognized as traditional stakeholders in the GSR’s future. To them, “The reef is our heart and soul,” Leone said.

That unshakable faith is evident in the family’s nurturing of Nukubati, which has withstood cyclones, a fire, the COVID-19 pandemic, and more. Throughout the trials the property has come out the other side, a timeless hideaway that accommodates a maximum of just 14 guests. The strong family and community bonds have kept it going; 100 percent of the Nukubati staff are local. Sustainability is another defining aspect, as Nukubati has run on solar panels, a system hand-engineered by co-founder Peter, since its opening day in the 1990s. Fast forward to now: In September 2026, Nukubati and its in-house operator, Great Sea Reef Divers, were recognized as a PADI Eco Center, a designation awarded to properties that demonstrate a significant commitment and investment to conservation and sustainability.

Now, after their dives, Leone and his team log the sharks and rays they’ve seen in the new global census, and encourage visitors to join. “There's no looking back now,” Leone said, rubbing his hands together. Ahead of him, the Great Sea Reef—colossal, colorful, teeming with sea life and yet empty of humans—waited just below the surface.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

While it would be a dream to get to every new hotel within days of opening to be among the first to experience special properties around the world, the reality is, that’s not always possible. When it is, though, you can bet we jump on the opportunity. Especially when it’s a flagship new points hotel.

That’s how I ended up staying at the gorgeous new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur within a week of its opening on Oct. 30, 2026. To be clear, I understood that not all the hotel’s restaurants would be open, nor would its spa, so this is not a full review, rather a first glimpse at what’s sure to be a favorite Hilton points redemption option soon.

Although it’s the Malaysian capital’s newest hotel, the Waldorf Astoria actually occupies the site of the storied former Hotel Istana in the heart of city’s Golden Triangle district — so called because it is the capital’s main financial and shopping district, with luxury megamalls galore — which means it’s centrally located, but tucked onto a quiet stretch of Jalan Raja Chulan.

Because of that, the hotel feels secluded and quiet, but plugged into the rest of the city, and easily accessible to most of the activities international visitors are likely to seek out while in town.

The hotel feels like a destination unto itself, too, though, thanks to its palatial suites (no mere rooms here) and an impressive slate of bars and restaurants, including outposts from celebrity chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten and Bangkok-based Garima Arora. The hotel will also be home to Malaysia’s first and only La Prairie spa, and the outdoor pool is the perfect place to while away a tropical afternoon.

Here’s what else you should plan to do during your stay at the new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur.

During my stay, only a fraction of the accommodations were ready for guests, but the hotel should be at full strength soon. There are no rooms here, just suites, which start at an impressive 80 square meters (861 square feet).

Deboss Collective is behind the decor, and sought inspiration from traditional Malay construction and crafts, incorporating lots of natural stone and timber, woven textiles and wooden furnishings that feel like contemporary urban updates to what you might find in a traditional rumah kampung, or village house.

To wit, there are huge windows overlooking the hotel grounds and the city skyline, letting in plenty of natural light. The carpet patterns and hardwood are meant to evoke traditional Malaysian marquetry while colorful accent walls call to mind vibrant Peranakan shophouses you can still find in parts of the city.

My suite’s footprint was enormous, with a huge, welcoming living area that included a 65-inch flatscreen television, a breakfast table which could double as a workdesk thanks to a panel of plugs, a rounded sofa and armchair and a low-slung wooden chair that blended colonial and midcentury influences.

In the separate bedroom, a king-size bed was dressed with crisp white sheets embroidered with a “WA,” just in case you forgot where you were. To either side were walls with a terete theme hearkening to the bamboo stalks that grow in gardens around the city. Another 55-inch flatscreen hung on the wall in there.

The bathroom was mostly white marble, including geometric floor tiling, but the countertops were a handsome darker hue. Anchoring the entire space was an elliptical standalone tub with a scalloped shell, while a water closet and separate walk-in shower stood close by. To lend a sense of place, the bath products are from Jo Malone’s Jo Loves line and scented with citrusy-fresh pomelo, which is a staple in Malaysian cuisine.

Considering this was a standard category room, it felt positively palatial, with a huge amount of real estate that provided a variety of distinct spaces to enjoy within the suite at different times.

The Waldorf Astoria isn’t the biggest hotel in town, but it fields an outsize roster of restaurants that should be a draw for guests and Kuala Lumpur locals alike.

You can’t call your hotel a Waldorf Astoria if it doesn’t have a version of Peacock Alley, the famous lobby lounge from the New York City original. The one here sits smack dab at the hotel entrance and has soaring ceilings, sculptural marble columns, dramatic overhead chandeliers and a variety of seating vignettes that feel homey yet upscale.

The all-day menu offers items like chicken skewers with lemongrass and coriander ($10.50), a Waldorf salad ($14.50), a smash burger ($22) and Malaysian nasi goreng ($17) among other options.

Named after the previous hotel to occupy this spot, Istana is the hotel’s all-day dining restaurant and is adjacent to the lobby. Breakfast includes an extensive buffet and both Western and Asian dishes. For lunch and dinner, you’ll find specialties like spiced Borneo chicken wings with a honey glaze ($10.50), chargrilled red snapper with wild ginger chili sambal ($23.75) and fresh fiddlehead ferns from the Cameron Highlands sauteed in coconut milk with tongue-torching bird’s eye chili ($8.75).

If you’re up for it, the durian dessert with coconut cream and a palm sugar compote and served with toasted buttery buns is a rich way to end the evening ($12).

This is Vongerichten’s farm-to-table concept, so you’ll find a menu focused on seasonal fruits and vegetables. The signature eggplant dip is smoky and smooth with tangy coconut yogurt and tomato chutney served with fluffy pita ($9.75). There are also tartines like a king crab crostini with tart lemon aioli and dill ($16.50), various pizzas and pastas, and an array of plant-based dishes including pistachio-crusted broccoli with hazelnut vinaigrette ($14.50).

At the entrance to ABC Kitchens KL, there is a bright, casual area with a cocktail bar and small plates.

Jean-Georges Vongerichten has a longstanding relationship with the Waldorf Astoria brand, so it should be no surprise that the signature restaurant here is a French-Malaysian fine-dining fusion restaurant courtesy of the chef. It is only open for dinner Tuesday-Saturday. I did not have the opportunity to dine here, but the menu features an entire caviar section, starters like diver scallops with caramelized cauliflower and caper-raisin emulsion ($29.50) and spice-charred duck breast with roasted cabbage and chili-lime broth ($39.50).

It was not yet open during my stay, but Yaari will be the hotel’s sophisticated Indian restaurant and will only be open for dinner from Wednesday-Sunday. The chef is Garima Arora, whose Bangkok restaurant, Gaa, holds two Michelin stars.

Located on the fourth floor, Coda feels like a swanky hideaway for those in the know. Glossy dark stone surfaces and emerald-green velvet chairs and banquettes give the space a swanky vibe, as does the menu of libations inspired by various vinyl albums, one of which will likely be spinning on the record player during your visit.

Even the classics get a Malaysian twist, like an old fashioned crafted with jerky-like beef bak kwa-washed Michter’s bourbon, cardamom, clove and cascara distillate and mandarin-infused jaggery for a sweet finish ($20.50).

Here are some of the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur’s other amenities:

Nightly rates at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur start at around $520 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is part of  American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, so if you have or , you can make a booking through amextravel.com and receive perks like availability-based upgrades, up to a $100 credit to use on-property during your stay for things like drinks or meals, complimentary daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

Both cards now offer a biannual $300 (up to $600 per calendar year) statement credit on prepaid stays at Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts, so you could save $300 on a reservation at the hotel if you are able to take advantage of one of these cards’ credits. Just note that this benefit is changing in 2027 and will require cardholders to book two nights or more to take advantage of the credit.

Related: Our favorite American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts around the world

All public areas at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur are wheelchair-accessible thanks to elevators (with wheelchair-height buttons), ramps and wide pathways. The hotel has accessible rooms in the King Urban Deluxe category. These accommodations feature audio and visual alarms, an automatic door closer, and wheelchair-height door viewer.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is an exciting new points option in the Malaysian capital, and one with plenty of award availability. While 100,000 points is a lot to pay, considering the sheer size of the suites here and the relatively high (for Kuala Lumpur) price point, it might be well worth it. Once the hotel’s restaurants and spa are all open and operational, this should become one of the city’s most popular luxury hotels.

#6228. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6227. A Wonderfully Relaxing “Afternoon Matinée” In SAS A330 Business Class

Our SAS A330-300 Business Class flight from Copenhagen to Chicago could not have been better and it really was one of the most relaxing flights I’ve had in a long time, during which I enjoyed great food and watched two excellent movies when I could not sleep.

Unless I’m flying on a plane with Starlink, I assume that the internet is not going to work onboard (especially on SAS). If it does, it is a pleasant surprise. If not, in most cases I will have already completed essential tasks so that I’m not spending my flight dreading unfinished work.

We flew home on Sunday afternoon, also a day off for me, and I decided that I’d just relax and watch some movies during the flight if I could not sleep between meals.

Lunch, by the way, was delicious. I pre-ordered “ASC” salmon with tomato vinaigrette, summer cabbage with brown butter, Jerusalem artichoke soufflé, and chive oil while Heidi pre-ordered beef with osso buco sauce, polenta cake, butter-and-thyme carrot, grilled artichoke and gremolata. We shared. Both dishes were perfect.

The appetizer and dessert were also excellent, as was the coffee:

I find the catering consistently excellent on SAS.

I did try to sleep, but could not, but that turned out to be a blessing in disguise on this flight. First I watched a Japanese movie called A Pale View of Hills, which I found riveting and very well-done. It trace the story of Etsuko and has a beautiful twist that left me profoundly moved. Highly recommended.

Meanwhile, Heidi was watching a German movie called Sound of Falling, a psychological drama spanning a century at a farmhouse in rural Germany. I then watched that while she watched the Japanese move. Wow, also excellent. Riveting and thought-provoking.

We don’t have a TV at home and I do not watch movies or anything at all unless I’m on a plane, but watching movies like this makes me think that I may be missing out…both were so well done and absolutely worth the time. I honestly could not stop thinking about either one for a couple days.

Before a landing, a delicious open-face sandwich was served with eggs and shrimp.

The flight crew was excellent and the kids were again very well-behaved, so I really don’t think it could have been a better flight. SAS does not have a cutting edge business class seat, but between my six hours of sleep on the way to Copenhagen and my restful flight on the way back, I was reminded again how much I love fly SAS Business Class and hope that I can find a way to replenish my EuroBonus account once we spend down the rest of the two million points.

I’m not sure whether I will offer a full review of this flight…I took a lot more pictures, but I’ve reviewed this product recently and little has changed. Bottom line: I do strongly recommend SAS for intercontinental travel.

Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

“We don’t have a TV at home and I do not watch movies or anything at all unless I’m on a plane” is the most interesting line of this article. I guess with laptops and tablets, a TV is not indispensable like before though there’s something about watching movies and shows on a big screen. You never have the desire to watch classic films, mini-series, or TV shows unless you’re on a plane?

Cozy. Enjoy those moments when they happen

#6226. Report: Google Accepts Privacy Safeguards for Spirit Data

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the proposed sale will exclude personnel records, including medical files, results of drug and alcohol tests, performance reviews, payroll information, and grievance and arbitration filings.

Unions representing former Spirit pilots and flight attendants had objected to the inclusion of that data, noting Google’s plans to use the information to train its artificial intelligence models. The agreement reached this week resolves the unions’ concerns, the Journal said.

Google and Spirit initially planned to have an outside company “deidentify” the airline’s records. That process will still take place, though at a higher standard than Spirit intended to use, and Google will be prohibited from attempting to “reidentify” the data.

Spirit went out of business in May following a dramatic rise in jet fuel prices. The decision to auction off its internal records for use by AI was a first for the airline industry and opened up a new realm of contestation for workers and employers.

#6225. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

Given the dire state of the BA offer with still flaky IT, dirty badly maintained cabins and dysfunctional (if at all) customer services a great option for those in the UK.
