#6212. 17 Best Airbnbs in Bangkok for Your Next Trip to Thailand's Capital

A vast metropolis where modern skyscrapers mix with antique wooden houses, Bangkok is, in my opinion, one of the best cities in the world. Whether you’re on the hunt for boat noodles or Thai massages, there’s so much to do and no bad time of year to visit. And when it comes to where to stay, travelers will find just as much variety among the excellent lodging options. While this Thai city delivers a sensory overload of epic proportions, there are plenty of peaceful pockets and quiet corners perfect for catching your breath after a long day of exploring. One of the best ways to get a bit of solitude is by renting a dreamy Airbnb in the area.

Over the years, I’ve spent months in Thailand’s capital city. I've visited for weekend girls trips, concerts, and trips with family, staying everywhere from Siam to Chinatown. I've experienced the city's endless ways to fill your days, from world-class museums to addictive street food to some of Asia’s best cocktail bars. If you're planning a stay and want a little more elbow room than the city's hotels might allow, there are plenty of charming rentals to lay your head down at, from studios with incredible river views to massive homes for the whole family to shophouses in Chinatown. Read on for some of the best Airbnbs in Bangkok.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Spacious design, hot tub, screen projector

Baan Konja sits at the end of a cul-de-sac in the café-crazed neighborhood of Ekkamai. This stylish four-story home is an ideal launching pad for families or groups of friends looking for a peaceful stay. Guests will love how well laid out and spacious the setup is, with elegant tiled bathrooms, a rare private hot tub, four plush bedrooms (three kings and a room with two singles), and a comfy outdoor balcony area. According to past guests, the host, Michael, goes above and beyond to address any issues, including providing toothbrushes and slippers if you forget yours at home. He’s also able to suggest great cocktail spots.

Neighborhood: EkkamaiThings to do nearby: Wat That Thong Buddhist temple; top restaurants, cafés, and bars

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Incredible river and temple views, Thai design, trendy location

Ideal for couples and digital nomads, this large studio apartment is high up in a residential building surrounded by some of the city’s best spots for eating and drinking. Outfitted with a comfortable bed and couch next to a floor-to-ceiling window, it's designed with local touches like Thai art, colorful throw pillows, and a hand-carved wooden headboard. But travelers are really booking this room for the incredible views over the river and the nearby temple. Just outside, Michelin-star restaurants, riverside cafés, and trendy boutiques are steps away.

Neighborhood: Talat NoiThings to do nearby: Talat Noi street art, Chinatown, Wat Traimit Buddhist temple

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beautiful design, large soaking tub, open-air spaces

The Clay Room is one of six short-term rental units in this newly renovated apartment building formerly owned by the host’s grandfather. This studio-style room is cozy with a comfortable bed and couch area, a large TV, and floor-to-ceiling glass-block windows. But to me, the best part of a stay here is the glass-block bathroom that looks like it could be out of a ’70s design magazine. Separated by a large velvet curtain, it has handcrafted clay-colored tiles, natural mineral paint, a huge soaking tub, and two curved glass-block partitions separating the toilet area and shower. There’s also an outdoor kitchen and a washer and dryer in the leafy backyard area.

Neighborhood: Thon BuriThings to do nearby: Wongwian Yai Park, IconSiam mall, Wat Arun Buddhist temple

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Quality craftsmanship, detailed design, first-floor spa

Located near the Jim Thompson House Museum, Chinatown, and Lumphini Park, this two-bedroom apartment is perfectly situated for exploring the best of Bangkok. Modern and stylish, its Scandinavian-style furniture is made with high-quality craftsmanship, according to past guests. The sleek style is accented with traditional pillows and throws woven with Thai patterns. Its main bedroom is huge with a king bed, while the second is smaller and has a set of bunk beds, making it ideal for a family with small children. When your feet get tired from exploring, walk down to the first-floor spa for a sublime Thai massage. (Of note, the apartment is on the second floor and there is not an elevator.)

Neighborhood: Hua LamphongThings to do nearby: Chinatown, Jim Thompson House Museum, Lumphini Park

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Central location, high ceilings, historic design

Steps from the Chao Phraya River, this 130-year-old heritage shophouse is in the pulsing heart of Bangkok. The city's best bars, cafés, shopping, and public transport are practically at your doorstep, but the Airbnb’s effortlessly cool design makes it hard to leave. Fun yellow and white checkered flooring, a coral-colored spiral staircase and matching ceiling, painted cement walls, and retro Thai art are a few of the standout elements of this cozy one-bedroom. Although the listing says it can accommodate up to five with a king-size bed and a sofa bed in the lofted bedroom, as well as a king-size sofa bed in the living area, guests say the house is compact, so I recommend it for couples or small families.

Neighborhood: Bang RakThings to do nearby: Sathorn Pier, IconSiam mall

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Private driveway with EV charging station, 60" smart TV, large kitchen

After years of working in European hotels, host Chureerut moved back to Bangkok to live with her mother and open her own Airbnb. Located between Bangkok’s two airports, slightly outside the city down a quiet alley, it’s a great setup for a peaceful family escape. Chureerut lovingly combines Scandinavian tiles and lighting with traditional Thai design elements, such as teak and rattan furniture. The two-bedroom house (a king and a queen) sleeps up to seven and is fully equipped with everything you could ever need, from a washer and dryer to a fully stocked kitchen and a dreamy outdoor patio with traditional Thai windows. Should you need any Bangkok recs, Chureerut and her mother are right next door.

Neighborhood: Khet Lat PhraoThings to do nearby: Central EastVille shopping center, Crystal Design Center

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Japanese-style design, pool, modern building

This full-service apartment on Bangkok's ​​Phahonyothin Road offers a quiet stay and easy access to the rest of the city. A seven-minute walk or a free tuk-tuk ride (provided by the building management) will take you to Sanampao Station, and from there, Bangkok is your fire-grilled oyster. The host has multiple one-bedroom apartments spread throughout the building, each with a subtle Japanese design: light timber, low beds (this one is a king), neutral tones, and large glass windows. Top-notch building amenities include a gym, outdoor swimming pool, and a massage parlor—a perfect tonic after a long flight.

Neighborhood: PhahonyothinThings to do nearby: Victory Monument, Jim Thompson House Museum

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Stylish design, natural light, convenient location

This artfully curated apartment incorporates Scandi-chic touches throughout. Situated near Lumphini and Bechakitti Parks and just a short walk to the BTS, past guests have raved about the location. But its interiors are what really will catch your eye. The main living room has floor-to-ceiling windows with green views, rattan chairs, and a mustard-colored couch with colorful pillows. Find ocean-blue tiles in the kitchen for another fun pop of color. Its two king bedrooms have concrete floors, wooden furniture, and light pastel sheets. Black slate and white mosaic tiles adorn the bathroom, which includes a large tub. Keep in mind that it's located on the third floor and there is no elevator, so pack light!

Neighborhood: LumphiniThings to do nearby: Lumphini Park, One Bangkok, Benjakitti Park

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor bathroom, quiet workspace, tons of character

As soon as you check in here, you can tell it’s owned by an artist. Located in the historic center of Bangkok, chaotic Khaosan Road is a 10-minute walk away, but this two-bedroom renovated shophouse is a peaceful reprieve. Filled with fun art and an eclectic style, this cute and compact space includes a shared bedroom and living room, plus a second bed in a loft. Its large, exposed-brick dining room is ideal for a couple working remotely, and its outdoor bathroom is among the most unique I’ve seen in Bangkok.

Neighborhood: RattanakosinThings to do nearby: Khao San Road, The Grand Palace, Wat Pho temple, Loha Prasat “metal castle”

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Lush garden, badminton court, brushed concrete interiors

Tucked into a local area in Samrong on the far outskirts of Bangkok (accessible via the BTS SkyTrain), this one-bedroom Airbnb is perfect for travelers who want to escape the chaos—at least for a little while. The owners have outfitted their backyard guesthouse with cooling brushed concrete, vintage wooden doors, and comfortable bedding, including a contemporary pullout sectional. Reach out to the hosts for help arranging a badminton game at the nearby court, a market tour, or a few other neighborhood experiences. Plus, the fridge is stocked with drinks and snacks to enjoy while relaxing under a banana tree in the large garden.

Neighborhood: SamrongThings to do nearby: Pak Nam fish market, Talad Rot Fai Srinakarin night market, Bang Krachao man-made island

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Great nearby food options, trendy tiles, access to hotel amenities

It’s all about coziness and convenience at this quaint two-bedroom (each with a queen) apartment near the SkyTrain and the Sathorn Central Pier. White walls, lofty ceilings, bamboo light fixtures, and handwoven wall tapestries make its newly renovated spaces feel airy and bright. Major brownie points go to the host, who can help with just about anything, including arranging an airport transfer, providing tips for the best local restaurants, and securing passes to use the neighboring hotel’s outdoor pool and fitness area (for a small daily fee).

Neighborhood: SilomThings to do nearby: Sathorn Pier, IconSiam mall

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Sophisticated decor, powerful AC, designated workspace

Digital nomads flocking to Thailand—thanks to its visa—will love this fully-equipped house. During your stay here, you’ll find comfortable working areas, powerful AC, a stocked fridge, and even a printer. Located in a residential area outside the city center, the Ratchadaphisek MRT Station is just a five-minute walk away, connecting you to the city’s hotspots after office hours. Newly renovated, its trendy midcentury-modern decor is another stay highlight. Mismatched furniture, concrete floors, matte black fixtures, and pencil-strip bathroom tiles are all smart additions. It sleeps up to four with a queen in the bedroom and a sofa bed in the living room.

Neighborhood: RatchadaphisekThings to do nearby: Chatuchak Weekend Market, Jodd Fairs market

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor patio, eclectic design, tons of natural light

You'll find this delightfully eclectic three-bedroom respite on a quiet, tree-lined street in the residential Din Daeng area of Bangkok. Decorated with the owner’s paintings, parquet floors, and an eclectic blend of furniture, this homey abode is perfect for a young family or a group of friends. Its three bedrooms (two with kings, one with a queen) have unique styles, from wacky wallpaper to shiplap and fully tiled bathrooms. Each has a desk for working, but the peaceful patio with mango trees and ferns is a much better place to get the creative juices flowing.

Neighborhood: Din DaengThings to do nearby: Huai Khwang market, Ganesha Shrine, Thailand Cultural Center

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beautiful design, luxurious bathroom, fantastic location

As far as neighborhoods go, Bangkok’s Chinatown is hard to beat. The city’s best street food, hippest bars, and most vibrant shops are all steps from your door. Inside an ornate shophouse, this two-bedroom, one-bath home offers more modern finishes than its exterior implies. Its bathroom includes a high-tech rain shower, luxurious soaking tub, and cool Oxford encaustic tiles. The bedrooms here are huge, with chic black and rattan furniture, handwoven decoration, king beds, and large TVs. It’s ideal for families, friends, or two sets of couples. Situated on the 36th floor of the famous State Tower (you may remember the building’s rooftop bar from The Hangover 2), the unbeatable city views are enough of a reason to book this high-rise. Neighborhood: RatchathewiThings to do nearby: Jim Thompson House Museum, Victory Monument

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Unique design, open-air living, stylish bathrooms

Neighborhood: RattanakosinThings to do nearby: Phra Sumen Fort, Khao San Road, The Marble Temple

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Bangkok?

Chinatown and Talat Noi are always my go-to neighborhoods when I'm in Bangkok. They are full of fun, trendy bars, restaurants, and cafés worth spending some time wandering around. Sukhumvit is a great neighborhood for first-timers, with plenty of restaurant options, rooftop bars, and access to the MRT.

When is the best season to visit Bangkok?

Many people suggest that the best time to visit Bangkok is at the end of the rainy season—October through December—before the smog gets bad in January. March to May is the hottest time to visit, so it may be best to avoid if you don't do well in the heat, but I highly recommend planning a trip around Songkran (April 13–15), a.k.a. Thai New Year. It's known for hosting the world's largest water fight, and in my opinion, is one of Asia's best festivals.

#6211. Singapore Airlines Could Have Made Business Class Look Like This. Why Did It Choose Black And Yellow?

For some backstory, you may wish to read my earlier coverage on the seat, namely that CEO Goh Choon Phong has now stated that Singapore Airlines is open to rethinking the design.

> Read More: Singapore Airlines CEO May Rethink New Business Class Colors, And He Should

But are we really making a big deal about nothing?

“A yellow strip. A color palette. My god, seriously? Do you all stand there and stare at the seat for hours to gain some sort of energy transference? Personally, I sit down on it, eat the food, sleep and arrive somewhere I need to be. It’s a tiny cocoon of transport. Not a hotel room. Yes, I want comfort and decent things to pass the time. But anyone who obsesses over feeling less comfortable given a yellow stripe needs to seriously assess priorities.”

I understand that sentiment and agree that the comfort and quality of the seat, bedding, food, and drinks is far more important the color of the seat. Even so, the issue is that Singapore Airlines prides itself on the small details and the current mockup looks like a sloppy and callous oversight.

That’s certainly a matter of opinion, but what strikes me is that “the internet” has had a field day creating alternate design schemes. Look at this collage of alternatives, for examples:

A post shared by Dennis Chong (@dennischongofficial)

Every one of those strikes me as preferable to the chosen design and some look downright luxe and in the rich tradition of Singapore Airlines. This one is my favorite:

People are joking about what’s next, wondering if we might soon see new flight attendant uniforms to replace the sarong kebaya?

(Ironically, these looks like Starlux uniforms, which BMW/Designworks also designed).

I’ll leave it here, but I’d still really like to know the thought process that drove this seat design. Who agreed that this was a great new design, especially when it truly looks like Scoot, your low-cost subsidiary?

I’m still betting that SIA is going to scrap the black/yellow design and come up with something new, but that’s about as theoretical at this point as the “new uniforms” above.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Is this the most important thing in life? Obviously not. Has no impact on my life.

But it’s just a complete and abject failure of maintaining a luxury brand. A case study in stupidity. And sorry folks, branding matters.

The shame of it is that what looks like a beautiful new first class design has basically been completely ignored in favor of commenting on this spectacular failure. “Here’s our new profit center – great news, we made it look cheap and bland and just like our low cost airline” is the sentiment that is being put forward. That’s unbelievable!

This wasn’t a complicated assignment. The fact that they bungled it so badly is incredible. Someone at the airline will surely be held accountable for this, whether the internet thinks that’s fair or not.

Given that BMWs are the most super-mega-fugly vehicles on the road, it’s no surprise that this design is a total flop. That said, the mystery of why SQ management signed-off on it does still remain.

What in the world is the basis of the new yellow stripe and gray design? Is it some type of “ode to Spirit Airlines”? Certainly not aligned with a premium product. Singapore Airlines was a special experience. It’s going to be difficult to watch Singapore Airlines’ Bud Light moment.

As soon as you apply for a credit card, your application is processed by a computer. You’ll typically receive one of three responses: immediate approval, some form of “pending” status or denial.

Receiving instant approval doesn’t guarantee that you can begin using your card immediately. If you receive instant approval, you may be able to view your card number right away; otherwise, you’ll usually need to wait until your physical card arrives in the mail before you can begin using it.

It can take five to 10 business days to get a new credit card after approval. However, that timeframe varies by card and issuer. For instance, American Express offers overnight shipping for its top-tier cards. Some issuers offer expedited shipping on request, but there’s no guarantee. You may need to pay when requesting expedited shipping from some banks (including Barclays).

Getting approved for a new credit card is exciting, but waiting a week or more for it to arrive in the mail isn't. Fortunately, some issuers let you start using your new card immediately after approval, either by providing an instant card number or by allowing you to add your card to a digital wallet.

That instant access can give you a head start on meeting the welcome bonus spending requirement, since the clock starts ticking as soon as your account is approved — not when your physical card arrives. It can also come in handy if you need to make a purchase right away, whether you're booking travel or taking advantage of a 0% introductory APR offer. For cobranded store credit cards, you may also receive a discount on your purchases, starting as soon as you use the card.

Here's a look at which major credit card issuers offer instant card numbers, digital wallet access or both.

Some issuers provide an instant card number, while others, like Chase, instead let eligible cardholders add their new card to a digital wallet immediately after approval. Both options let you start using your card before the physical version arrives.

While there are too many cards to list that offer instant card numbers or access, here are six of our top picks.

American Express provides your new account number immediately after your online application is approved, provided your identity can be verified.

The instant card number will be the same as the physical card you’ll get in the mail, but the four-digit card identification number on the front of the card will be different. Because of that, you may want to wait to set up recurring payments.

Note that instant card numbers for some cobranded cards may only be used with the cobranded company (like Delta, Hilton or Marriott).

In addition to instant numbers for new cardmembers, Amex gives existing cardmembers access to their card information when ordering replacement cards.

Most Amex personal and business cards offer instant card numbers; notable exclusions include the Amazon Business Card and the Amazon Business Prime Card.

#6209. How a Trip to India Helped Me Find Peace With a Life-Changing Diagnosis

After spending nearly 25 years away, Tina Aswani-Omprakash, 43, finally traveled back to India, confronting long-held fears about traveling with Crohn’s disease. Along the way she reconnected with her roots, her family, and the food she had spent years afraid to eat. Following more than 20 surgeries and years of debilitating illness, going on the trip was a hard-won milestone for Aswani-Omprakash, made possible through careful preparation and her doctors’ support. Involving everything from exploring historic palaces and temples to meeting some relatives for the first time, the experience reminded her how travel can help us feel connected to culture and live life to the fullest. Here is Aswani-Omprakash’s story, as told to health writer Katie Camero.

The tuk-tuk ride up the Chamundi Hills near Mysuru, India, took about half an hour. My husband, brother-in-law, and some of my colleagues were split between two rickshaws, winding our way up a massive hill toward the Chamundeshwari Temple. I used to love taking tuk-tuks as a kid, but at age 41 I found that the ride felt like so much more than a fun adventure.

I could feel the air on my face, and I remember thinking, I can’t believe it, but I’m really doing this. After over 20 surgeries and some near-death experiences, I had somehow worked up the courage to travel and live my life again.

Gopuram of Sri Chamundeshwari Temple, Chamundi Hill, Mysore, Karnataka, South India

Since childhood I’ve experienced a lot of what doctors call extraintestinal manifestations, which are symptoms that occur when an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects parts of the body outside the gut. I dealt with issues like severe joint pain and eye issues alongside constipation and GERD, but at the time doctors didn’t think to refer me to a gastroenterologist. The discomfort and unpredictability of my condition meant I was always scared to travel, even if it was just a road trip.

The last time I visited my family in India was in 2000 at age 16. We took a day trip from New Delhi to the Taj Mahal and ended up eating street food because we were starving. We all got sick, but I fared so much worse than the others and lost about 20 pounds in the weeks that followed because I was so ill. I eventually was diagnosed with IBD—specifically, ulcerative colitis—in 2006. (Although later I learned I actually had a different type of IBD.) Nearly two years later, my husband, who was my boyfriend at the time, took me to Mexico and we both came down with traveler’s diarrhea after eating some sliced fruit. He threw it all up and recovered just fine, but it took me months to get better.

What followed was a lot of pain, shame, and silence. I worked on Wall Street at the time as a financial-services compliance officer, and it was very tough to figure out the diagnosis, accept it, and try to get on medication while navigating such a stressful career. I was on disability for many years before I eventually had to stop working. I didn’t know what to do with my life because I truly thought this disease and the complications associated with it would kill me.

Over two years, my condition went from mild to severe. During this time I experienced severe bleeding, weight loss, and other debilitating symptoms. I finally had my colon removed on July 4, 2008—which I often call my very own Independence Day. However, complications from this operation, as well as my IBD itself, required me to have dozens of additional operations including one to create a permanent ileostomy in 2011. It was through this process that I learned I actually have Crohn’s disease, another type of IBD.

It wasn’t until late 2024 that my doctors finally gave me the green light to travel to India—and I was terrified. The extra-long flight plus cuisines that include many trigger foods for my condition created a hurdle I worried was impossible to overcome. Although I had taken a few trips around the U.S. and Europe since my diagnosis, I had not conquered my fears of traveling back to India and enjoying the foods my family and I love without getting sick.

After all this time, I thought I couldn’t do this because of my Crohn’s disease. Yet there I was almost 25 years later. I did it—albeit with lots of preparation.

My doctors did an intestinal ultrasound and other tests to make sure nothing was brewing in my gut, and they gave me antibiotics, steroids, and probiotics in case I had a flare-up or bad case of traveler’s diarrhea. My husband and I also booked a hotel, which our relatives didn’t love, but it gave me easy access to filtered water (tap water could have been contaminated with harmful bacteria that could make me really sick) and a private bathroom in case I needed to make frequent trips overnight, along with other perks that kept us feeling safe and comfortable. I stayed clear of street vendors and only ate hot foods to reduce my chances of getting ill.

Even with those restrictions I enjoyed delicious, authentic food. In Mysuru, there’s a restaurant called MTR that offers South Indian cuisine like dosas, which I love. Though the lentil soup they come with can be a little spicy (a common IBD trigger), you can ask for a plain dosa with potatoes inside, which actually works pretty well for people with IBD. It’s a good way for us to enjoy the local cuisine while avoiding a flare-up.

Though it may seem like a lot of work, it honestly felt like such a huge accomplishment to go back to where my family is from and connect with my culture and relatives, some of whom I’d never met before, without getting sick.

However, it took a lot to get to that point. I faced many cultural challenges, not just during my journey to a diagnosis but also to starting treatment. My family survived the 1947 partition of India and Pakistan—my relatives were displaced from Pakistan and became refugees in India. As a result my family lost their trust in the West, and they certainly did not trust Western medicine. My condition got more severe than it needed to because my family was so against medicine or surgery. Marriageability and how others will perceive the family is also something my community worries about a lot. So I had to consider how my diagnosis would impact my sibling’s ability to find partners.

I felt a lot of fear as well because my dad died when I was 8 years old from Crohn’s disease that turned into colorectal cancer. Despite having this family history, I had to do a ton of self-advocacy to finally get the colonoscopy that started to give me much-needed answers and treatment options.

Through all of this I’ve learned that fear is just a mindset and we can accomplish whatever we want if we believe in ourselves. It also really takes a certain mindset to travel such a long distance and eat foods you haven’t been able to eat in so many years without feeling completely terrified you’re going to get sick.

Because of the stigmas I faced in my own journey with IBD, I co-founded, alongside other patient advocates and clinicians, the Strategic Alliance for Intercultural Advocacy in GI, a nonprofit that offers culturally sensitive resources for patients with GI conditions, caregivers, and health care providers to improve treatment and access to care. Many patients I speak with ask why I push past my comfort zone through my travels. My answer is simple: It makes me feel alive. With everything I went through in my 20s and 30s with this disease, I felt like I wasn’t really living. But when you go through so much disability, all you want to do is feel alive again.

Of course, trips like these aren’t feasible for everyone with inflammatory bowel disease. But if you start slowly, you might just surprise yourself. Growing with and owning your chronic illness is a process, and travel has helped me with that immeasurably.

#6208. My SAS Flight Attendant Wore A Greenland Flag To Send Americans A Message. I Agreed, But Not With His Approach

On my recent SAS flight from Chicago to Copenhagen, the purser wore a Greenland flag pin. When I asked about it, he explained that he wanted to make a statement, especially on flights to the United States. I agreed with the statement. But that does not mean I thought his uniform was the appropriate place to make it.

I mentioned an interesting flag pin in my account of our excellent SAS Business Class flight from Chicago to Copenhagen. Here is the story.

The purser was working my side of the aircraft, and I noticed a Greenland flag pinned to his uniform. Naturally, I was curious, especially considering I had just been there.

I asked whether he was from Greenland. He was not. Did he speak Greenlandic? No.

“To send a statement, especially on flights to the U.S.”

Well, there was my answer. This was a deliberate political message, and he was quite candid about it.

Let me be clear: I find the Trump administration’s saber-rattling over Greenland among its most offensive actions.

Denmark is a NATO ally. Threatening to take control of territory within the Kingdom of Denmark is an appalling way to treat a partner. Greenlanders also have a right to determine their own future. I understand why someone working for a Scandinavian airline would feel strongly about this. I do too. Sometimes the only way to deal with a bully is to stand up to him.

Thankfully, diplomacy has produced a more constructive path. The United States, Denmark, and Greenland signed a security agreement in September that recognizes Danish sovereignty and Greenlandic self-determination while strengthening Arctic security.

Our flight took place before Greenland’s parliament ratified the agreement on November 3. Denmark’s parliamentary vote is scheduled for November 19, so the ratification process is not yet complete.

I cautiously welcome that progress. Cooperation with an ally should have been the approach all along.

I have criticized political flag pins before, including Palestinian flag pins on Delta Air Lines and a similar incident on an American Airlines flight operated by SkyWest.

My position has been that a crew uniform should not become a platform for an employee’s personal political advocacy. I cannot abandon that position because this time I happen to agree with the cause.

A Greenland flag is not inherently a political protest. It can signify someone’s home or heritage. A flag or badge might also serve an airline-approved purpose, such as identifying a language spoken.

Here, however, I did not have to speculate about his intent. I asked, and he told me. He wanted to send a message, particularly to an American audience.

Sorry, but I take issue with that. Just wear the uniform as prescribed so everyone looks…uniform. The airline should determine what belongs on it. Individual employees should not decide which geopolitical causes deserve an exception.

I have not established whether SAS permits this particular pin, so I am not claiming a confirmed uniform-policy violation. My objection is to using the uniform for the purpose he described.

This did not change my assessment of the flight. We enjoyed excellent food, slept very well, and received attentive service. I have already praised the crew, including this purser who made a great cappuccino, and that praise stands.

Nor do I think a small pin requires turning an otherwise enjoyable journey into a confrontation…it was not my fight to wage.

But it is worth discussing precisely because I sympathized with him. Consistency is easy when you dislike the message. The more useful test comes when someone expresses a view you share. If I want political advocacy kept off crew uniforms, that has to apply here too. Otherwise, my position amounts to allowing the messages I like while objecting to everyone else’s.

My SAS purser wore a Greenland flag pin and openly acknowledged that he wanted to make a statement, especially on flights to the United States.

I understood his frustration and agreed with the underlying sentiment. I still do not think his uniform was the right place to express it. He helped deliver an excellent flight. I would happily fly with him again, but hopefully next time he’ll leave his Greenland pin at home.

#6207. United Clears Halfway Mark on Starlink Rollout

Starlink satellite internet service is now available on more than half of United Airlines’ daily flights, the carrier announced Thursday.

The airline said it accelerated Starlink installations ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period. It expects to fly an average of 500,000 people per day between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1.

Customers can use United’s Starlink Wi-Fi tracker to check whether their upcoming flight is equipped with the service up to three days before their departure.

United selected Starlink as its onboard wireless internet provider in 2024. It first installed the technology on its regional jets and is now working on its long-haul widebody fleet.

Starlink Wi-Fi is free for MileagePlus members.

United expects to have Starlink on nearly 64% of daily flights by the end of the year. Installations should be complete by the end of 2027, officials said.

#6206. Half Cruise, Half Cargo Ship? What It's Like to Sail French Polynesia Aboard a Local Freighter

It’s certainly a romantic notion to hop a freighter and sail to the distant South Pacific. One could spend days at sea staring at nothing but seabirds and cargo pallets, waking up to the sound of those pallets being offloaded onto a tiny concrete wharf, meeting a community nestled among palms. One could take the day to hike or tour the island, or feast on fresh catches with the locals, while the offloaded pallets are filled with grapefruits, dried coconut husks, and flowers to be sold elsewhere—Tahiti, perhaps.

It might come as a surprise to know that one company has been offering dedicated cruises built around that very premise for over 40 years. In French Polynesia, the locally owned cruise line Aranui Cruises offers combination passenger and cargo services from Papeete, Tahiti, to the dramatically jagged volcanic pitons and pastoral scenes of the Marquesas Islands.

Fatu Hiva in the Marquesas Islands has no airport and is only accessible by sea.

The idea is simple: a ship operates a cargo service to the remote islands (two of them, Fatu Hiva and Tahuata, have no airport and are only accessible by sea), and while the inbound cargo of soft drinks, groceries, building supplies, and even racing canoes is unloaded in the port, the passengers can use the time to go touring. In March 2026, I joined one such sailing, onboard the purpose-built Aranui V to see exactly what the 12-night, nearly-thousand-mile journey to the Marquesas looks like.

I like to refer to the vessel as the “mullet ship”— cargo up front, cruise in the back. During the voyage, when I wasn’t swimming in the onboard pool, or enjoying a cocktail from the bar, I filled my days with lectures Dr. Carole S. Ivory, professor emerita from Washington State University, who specializes in the study of Marquesan culture and art.

I got to witness that culture up close on Aranui’s included shore excursions. The experiences were visits to archaeological sites and volcanic pitons by car on Nuku Hiva, or various organized hikes on several of the other islands. There are also optional excursions for an additional fee, like the scenic drive between two sides of the island on Fatu Hiva. The drive, which traced a narrow mountain road between villages, offered spectacular vistas from the sea cliffs and, to rejoin the ship, a bonus sunset barge ride—a worthy add-on.

The Aranui V ship is a passenger cruise in the front and a cargo ship in the back.

Local residents hired by Aranui guide passengers in their personal cars as these tiny islands have no buses. On tiny Ua Huka, our mahu driver (a person of third-gender common in Polynesia) wearing a red flowered dress and straw hat, spent the day chatting with passengers and eating. And oh, how we ate! Baguette sandwiches during a morning stop at a craft center. A plate of chow mein from the snack bar at the botanical garden. A tour-of-the-island plate from the buffet heaped with coconut milk-roasted goat, the raw fish salad poisson cru, steamed taro, rice, and magenta-colored mashed banana swimming in sweet condensed coconut milk.

On each of the islands, we passengers from the Aranui V were greeted with local musicians and artisans, typically in a community pavilion. The Marquesas are noted for their skilled carvers, working in both wood and bone to create intricately decorated bowls, decorative canoe paddles, and jewelry. Carvers also work in stone called te ke’a pua (flower stone), also known as garnet phonolite, a polished volcanic rock that has the natural appearance of being covered in crystalline flowers. The rocks themselves are found on the island of Ua Pou, and are worked into a variety of shapes: ornamental fish hooks, decorative whales and birds, and pestles used to smash taro called kea tuki popoi.

Unlike most cruise lines, which have multinational crews, Aranui instead runs a local cargo service that just happens to have a large international tourism component. This means all of the onboard crew are Polynesians, many of them originally from the Marquesas themselves. The service is friendly and informal, and I was often greeted on a first-name basis. A couple of the crew recognized me from my previous sailing to another island group, already some four years hence.

The passenger half of the ship has basic amenities like a pool and cocktail bar.

Aranui also doesn’t enforce the same separation between passengers and crew that is prevalent on other ships—passengers and crew can freely mingle. After dinner, many crew members and officers end up in the bar for nightcaps right alongside the passengers. On my previous voyage with Aranui, to the Austral Islands, I joined an impromptu card game in the onboard pearl boutique and watched the head of housekeeping handily clean out the ship’s captain over the course of several hands of poker, all while we and the silken strands of Tahitian Pearls in the display cases bore witness.

When my only pair of sandals broke alighting from the landing craft on Ua Huka, Aranui staff directed me to the ship’s French doctor, who fixed it with tape from his medical bag. “Come back later onboard,” he said, “and we’ll do surgery on the shoe.” While I waited, I took great amusement with a large notice on the door of the ship’s infirmary, warning that many of the fruits served onboard and in the islands have “diuretic and laxatif (sp) effect,” urging passengers to consume in moderation. I wondered how many passengers had visited the infirmary over the years with the same complaint before they felt the need to put up a sign.

At the end of our stop on Ua Huka, we all gathered on the deck of Aranui V. We still had calls on the islands of Rangiroa and Bora Bora scheduled, but it was time to bid our goodbyes to the Marquesas in a traditional manner. A member of the onboard staff invoked a prayer of thanks for the voyage and fond farewell to these magnificent islands, which we did with armfuls of local flowers and plants cast into sunset-dappled sea to watch float ashore.

That, however, wasn’t the lasting image of the Marquesas for me. For weeks after my trip, I awoke each morning in a home that seemed suddenly foreign, recalling the smell of the straw hats, the taste of the baked banana, the green of the mountains, the red floral dress of the snacking mahu, and the pallets of coconuts and grapefruits stacked on the tiny wharf.

#6205. FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop, But The Airline Meltdown Is Far From Over

The FAA halted departures nationwide Friday afternoon, November 13, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Friday evening that the system had reopened at 8:15 pm ET.

That is welcome news for everyone waiting to travel. It does not, unfortunately, put aircraft and crews back where they need to be…

During the evening press conference, Duffy attributed the disruption to aging air traffic control communications equipment that became overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials were also examining how older equipment interacts with newer technology. That, of course, is a preliminary explanation, not a completed technical investigation. We still await a detailed account of what triggered the failure and why the system could not absorb it without such an extraordinary interruption.

Duffy warned that restoring airline operations would take time. The government and airlines would try to move flights Friday night, with recovery efforts continuing Saturday.

Mullin offered a more reassuring assessment of the security question:

“We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack.”

There has also been speculation about the FAA’s newly introduced SMART traffic-management tool. Its developer, Air Space Intelligence, denied that its software or integration caused the ground stop.

I would wait for the technical findings before assigning blame to a particular product or contractor, though the timing is certainly suspicious.

By 8 pm ET, FlightAware showed more than 10,000 delays and 5,000 cancellations involving U.S. flights.

The operational problem is obvious: a flight that could not depart may leave another airport without the aircraft needed for its next departure. Crews can reach duty limits while waiting. Passengers miss connections, and the remaining seats fill quickly.

Lifting the restriction allows airlines to begin untangling that mess, but of course does not instantly resolve it. Expect continued disruption tonight and check Saturday flights carefully too…this could go well into the busy Thanksgiving travel week.

The Department of Transportation explains that passengers are entitled to a refund when an airline cancels a flight and they decline the alternatives offered, regardless of the reason for cancellation. Qualifying significant delays also trigger refund rights when passengers choose not to travel.

Among the qualifying changes are scheduled arrival delays of at least three hours on domestic itineraries or six hours on international itineraries. You do not have to accept a voucher instead of a refund when a refund is owed.

That refund right is separate from whether the airline must pay for your hotel or dinner.

The FAA has lifted its nationwide departure restriction after a communications outage brought U.S. air travel to a halt Friday. Duffy pointed to overloaded older equipment, and Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Flights can resume, but the recovery will take longer. Check your individual itinerary, use any applicable waiver, and understand your refund rights before accepting an alternative that no longer works for you.

The FAA just froze every departure in the US over a communications failure at air traffic control centers. Here is what we know and what to do right now.

This is the kind of alert nobody in travel wants to see on a Friday afternoon. The FAA has ordered a nationwide ground stop for every airport in the country, effective 3:54 p.m. Eastern, according to the Air Traffic Control System Command Center as reported by Gizmodo.

The notice to operators is blunt. It cites “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” and says “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice,” per WCVB. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis.

Aircraft already in the air are not being ordered down immediately and can continue to their destinations, according to Reuters reporting cited by IBTimes. The hold applies to departures.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy put the cause in plain terms on X: a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” He added that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” Those centers handle high-altitude, en route traffic across the country, so a problem there is not a local hiccup. It touches nearly every flight plan in the system.

There is one wrinkle worth flagging. An FAA spokesperson described the problem as affecting “multiple” centers, while Duffy said “all,” per Gizmodo. Just before the national order, both Chicago airports were placed under a ground stop for an “equipment outage,” according to NBC Chicago. The government has not provided further detail, and as of this writing (5:12pm EST) nobody official has said whether a cyber event has been ruled in or out. I would not speculate in either direction until the FAA does.

The timing is awkward. Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize air traffic control communications, and the FAA and White House have asked for another $30.1 billion, as IBTimes notes. That money has not been applied to a solution yet so it’s unclear as to whether a future system would be able to avoid such a critical infrastructure system.

Extremely. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, according to the AP via ABC7. Reuters counts it as only the second nationwide halt of departures since September 11, 2001.

That 2023 event came from the failure of the NOTAM system, which pilots rely on for safety notices. The FAA lifted that order just before 9 a.m. Eastern, but the damage was done: more than 3,700 flights were delayed and more than 640 canceled, per the AP report at the time. That stop hit on a Wednesday morning. This one hit a Friday afternoon heading into a weekend, with aircraft and crews about to be stranded out of position. Even a short pause will ripple into Saturday.

For what it’s worth, SpaceX just started its launch channel ahead of a 5:45pm EST planned launch in which it will “double catch” both the booster and Starship. Space launches likely have its own windows but cross shared airspace.

If you are flying tonight, do not head to the airport on faith. Check your airline app first. Airports themselves are deferring to carriers, with Boston Logan telling passengers to “check with their airlines for the latest flight updates,” per WCVB. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey could not even say whether planes were leaving JFK, according to Gizmodo. However, this amount of departures will take a long time to untangle and you’re unlikely to get out this evening.

Rebook if you can, and do it right now. The first people to grab the remaining seats on tomorrow morning’s flights are the ones who get out. If you have a cruise departure or a nonrefundable hotel tied to tonight’s flight, call the supplier now rather than after midnight. From the agency side, this is exactly when a travel advisor earns their keep, juggling the hotel, the ship, and the airline while you wait in line.

Keep your receipts for meals and hotels too. Airline policies on what they cover vary, and having the paperwork makes any claim easier. It’s unlikely the airlines will cover for an event out of their control but credit cards used to purchase this travel might.

A nationwide ground stop driven by a communications failure at the centers that run en route traffic is about as serious as an operational problem gets. The FAA has offered no time for departures to resume, and even when they do, Friday night’s schedule is effectively gone and Saturday will be messy. The bigger story will come after the planes are moving again: what failed, why there was no backup to keep traffic flowing, and whether the billions already earmarked for modernization are arriving fast enough.

We will update as the FAA and the airlines share more.

Where has the president been the last few hours of this crisis? Hiding in a beverage cart?

Frontier Airlines not giving a passenger what he paid for is not a political issue. This is. The current administration inherited a series of disasters: an Oval Office that was insufficiently gilded. A public golf course that was excessively public. A reflecting pool that was not blue enough. An East Wing without enough marble. A memorial to a former president that ignored the needs of the current one, and a traffic circle that was missing an Arch. Plus also an air traffic system from before color TV, which is so strained that there are now regular near-accidents. The President has dedicated vast amounts of energy and political capital to some, but not all, of these problems. How he has prioritized is his to explain.

Flights to Europe are operating with slight delays. AA’s JFK to LHR and MIA to LHR departures are in the air. Just two examples. It seems to be affecting domestic flights in large part, rather than some international flights.

My flight on Friday evening was one of the ones impacted. We took off right before the ground stop was officially lifted. Perhaps because it was an international flight over the Atlantic.

Im anxious to see which airlines recover the fastest and which dont

Call it the ultimate Nile River cruise experience.

River cruise giant Viking has unveiled an epic new itinerary that sails the entire 600-mile stretch of the waterway between Cairo in the north and Aswan in the south.

Dubbed the Grand Nile Journey, Viking's 19-day trip revives a longer Nile cruise route that dates back to the late 1800s, when paddle steamers carried travelers from Cairo on the 465-mile journey south to Luxor, home to some of ancient Egypt's most famous temples and burial grounds.

From there, the vessels would continue to Aswan, another 130 miles to the south, with stops at ancient temples along the way.

Nowadays, most Nile River sailings skip the first 465 miles of this historic route, with ships only traveling along the 130-mile stretch of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan. Passengers reach the ships by flying from Cairo to Luxor, typically after a few days exploring Cairo.

Related: The ultimate guide to Nile river cruises and cruisetours

Only a handful of vessels currently operate a longer itinerary of the sort that Viking has announced — and none at the luxury level for which Viking is known on the river.

Kicking off in 2028 but available to book now, Viking's new Grand Nile Journeys will begin with a three-night stay at a luxury hotel in Cairo (the line often puts guests in the elegant Fairmont Nile City, along the banks of the river). Then, passengers board the line's one-of-a-kind, all-suite vessel Viking Ra for the 14-night journey south to Aswan.

The voyages will include stops at ancient sites along the 450-mile stretch from Cairo to Luxor that most Nile River travelers never see, including the 4,600-year-old Meidum Pyramid near Beni Suef and the striking cliffside Noble Tombs of Beni Hasan.

Other rare stops will include a visit to Tell el-Amarna, the once-lost royal desert capital founded by the Pharaoh Akhenaten, and the Abydos Temple, famous for drawings of ancient pilgrims to the sacred Festival of Osiris.

After a week traveling south along this lesser-visited stretch of the Nile, the Viking Ra will arrive in Luxor for another week of travel southward along the more popular parts of the river.

An extended stop in Luxor will bring visits to the temples of Luxor and Karnak, the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Seti I at Abydos.

Additional stops include the Temple of Horus in Edfu and the Temple of Philae near Aswan, among other sites in this area.

Related: The 5 best destinations you can visit on a Viking ship

By following this long route from Cairo to Aswan, the new Grand Nile Journeys will echo the long Nile sailing that Agatha Christie made famous in her 1937 novel "Death on the Nile." She wrote the book after taking one of the long journeys in 1933 on the Thomas Cook & Son luxury paddle steamer S.S. Sudan.

The first few days of each of the new Grand Nile Journeys in Cairo will include visits to the Great Pyramids of Giza, the Great Sphinx and the Grand Egyptian Museum.

At the end of the trip, passengers will also spend a final night at a hotel in Cairo before departing.

Passengers can extend their trips with optional pre- and postcruise land tours that include an extra two-night stay in Cairo and a four-night, fully guided excursion to nearby Jordan for visits to the Dead Sea, Petra and Amman.

While dating back to the late 1800s, when Thomas Cook & Son introduced "rapid steamers" that sailed the Nile from Cairo to Aswan, such longer Nile itineraries continued to be common until 1994, when the Egyptian government officially closed the 465-mile stretch of the river between Cairo and Luxor to overnight passenger ships due to security worries. Low water levels and shifting sandbars in the river also played a role.

After nearly 20 years of closure, the Egyptian government reopened the Cairo-to-Luxor stretch of the river to cruise vessels in 2012, following extensive river dredging, irrigation upgrades and major security overhauls. But long sailings from Cairo to Aswan have been slow to rebound.

Among the handful of other companies offering such trips is Movenpick Hotels & Resorts, which markets 14-night sailings from Cairo to Aswan on the 52-cabin MS Darakum.

#6203. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly A KC-135 Stratotanker?

First flown in 1956, the Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker has spent decades refueling US military aircraft in flight. Despite its age, it remains a major part of the United States Air Force's tanker fleet, supporting fighters, bombers, and other aircraft on missions around the world. But how many people does it actually take to operate an aircraft responsible for such an important job? The answer raises some interesting questions about how the Stratotanker was designed and how its crew responsibilities have changed over the years.

The KC-135's crew arrangement is not quite as straightforward as it might seem. Its refueling missions require close coordination between the cockpit crew and the operator responsible for transferring fuel, while other missions can bring additional personnel aboard. Its history also raises questions about why it differs from commercial aircraft of the same era and how its crew compares with that of the newer KC-46 Pegasus. Looking at these differences helps explain how the Stratotanker has continued to serve for so many decades.

For a normal refueling mission, according to the US Air Force's KC-135 fact sheet, the standard crew is three. The KC-135R and KC-135T normally operate with a three-person crew: a pilot, a copilot, and a boom operator. The two pilots occupy the cockpit, while the boom operator works at the rear of the aircraft, controlling the flying boom used to transfer fuel to the receiving aircraft. The National Museum of the US Air Force confirms the same crew number for the KC-135R. The more interesting question is how those three people divide the work.

The workload is substantial. The Air Force fact sheet gives the Stratotanker a maximum takeoff weight of 322,500 pounds (146,285 kg), with up to 200,000 pounds (90,719 kg) of transfer fuel and, depending on configuration, as much as 83,000 pounds (37,648 kg) of cargo. The aircraft carries all of that on a wingspan of 130 feet, 10 inches (39.88 meters), yet the normal crew is still small enough to sit around a kitchen table.

That was not always the case. Early KC-135s carried four people, with a navigator joining the two pilots and boom operator, before advances in navigation and avionics removed that position from the standard crew. The aircraft has nevertheless remained in service for decades. According to Simple Flying, the Air Force still operates roughly 396 Stratotankers across active-duty wings, the Air National Guard and the Air Force Reserve.

More recent Air Force figures cited by the Government Accountability Office put the fleet at 373 aircraft as of early March 2026, before accounting for the losses and damage sustained during Operation Epic Fury against Iran. The Congressional Research Service later listed seven KC-135s as lost or damaged during the conflict. With hundreds of Stratotankers still in the inventory and the basic crew arrangement remaining central to their operation, the obvious next question is what each crew member is actually responsible for.

The three-person crew arrangement makes more sense once the KC-135's refueling system comes into view. Aerial refueling requires two aircraft to maintain close formation while a rigid boom connects them in flight. The Air Force lists the KC-135's maximum speed at 530 miles per hour (853 km/h) at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), although fuel transfer takes place at speeds appropriate to the aircraft involved. The receiving jet moves into position below and behind the tanker, the boom extends, and the final connection is made from the rear of the Stratotanker.

Each crew member has a specific responsibility. The pilot flies the tanker and maintains a stable flight path, while the copilot shares flying duties, handles communications and checklists, and monitors aircraft systems. At the back, the boom operator, an enlisted airman, controls the boom and guides its nozzle into the receiving aircraft. The National Museum of the US Air Force explains that the operator uses small wing-like control surfaces called ruddervators to steer the boom into position. Working from a prone position and looking through a window, the operator effectively flies the boom itself. The system can transfer nearly all the KC-135's usable fuel, while a drogue attachment can be fitted to support aircraft equipped with refueling probes. The arrangement has proved capable of some extraordinary missions.

The museum's KC-135R earned the Mackay Trophy for a sortie flown on May 31, 1967, after a Navy pilot was shot down in Southeast Asia and a rescue operation ran into fuel difficulties. Two US Navy Douglas KA-3 Skywarriors kept a pair of Vought F-8 Crusaders airborne, but both the tankers and the fighters were running low on fuel. The KC-135 crew began refueling the KA-3s while continuing to pass fuel to the F-8s. In effect, one tanker was refueling another tanker that was simultaneously refueling a fighter. The KC-135 subsequently provided additional fuel to two McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom fighters on its way to an alternative landing base.

Interestingly, although the KC-135 could operate with a basic crew of three, the aircraft involved in this award-winning mission carried four. Its crew consisted of Major John H. Casteel, aircraft commander; Captain Richard L. Trail, copilot; Captain Dean L. Hoar, navigator; and Master Sergeant Nathan C. Campbell, boom operator. This historical example illustrates the distinction between the aircraft's earlier four-person arrangement and its modern standard crew. The additional crew member was a navigator, not a flight engineer.

Here’s how the B-52’s crew works and why the United States Air Force wants fewer airmen.

The navigator's presence on earlier KC-135 missions helps explain how the tanker's crew evolved over time, but it also highlights a more fundamental difference between the aircraft and its civilian contemporaries: the absence of a dedicated flight engineer. The tanker was developed alongside the Boeing 707, and many airliners of the period used a third cockpit crewmember to monitor engines and systems. Yet Air Force records for the KC-135 identify pilots, a boom operator and, on earlier versions, a navigator.

The absence of a flight engineer from the standard KC-135 crew does not mean the aircraft never employed one. In a 2017 Air Force profile, Master Sgt. Robert Self was described as the service's last KC-135 flight engineer, following a career that included assignments on specialized NKC-135 and KC-135 aircraft used for testing and support programs. His responsibilities included operating the fuel panel, monitoring aircraft systems and advising the pilots. He also recalled that earlier KC-135 configurations had carried both flight engineers and navigators, positions that gradually disappeared as onboard computers and avionics became more capable.

Two pilots were always intended to occupy the front seats, with the boom operator handling refueling from the rear. Then the avionics changed. As reported by the National Guard in a story about Iowa's 185th, PACER CRAG brought compass, radar, and GPS improvements to the fleet by the early 2000s, while modern GPS removed the need for the navigator on standard missions. GlobalSecurity's overview of the program likewise notes that the commercial off-the-shelf upgrade eliminated the navigator requirement on most missions. The Simple Flying report mentioned earlier adds that digital flight decks and enhanced autopilots have further reduced the workload.

The tradeoff is workload. A base spokesman at Fairchild told the Spokane Journal that, while the upgrades were arriving,it basically meant more responsibility for the pilot and copilot. Navigation functions moved into the avionics, while some tasks previously handled by another crew member became part of the cockpit workload. This distinction is important when comparing the KC-135 with the Boeing KC-46, which was designed from the outset around a very different refueling station and a more modern approach to crew responsibilities.

The easiest way to see the difference is to look at the boom operator. On the KC-135, that person works at the rear of the aircraft and looks outside through a window. On the KC-46 Pegasus, there is no comparable window to look through. According to Air Mobility Command's KC-46A fact sheet, the Pegasus uses a fly-by-wire refueling boom and gives its Air Refueling Operator panoramic displays with wingtip-to-wingtip situational awareness. From that station, the operator controls the boom, centerline drogue, and wing aerial refueling pods.

The screen-based system was intended to offer advantages, but it also created problems that required a major redesign. The same fact sheet says that the Air Force and Boeing agreed in April 2020 on the final Remote Vision System design, known as RVS 2.0, after deficiencies had affected safe and effective refueling. The issue has not disappeared completely: as Simple Flying reported, the Pegasus still has refueling limitations with some US Air Force aircraft, including the FairchildA-10 Warthog, while Boeing works on boom and vision-system fixes. The KC-135's window may look primitive alongside the KC-46's cameras, but it also offers a remarkably direct view of the aircraft being refueled.

The contrast does not mean the KC-135 is about to disappear. According to Simple Flying, the Air Force originally planned to field 179 KC-46s, but that figure has since grown substantially. The current program calls for 263 Pegasus tankers, almost 100 more than the original requirement, as the service looks to replace much of its aging KC-135 fleet. As of early March 2026, the Air Force had 373 KC-135s and 103 KC-46As in its inventory, according to the Government Accountability Office. The Pegasus is the newer design, but the Stratotanker remains a major part of the force and is being kept in service for decades longer than originally intended. That creates an important question about the three-person crew: is it sufficient for every mission the aging tanker is now being asked to perform?

How many crew members does the V-22 Osprey need? The answer depends on the military service, the mission, and the demands of each variant.

The three-person crew is a starting point, not a fixed rule. The Air Force fact sheet notes that some missions require a navigator and that only a limited number of navigator suites are available for those specialized tasks. It is an uncommon arrangement today, but it shows why the published crew number needs a little context: the KC-135's staffing changes with the mission.

Aeromedical evacuation is the clearest example. The KC-135 can carry litter and ambulatory patients on patient support pallets, and the fact sheet says an aeromedical evacuation mission adds a basic medical crew of five: two flight nurses and three medical technicians. That number can change according to the patients being carried. In the basic configuration described by the Air Force, a hospital mission can therefore put eight crew members aboard before the patients themselves are counted.

For aeromedical evacuation, the KC-135's cargo compartment can be fitted with a stanchion litter system, allowing patients to travel on a secured litter rather than ordinary passenger seats. The system must be assembled and attached inside the aircraft by support personnel, while the medical team brings the equipment needed to monitor and care for patients during flight.

Another issue that is harder to solve with crew changes is age. The last KC-135 was delivered in 1965, so even the newest aircraft are now decades old. As reported by ExecutiveBiz, SNC has assembled a team with BAE Systems, Collins Aerospace and GE Aerospace to pursue the Air Force's KC-135 Center Console Refresh, a program aimed at replacing aging fuel-system equipment, flight displays and computing architecture. SNC announced the consortium in November 2026.

BAE would design the fuel management system to reduce pilot workload; Collins, which has supplied KC-135 avionics for more than three decades, would add new displays and computers built on an open architecture; and GE Aerospace would contribute avionics already flying on the KC-46 and Lockheed C-130 Hercules. The proposal also includes autothrottle capability, with performance projected from July 2028 through June 2038 and the award still anticipated. In other words, the same aircraft that learned to do without a navigator decades ago may soon get another set of tools designed to make the remaining crew's jobs easier.

The standard KC-135 Stratotanker crew consists of three people: a pilot, a copilot, and a boom operator. Earlier configurations commonly included a fourth crew member, a navigator, whose position gradually disappeared as navigation systems and avionics improved. Specialized missions can still require additional personnel, while aeromedical evacuation typically adds five medical crew members to the basic crew. Flight engineers also served aboard certain specialized KC-135 aircraft, but they were not part of the standard operational crew. The result is an aircraft that has retained its essential three-person operating arrangement while adapting to decades of technological change.

That makes the boom operator the most distinctive member of the crew. From the rear of the tanker, one person is responsible for the final connection between two aircraft moving in formation, doing it through a window that has been part of the KC-135's design for generations. The KC-46 approaches the same task from the opposite direction, replacing that view with cameras and displays. The basic mission has barely changed; the way the crew carries it out has.

The KC-135's story is not yet finished simply because the KC-46 is entering the force. Looking ahead, Air & Space Forces Magazine reports that the Air Force plans to keep the KC-135 until at least 2050, even as it considers a bridge tanker and a future Next-Generation Air-Refueling System. If the cockpit refresh moves forward, the old tanker could receive a substantially modernized flight deck under the program's 2028 to 2038 timeline. For a design that first flew in the 1950s, the next chapter may be less about adding people and more about giving the same three-person crew better tools for the job.

#6202. 10 Vacation Rentals Across North America For Your Next Family Reunion

Family reunions can be stressful. There’s much to consider, from dealing with a motley of personalities to making sure the kids are looked after. But things get much easier when you land on the perfect vacation rental, one in a crowd-pleasing location, with a spacious layout and plenty of amenities that will keep everyone happy. Whether you’re bringing the gang together for an outdoor adventure at Yosemite National Park, or seeking a laid-back sojourn in the Caribbean, the rentals on this list satisfy every kind of trip. Each featuring four bedrooms or more, these properties are sure to fit the entire clan with luxe amenities worth traveling for: think saltwater pools, golf simulators, and private beach access. What’s more, many are within the top 1% of guest reviews in their area, which means they’re loved by the people who have visited (and are often booked for return trips). Below, the best vacation rentals for family reunions across North America.

We've selected these listings based on ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 20Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 5.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private pool, proximity to beach, game room

Just steps away from Alys Beach, located on Scenic Highway 30A, this sunny and spacious six-bedroom home was designed for families: four king bedrooms with en suite bathrooms (one of which houses two extra twin beds); a bunk room with a double and four additional twin beds; and a queen with a trundle. There’s a game room, complete with ping-pong and Foosball tables, plus large-screen TVs. The little ones can enjoy amenities too, like mini cribs and pack-and-plays. If the family would rather swim at home, there’s a gorgeous heated pool for everyone to wade in, with sun loungers, an adjacent barbecue, and even a little tanning ledge for kids to take their first steps in the water.

Location: Inlet Beach, FloridaThings to do nearby: Seacrest Beach, Deer Lake State Park, Alys Beach

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Study area, in-unit washer/dryer, outdoor patio

Nantucket, with its pristine beaches and vibrant historic town, makes for an excellent family gathering. This classic, cedar-shingled home features an abundance of windows that bring in natural light, spotless interiors, and plainly chic furnishings. There are five bedrooms with high ceilings (some offer glimpses of the harbor), four full bathrooms, and a spacious kitchen. On the first floor, French doors open out to an outdoor entertainment area, with sectional seating, a dining table that seats 10, a gas grill, and an outdoor shower, all enclosed by a landscaped lawn—the perfect place for the group to kick back and relax.

Location: Nantucket, MassachusettsThings to do nearby: Nantucket Atheneum, Quaker Meeting House, Children's Beach

Number of guests: 20Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 6 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, proximity to ski resorts, golf simulator

This dreamy A-frame home in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands offers adventurous family members proximity to the slopes at Hidden Valley and Seven Springs resorts. With seven bedrooms spread across three floors, there’s enough space for 20 guests to spread out, plus a fully equipped kitchen, dedicated theater area, game room, and even a golf simulator. After a long day of activities, there’s no better place to relax tired muscles than the hot tub outside, fit for six, or the firepit, surrounded by cozy loungers. Keep in mind the area does get icy over the winter, so 4WD is recommended.

Location: Somerset, PennsylvaniaThings to do nearby: Hidden Valley Resort, Seven Springs Mountain Resort, Ohiopyle State Park

Number of guests: 20+Bed and bath: 9 bedrooms, 8.5 bathsWhy we love it: Gazebo, valley views, fireplace

Located in the heart of Ohio’s Amish country, Hillside Villa is a bucolic escape for the extended family. While the entire villa can be booked (check for availability on the “Premier House” option), you can also opt for individual units, from a deluxe room for two with a jetted hot tub to a junior room that sleeps up to four. Each comes with scenic views of the hills, along with shared kitchen access (coffee and tea maker provided). There are 55-inch flat-screen TVs too, along with features like fireplaces and porches. In the backyard, you’ll find a gazebo with a firepit, perfect for watching the sunset descend over the farm-filled valley.

Location: Millersburg, OhioThings to do nearby: Country Acres Mini Golf, Pro Football Hall of Fame, Belden Village Mall

Number of guests: 14Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Contemporary interior design, private lake access, barbecue

Offering 200 feet of private lakefront in Austin, this modern four-bedroom is a rare retreat. Ideal for a multigenerational family, it’s composed of a main house with two king bedrooms and a guesthouse with a king bedroom, plus a large bunk room with eight twin beds. Spend your days gliding along the lake on a kayak or paddleboard, floating on the 16-foot lily pad, or taking a hike through the surrounding Balcones Canyonland Preserve. End the fun on the two-story party dock, where you can enjoy a meal outside, with s’mores for dessert around the firepit.

Location: Austin, TexasThings to do nearby: Lake Austin, Sixth Street, University of Texas at Austin

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hiking trail access, pool table, forest views

This Yosemite home, with its breathtaking cathedral windows and stone fireplace, will offer the family a stay they won’t forget. The perfect place to retreat to after a day spent at Yosemite National Park, this four-bedroom is wonderfully western, with its hanging deer antlers, wooden furniture, and tons of colorful textiles. Your group can spread out between two queen beds, two twin beds, and two bunk beds (one with a trundle). Prepare meals in the fully equipped kitchen, then enjoy some family time at the dining table, which seats up to 10. Up in the loft, you’ll find a mini arcade, a number of board games, and a pool table.

Location: Yosemite National Park, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Yosemite National Park, Yosemite Valley, Yosemite Arch Rock Gate Entrance

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Mountain views, gym, wildlife sightings

Cozy, inviting, and lived-in, this Jackson Hole property is the ultimate mountain escape. Located in Spring Creek Ranch, the home is in a 1,000-acre ranch community, perched atop East Gros Ventre Butte, 800 feet above the valley floor. The first thing you’ll notice upon walking in is a kitchen and dining area that flows into the living room, with large windows overlooking the mountains. There are four bedrooms (three kings and one with two twin beds), each with views of the Tetons. Poke around the woods, watch a movie around the fireplace, and look out for elk.

Location: Jackson, WyomingThings to do nearby: Jackson Hole Valley, Jackson Hole Wildlife Safaris, Jackson Town Square

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Scenic views, in-unit washer/dryer, beach access

In Quebec City, the Saguenay Fjord stretches over 62 miles and is surrounded by dramatic granite cliffs. This charming, four-bedroom home will place you right in front of the action. Settle back on the front porch with your loved ones and watch the tides roll in, or take sunset walks along the beach. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need for meals at home, while the grand dining table looks out into the water. Outside, there’s a swing for little ones, plus a few Adirondack chairs for the adults to continue savoring the view.

Location: Saguenay, Quebec City, CanadaThings to do nearby: Saguenay River, Theatre du Palais Municipal, Okwari Le Fjord

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathroomsWhy we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, chef available upon request, beach access

Dreaming of a family reunion across the border? At this bungalow in Placencia, Belize, you’ll have the Caribbean Sea right at your doorstep. Ideal for two families, the four bedrooms (one king and three queens) are spread out in such a way that two of them have their own separate entrance. Spend your days soaking up the sun, swimming in the saltwater pool, gliding along the water on a stand-up paddleboard, or preparing a fresh lunch in the outdoor kitchen. And if you truly want to leave your worries at the door, in-house chef services are available upon request.

Location: Placencia, MexicoThings to do nearby: Placencia Beach, Placencia Pier, Maya Beach

Number of guests: 18Bed and bath: 8 bedrooms, 7 bathsWhy we love it: Panoramic windows, hot tub, in-unit washer/dryer

For extra-large families with great taste, this eight-bedroom beach house is a no-brainer, with jaw-dropping, panoramic views of Lake Michigan and plenty of luxe amenities, from a hot tub and game room to a heated pool. There are gorgeous design details throughout, like vaulted wooden ceilings and circular ship-style windows. Rooms are split between the main house and guest house, with two separate kitchens. Just an 11-minute walk from Saugatuck Dunes State Park, the house provides access to endless scenic trails. Bonus: It’s pet-friendly too.

Location: Saugatuck, MichiganThings to do nearby: Kalamazoo River, Saugatuck Dunes State Park, Oval Beach
