#6201. The Moment I Saw This Gorgeous Lake Como Airbnb, I Knew I Had to Plan a Trip to Perledo

Maybe it’s because I’m a dreamer, or maybe it's because I’m slightly impulsive, but whenever I'm planning a trip, I start by browsing Airbnb. I find it the easiest way to envision my time away, and I dropped the notion a long time ago that you don’t actually spend time in your accommodations. That's how I ended up finding myself in a teeny town called Perledo this past summer—my mom had always dreamed of visiting Lake Como for her birthday, so I decided to see what great accommodations I could find in the area for a visit in August, her birth month.

For a stay in Italy, if it’s sleek, minimalist, or modern, keep it away from me. I’m drawn to homes that feel like a reflection of the country I’m in—something uncommon with character and a story. So when I found this unbelievably charming rental in Perledo—a quiet village in the hills above Varenna, overlooking Lake Como—on the Airbnb platform, I booked it for my mom, sister, and I before we even had flights. I mean, look at it!

My family and I arrived in Lake Como on a scorching August day after spending seven days in Sardinia. After a flight, bus, train, and short taxi ride up and around the mountain, we were thrilled to land in our new home. A few days before our arrival, our host, Giulia (having the same name as her felt like a good omen to me!), helped us navigate getting to the apartment from the train, offering us multiple numbers for local taxis, as we hadn't wanted to rent a car. (I'm glad we went that route, because I wouldn't have wanted to deal with parking.)

Upon entering the home, after several trips up and down the stairs, we threw down our bags and immediately made our way onto the balcony. The sunlight beamed through the French doors with the mountains in the background, and the smell of crisp Alpine air made the three of us pause. Staring at the boats as they glided through the water, we all immediately forgot about the long journey it took to get there.

We discovered a bottle of red wine, taralli, and a bunch of Nespresso pods waiting for us on the kitchen table, and I was delighted to find the pantry filled with essentials—salt, pepper, olive oil, and vinegar. You know, those items you might need to complete a meal or a snack, but are annoying to buy on vacation.

The apartment felt warm from the sunlight, but also by design. The pearly walls, with green cabinets and warm wood accents, felt very grounding, like an extension of the atmosphere outside. The tile flooring in the living area reminded me of my cousin's house in Rome, and the pistachio-green-framed window in the bathroom opened wide for a clear picture of the mountains and lake.

After already spending a week with my mom and sister, I was ready for some space, so I opted for the sofa bed with a memory foam topper in the living room. The bed was already made, so it was easy to slip into the soft sheets for a nap after my shower. Throughout the stay, we were mindful not to let the hot water meter fall below a certain level, per Giulia's advice, but between the three of us, we rarely came close.

Giulia also gave us tons of information about the area, including ferry schedules, walking paths, and numbers for hairstylists (I'm always looking for a good blowout). Being able to communicate with her as a local resource felt like we had a personal tour guide with us at all times.

When we left the apartment on our first evening, we followed Giulia’s instructions to catch the complimentary Perledo Night Bus, a service provided by the town from 7 p.m. till midnight, to get to nearby Varenna, where we could grab the ferry to take us to other towns. Walking up and down the mountain, especially at night, would have been challenging and slightly dangerous, so we were happy to grab the shuttle, which was a 10-minute walk from our place.

Unlike Como town or Bellagio, Varenna is quieter, with restaurants that shut down around 9 p.m. Luckily, there are some places to eat and drink in Perledo too. For example, Bar Milano is where locals congregate for their morning espressos or evening nightcaps. For us, it was where we would grab our bus rides up and down the mountain, as well as breakfast (the apricot croissants are incredible).

The walk to Bar Milano was a deeply scenic experience for us—the sunlight glistening on the lake to our right; the lush green mountains dotted with homes to our left. We often noticed fountains and shrines to pray at on our journeys up and down, something consistent on most streets in the village. After arriving home with our breakfast every day, we would start our mornings slow, sitting on the balcony with our espressos and cornetti, taking in the postcard-perfect views of the lake. We often said hi to our neighbors just below us, families who were keen on enjoying the morning air too.

We made few plans for our days, except a reservation for my mom’s birthday lunch. We spent four hours indulging at Passalacqua, the boutique hotel in Moltrasio, and between the beauty of the space, the unhurried pace of the meal, and the kindness of the staff, it’s a memory we will all keep forever. Other afternoons were spent ferry hopping, exploring different towns. In Bellagio, it was imperative we walked down the most famous corridor—Salita Serbelloni. Filled with small artisanal shops and restaurants, it was here I bought a rosary necklace from a man named Filippo, the owner of Bellagio New Wave, a family business that has been in operation for over 100 years. He told me that he grew up above the building.

After days spent on our feet, ears buzzing from the large crowds, nothing was more serene than returning to the quiet of our apartment. Stepping off the shuttle and onto the street for our walk back to the Airbnb brought a sense of tranquility over our three days there, like we were truly going home. Being able to stare into the night sky, overlooking the stillness of the water while being hit with a slight breeze, offered a respite from the adventures of the day.

When I think of Lake Como, I think of two things: romance and luxury. Away from the noise but still close enough to the action, this Airbnb gave us a slice of that fantasy. I now recommend Perdolo to everyone. Safe to say, I’ll continue building my trips around great Airbnbs. The rest always figures itself out later.

#6200. FAA Lifts Multi-Hour Nationwide Ground Stop Linked To "Instability" Of Radar & ATC Communications

* Last Updated: 10:05 PM EST November 13, 2026 by Channing Reid

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a rare nationwide ground stop that halted operations at all airports late Friday. The ground stop was implemented by the agency due to communication failures affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. Citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns, the FAA suspended all departures in the multi-hour ground stop. International arrivals were handled individually while technicians investigated the disruption.

The FAA said "communication issues" impacted air traffic control (ATC) centers around the country on Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said late Friday that the cause of the ground stop was related to “instability" regarding radar and communications in the "TRACONS throughout the country.” Aviation watchdog JonNYC reported that the halt was not a “9/11 type of event,” which required flights to be forced to land at the closest airport available.

Simple Flying's Flight Tracker captured ATC first communicating to pilots that all departures had been stopped.

The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at around 8:30 PM EST. All flights are allowed to resume, but some warn it could take days before airlines can restore their normal schedules. The agency confirmed the lift in a statement around 10:00 PM EST.

"The safety of the flying public is always the FAA’s highest priority," it said. "The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming. Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."

Multiple sources have reported that the FAA's telecommunication infrastructure rebooted on Friday due to an update to a private communications network that handles connections between the US' nationwide ATC system. Amid the reboot, the system crashed, resulting in a communications outage, according to CBS News Political Reporter Olivia Rinaldi. The system is reportedly operated by L3Harris – the same company responsible for the security overhaul of the Air Force One bridge Boeing 747-8.

International flights are slowly resuming. According to Flightradar24, some eastbound transatlantic flights have been cleared to depart from airports across the Northeast.

The first flight from Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) also departed around 7:15 PM EST. Despite the gradual resumption, the ground stop still remains in effect, meaning all domestic flights have not been cleared to resume.

There is no evidence that the Microsoft outage that affected millions of people worldwide on Thursday is related to the ground stop.

"Microsoft has no indication that the FAA nationwide ground stop is related to the recent service disruption," an FAA spokesperson said in a statement obtained by NBC News.

Several major airports around the country issued statements and notices to passengers about the ground stop. Officials at Miami International Airport (MIA) told passengers to stay away from the airport until they confirm their flight's status with their airline.

"MIA is coordinating closely with airlines and safety and security partners to monitor evolving conditions, support affected passengers, and maintain operational readiness," the airport said in a statement. "Passengers are strongly urged NOT to come to MIA until they have confirmed directly with their airline that their flight is operating and have received updated travel instructions."

Friday's ground stop is the second nationwide halt since the September 11, 2001 attacks. The last time such action occurred was in early 2023 when the FAA's Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system failed. All departures were grounded for about an hour and a half before resuming. Investigators said that damage to a database file may have been the cause of the system failure.

Law enforcement officials say the ground stop is not the result of a cyberattack. However, personnel from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) around the country are monitoring the situation, according to CNN.

Friday's ground halt comes on the heels of the FAA rolling out a new AI system to manage air traffic. While it is not clear that the telecommunications outage was directly related, the agency has been criticized for implementing the system.

It is known as the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART), and "analyzes airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic airflows and identify potential conflicts before they occur," according to the FAA.

All airborne aircraft were allowed to continue flying until further notice. According to FlightAware, more than 6,500 flights are currently halted.

The FAA confirmed that the ground stop was implemented "out of an abundance of caution" in a statement.

"There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis."

Flightradar24 is reporting that more than 1,000 flights had already been canceled by 6:00 PM. Cirium data indicates that more than 11,000 flights were still set to depart across the US on Friday after the ground stop was put in place, so cancellations are expected to increase significantly as the evening progresses.

Ground controllers will also face growing difficulty as aircraft continue to land and none depart, putting pressure on already stressed infrastructure and increasingly scarce gate availability.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6199. 9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche

Any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward.

As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.

A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain

“I went [to the Basque Country] for the first time in 2013, but it was such a quick, rushed trip that I left feeling like I’d barely scratched the surface. I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. It’s inland cooking, built on what’s hunted, foraged, and grown right there in the mountains. And I'll be eating my way through plenty of pintxo bars too, of course. — Katie Button, chef/co-founder of Cúrate Bar de Tapas in Asheville, and author of Spanish Accent cookbook

“I’m in love with Erin French’s new cookbook [Seize the Supper], and wildly enough, Maine is one of the few states I've never been to. So, I'm plotting something for next summer. I love that it's a mostly female crew, a standout (unfortunately) in our industry. Erin’s focus on local produce and connecting to the earth speaks to my own regenerative cooking and inspires me constantly to dig deeper and deeper. I also admire her ethos of humble simplicity, distilling dishes to their core, filled with soul and properly honoring ingredients, with a nod to her family's heritage. I dream of her play on sweet and savory—like the soft polenta with honey and ricotta.” — Camilla Marcus, chef and founder of Westbourne

The seafood platter at the new Casa Juani in Boulder

Casa Juani's Spain-inspired sea urchin dish

“I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best New Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City

For cookbook author Rebekah Peppler, edomae-style sushi is a must-eat in 2027.

“[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author

Baekyangsa Temple, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan hosts meals

Freshly foraged ingredients, including mushrooms, herbs, and greens, used by chef Jeong Kwan

“Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P.

Street bread Ka'ak is the reason chef Mary Attea will be headed to Lebanon in 2027.

“I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City

A ceviche dish at Lima restaurant Al Toke Pez

“I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City

Traditional Assamese food items on sale at the annual Bhogali Bihu Festival in Assam

“I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L.

“I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats

A bowl of pollock soup, a dish local to Inje in South Korea

“Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food company Queens

I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia

Korean Air is adding a second New York-area gateway.

The SkyTeam Alliance carrier will land at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) with flights from Seoul’s Incheon Airport (ICN) in May 2027, Korean Air said on Thursday. The new route to east of the Hudson River complements its long-standing twice-daily service to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Korean Air will offer daily flights to EWR from May 22. It will fly a Boeing 777-300ER on the route.

The airline did not say what 777 configuration it will fly to EWR. It flies planes with several layouts, including an older configuration with eight first class suites.

United Airlines launched its first-ever nonstop from EWR to ICN in September. The Star Alliance carrier flies a Boeing 787-9 on the route.

Korean Air’s new EWR flight comes at a time of change for the airline as it wraps up a merger with fellow Korean carrier Asiana. Korean will complete the customer-facing integration of Asiana on Dec. 17, a combination that will significantly increase its market share at ICN.

While the merger does not add any new U.S. destinations to Korean Air’s map, it does increase its presence at JFK to up to four daily flights including Asiana, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

First look: Inside Korean Air’s stunning new flagship lounge at LAX

Future schedules show Korean Air continuing to serve JFK with four daily flights through June 2027.

The new EWR flight will complement Korean Air’s JFK services and create a new connection with joint venture partner Delta Air Lines. The carriers have expanded their transpacific options in recent years with new routes, including Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) to ICN on Delta.

The partnership allows Delta and Korean Air to coordinate commercial matters, including fares and schedules, between the U.S. and South Korea.

Korean Air highlighted the expanded flight options and New Jersey’s pharmaceutical, biotechnology, financial, and logistics industrial clusters for its new EWR route.

EWR is Korean Air’s first new U.S. destinations since it added Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) in 2019.

American Airlines will add new connections and cut others as it works to optimize its network at Los Angeles.

The carrier confirmed Friday that it will launch year-round service from LAX to Reno, Nevada, and seasonal service to Bozeman, Montana, and Grand Junction, Colorado.

LA-Reno will operate three times weekly, starting May 27, 2027, using Embraer E175 aircraft.

The routes to Bozeman and Grand Junction will operate from May 27 to Aug. 9, with Bozeman service using an E175 and Grand Junction flights using a Bombardier CRJ700.

An American official said Grand Junction is a “seasonal market addition” while service to Aspen/Pitkin County, Colorado, is temporarily suspended due to construction work there.

The carrier also confirmed that it will drop service from Los Angeles to Cleveland and Des Moines, Iowa, on February 11.

#6196. US Flights Have Been Grounded Nationwide

The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated in a press conference that there was “no indication as of yet” that anything “nefarious” caused the ground stop, and suggested that it was due to a broad was a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”

The halt on take offs and landing is in place for both domestic and international flights operating within the US. United Airlines, one of the four largest airlines in the nation, said that the order did not apply to in-transit aircraft: “United Airlines is responding to a nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. United flights that are already airborne will continue. New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place,” United Airlines said in a press release. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved.”

The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred in the US was in January 2023 following a computer outage in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) pilot notification system (NOTAM).

CNBC reported that the widespread server outages affecting telecommunications over the past 24 hours were to blame, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, there are 26,284 flights scheduled to depart on November 13 from the US. As of 5:50 p.m., 600 flights have been diverted so far, with 496 of those 600 flights (82.7%) returning to their origin airport and the other 104 diverting to a different airport. At this time 481 have been canceled or no fly nationally, representing 1.83%. This will grow today,” a company spokesperson said. “After 4 p.m. Eastern time today, there were still some 11,000 flight scheduled to depart from US airports today.”

#6195. Livery of the Week: Etihad Partners with McLaren

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

While traditional marketing theories advise airlines to avoid sponsoring events such as motor racing because of perceived associations with “danger” and “uncertainty” — concepts that could reflect negatively on air transport operators — the past couple of decades have seen several airlines establish partnerships with Formula One teams and events.

Today, some carriers are title sponsors of their home Grands Prix. Gulf Air, for example, has been the title sponsor of the Bahrain Grand Prix since its inception in 2004. Singapore Airlines, which has held the same role at the Singapore Grand Prix since 2014, has extended its commitment through 2028.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways has been the title sponsor of the UAE Grand Prix since the race’s debut in 2009. This year, it also entered into a partnership with McLaren Racing, bringing together “two organizations with a shared commitment to innovation, ambition, and delivering exceptional experiences for fans and customers around the world”.

To mark the partnership, Etihad has painted one of its Boeing 787-10 aircraft in a special livery, taking McLaren Racing’s distinctive color to the skies.

The livery features McLaren’s signature papaya orange across most of the fuselage — the same color used on its racing cars and team uniforms. The “Etihad” and “McLaren” names appear side by side above the cabin windows, while the McLaren logo is displayed toward the rear of the aircraft against a black background. The tail fin retains Etihad’s signature mosaic pattern, with its colors adjusted to complement the fuselage’s black-and-orange scheme.

Papaya has taken flight 🧡✈️Keep your eyes on the skies and let us know if you spot us 👀#McLarenF1 | #BeyondBorders | @etihad pic.twitter.com/NCHxsdAMTi

The aircraft chosen to showcase the special livery is a Boeing 787-10, registered A6-BMI. It was delivered to Etihad directly from the manufacturer on Oct. 14, 2020.

The aircraft features one of Etihad’s older cabin designs, introduced in 2018. It has 327 seats in a two-class configuration: 32 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout and 295 economy class seats in a 3-3-3 layout. The first 10 rows of the economy cabin are designated “Economy Space,” offering a seat pitch of 35 inches rather than the standard 31 inches.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

The  is one of the most recognizable premium travel rewards cards on the market, offering everything from airport lounge access and hotel elite status to a long list of travel and lifestyle statement credits.

But with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), it's also a significant investment.

The Amex Platinum offers plenty of opportunities to offset that cost, especially if you travel frequently and can take advantage of its statement credits. However, many of its benefits come with restrictions, and getting the full value requires some effort.

So, who can actually get enough value from the Amex Platinum to justify its annual fee? Let's take a closer look at who should — and shouldn't — consider adding this card to their wallet.

For frequent travelers, airport lounge access is one of the biggest reasons to consider the .

The card offers access to one of the most extensive airport lounge networks available through a credit card, making it especially valuable if you spend a lot of time in airports.

Cardmembers can access American Express Centurion Lounges, receive a Priority Pass Select membership (enrollment required) and visit Delta Sky Clubs when flying on eligible same-day Delta flights. Delta Sky Club access is limited to 10 visits per year unless you spend $75,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year to unlock unlimited visits. Access is subject to eligibility requirements.

Amex also operates Centurion Lounges at more than 20 airports, so the benefit can be particularly valuable if you live near or frequently connect through an airport with one.

If you travel frequently and would otherwise pay for lounge access, the Platinum could help you save money while making your time at the airport more comfortable. And when combined with the card's other travel benefits and statement credits, lounge access can help make the $895 annual fee easier to justify.

While the is best known for its premium travel benefits, it also offers a growing list of lifestyle statement credits that can help offset its $895 annual fee.

For example, cardmembers can receive up to $400 in Resy statement credits each calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter) at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants* and up to $300 in Lululemon statement credits* (up to $75 quarterly) at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online.

The card also offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment statement credits* (up to $25 monthly) for eligible subscriptions, along with up to $120 annually toward an Uber One membership to fully cover an auto-renewing $96 annual or $9.99 monthly membership*.

If you're already spending money on dining, shopping and entertainment in these categories, the credits can provide meaningful value without requiring you to change your spending habits.

However, many of these benefits are divided into monthly or quarterly credits, so you'll need to keep track of when to use them. The Platinum is a particularly good fit for someone who doesn't mind managing these benefits and can consistently take advantage of them year-round.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum

The Amex Platinum can also be a valuable addition to your wallet if you regularly stay at Hilton, Marriott or luxury hotels.

Cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status, which can provide benefits such as bonus points on stays and potential room upgrades. You'll also receive Leaders Club Sterling status with The Leading Hotels of the World, a collection of independent luxury hotels. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Beyond elite status, one of the Platinum's most valuable hotel-related perks is its up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (up to $300 semiannually).

Cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits every six months on eligible prepaid bookings through American Express Travel®, including stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection properties, as well as select Airbnb Luxe stays.

The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe require a minimum two-night stay, and beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging credit.

Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with valuable benefits, including daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, room upgrades when available and a property credit valued at $100.

If you regularly book these types of stays, the lodging credit and additional perks can go a long way toward offsetting the card's annual fee. Just be sure to compare prices with booking directly, since rates through Amex Travel aren't always the lowest.

Related: How to maximize the Amex Platinum hotel statement credit

Chase's unofficial 5/24 rule generally makes applicants ineligible for many Chase cards if they've opened five or more personal credit cards across issuers within the past 24 months.

Travelers who are still eligible for Chase cards may want to prioritize products such as the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees) before exceeding that threshold.

If you've already built a collection of Chase rewards cards, the Amex Platinum could be worth considering as your next premium travel card.

The card also earns Membership Rewards points, giving you access to a separate collection of airline and hotel transfer partners that can complement an existing Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy.

Many people just starting in the points world underestimate the stringency of Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you're just getting started with travel rewards and remain under Chase's 5/24 threshold, you may want to think carefully before applying for the Amex Platinum.

Opening the card could count toward your 5/24 total and potentially limit your eligibility for Chase cards in the future. That could mean missing out on valuable welcome offers or benefits from cards you planned to open later.

However, once you get over 5/24, it may be hard to get back under, and there’s a massive opportunity cost in doing so. Having a plan and sticking to it will serve you well in the long term.

Of course, that doesn't mean everyone under 5/24 should avoid the Platinum. If its benefits are a particularly good fit for your travel habits, it may still make sense.

The provides 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or with American Express Travel (on up to $500,000 of spending each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

A card like the or (see rates and fees) may be a better fit because their broader travel earning categories can include eligible third-party airfare bookings.

The offers a long list of statement credits, but that doesn't necessarily mean every cardholder will get enough value from them to justify the $895 annual fee.

Following the card's 2025 refresh, several of its benefits are geared toward specific lifestyle purchases, including dining at Resy restaurants, shopping at Lululemon and purchasing an Oura Ring. (Cardmembers receive up to a $200 Oura Ring statement credit each calendar year. This statement credit applies to ring purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. Enrollment is required.)

Many of these credits also come with restrictions. For example, the Resy and Lululemon credits are distributed quarterly, meaning you'll need to use them throughout the year rather than all at once.

If you don't already spend money with these merchants, or you don't want to keep track of multiple credits and enrollment requirements, the Platinum may not be the best fit.

Before applying, carefully consider just how much these credits are worth to you; if they provide little to no value, another Amex card might be a better fit.

Related: 4 different flavors of Amex Platinum — which one is right for you?

Business owners with substantial expenses may find that is a better fit than the personal Platinum.

Although both cards carry an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), their earning rates and statement credits differ in ways that could make one more valuable than the other.

For example, the Business Platinum earns 2 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases in select business categories and on purchases of $5,000 or more, on up to $2 million in combined eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

The Business Platinum also provides up to $1,150 in statement credits per calendar year for U.S. Dell purchases: up to $150 each calendar year and an additional $1,000 statement credit after spending $5,000 on Dell purchases with the same card each calendar year (enrollment required).

You can also access the Pay with Points redemption option on the Business Platinum card, which gets you a 35% bonus for eligible flights with your selected airline using your Amex points (up to 1 million points back per calendar year). This is notably not available on the personal Amex Platinum.

These business-focused benefits may be more useful for someone with significant company expenses, while the personal Platinum may be a better fit for travelers who can maximize its lifestyle credits.

New cardmembers can find out their offer and may be eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus could be worth up to $3,500, which is nearly four times the card's $895 annual fee.

While this is the card's standard welcome offer, now could still be a good time to apply if you're eligible for an offer you're happy with and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases.

Just make sure you'll also get enough value from the card's ongoing benefits to justify its annual fee beyond the first year.

Related: The best time to apply for Amex cards based on offer history

The offers an impressive lineup of premium travel benefits and statement credits, but its $895 annual fee means it won't make sense for everyone.

For frequent travelers who value airport lounge access and luxury hotel perks, and can consistently use the card's lifestyle credits, there's plenty of potential to get more value than the annual fee.

On the other hand, travelers who prefer straightforward rewards or don't regularly use the card's benefits may find better value with a lower-annual-fee option.

Ultimately, the Platinum is worth considering if its benefits fit your existing spending and travel habits — not because of the total advertised value of its credits.

#6193. Delta Air Lines Is Already Flying The Replacement For Its Aging Airbus A319s, But American & United Don't Have One

Wikimedia Commons, Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines all operate the Airbus A319. Together, the three operate over 250 examples, using it as a core aircraft slotting above their regional jets and underneath their larger narrowbodies. However, the aircraft is also old, having debuted in 1996.

The US carriers need to replace these aircraft soon, yet two out of the three haven't ordered the Airbus A319neo, Boeing 737 MAX 7, Airbus A220, or Embraer E2. Delta Air Lines has ordered 145 Airbus A220s, split between 45 A220-100s and 100 A220-300s. The 109-seat A220-100s are much smaller than an A319-100 and are really sized closer to the airline's Boeing 717-200s.

The 130-seat A220-300s, however, are almost perfectly sized to replace the 132-seat A319-100s. The other airlines have not ordered this aircraft, nor any others to replace their A319s (as well as the 737-700 in the case of United). However, they might not need these planes to replace the A319-100.

Delta first ordered the A220 back in 2016 when the aircraft was still being sold by Bombardier as the CSeries. At the time, the CSeries was a promising plane, but orders were relatively scarce, and Bombardier was desperate to break into the US market in particular. The original order consisted of 75 CS100s (now the A220-100), and Delta received the planes at such an attractive price that it prompted Boeing to file an anti-dumping petition, which was later overturned.

Delta got an amazing price for these planes that is unlikely to be matched. The aircraft is, of course, excellent for its intended missions, but capital cost plays a huge part in the economics of acquiring and operating an aircraft type. The circumstances of the order make the A220 more compelling for Delta than it would be if American or United ordered the type simply because they would need to pay more money.

This is especially true when considering that it would come with high integration costs. Delta has experienced excellent results with the A220, and has since added 70 orders in total. While the original order solely consisted of 75 CS100s/A220-100s, all subsequent orders have been for the A319-sized A220-300.

Meanwhile, the airline has converted 30 A220-100 orders to the larger variant. While the A220-100 is a competent aircraft in its own right, the A220-300 has more seats without burning significantly more fuel, and the aircraft doesn't even have a significant range penalty for most airlines' purposes.

While the US airlines operate large fleets of last-generation small widebodies, American and United have not ordered any current-generation examples. However, this is because their replacement for the A319-100 is the A321neo and the 737 MAX 10. Both airlines have been upgauging because the A321neo and 737 MAX 10 offer significantly better per-seat economics than other narrowbody aircraft.

This makes them much more compelling to operate than their smaller counterparts. American Airlines has ordered 206 A321neos in total while also acquiring ten used examples, and it's ordered 115 737 MAX 10s. United Airlines has ordered 210 A321neos, 224 737 MAX 9s, and 167 737 MAX 10s. Both airlines have also ordered the 737 MAX 8, but in smaller numbers (103 for American and 123 for United).

What will actually happen is the new large narrowbodies will take over the carrier's highest demand routes, displacing smaller aircraft down the network and sending the A319-100s to the scrapyard. Delta has done this exact thing, ordering 100 737 MAX 10s and 189 A321neos. While it is taking new A220s, these aircraft are not necessarily replacing the A319-100s one for one.

Instead, Delta will again use its new large narrowbodies to take over its busiest routes, which will displace other aircraft, including the A220s in some cases. Meanwhile, the A319-100s will go away. For all three airlines, it's their large narrowbodies that will enable displacements throughout the network.

Over the past 15 years, Delta has ordered 145 A220s, while it also leased 88 717s from Southwest Airlines for an exceptionally low price. American Airlines ordered 32 A319-100s new from Airbus. Otherwise, all of Delta's narrowbody orders have been for the A321-200, A321neo, 737-900ER, and 737 MAX 10. American has otherwise only ordered the A321-200, A321neo, 737-800, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 10.

Similarly, United has only taken the A321neo, 737-800, 737-900ER, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 9, while holding orders for the MAX 10. There has been a noticeable trend of US airlines favoring larger narrowbodies, and even the mid-size 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s have fallen out of favor.

These aircraft simply deliver superior economics to the shrinks in their families, as the added fuel burn is far outweighed by their increased revenue potential. The tradeoff is shorter range and runway performance, but only a handful of mainline stations have truly challenging conditions. At the same time, the A320neo and 737 MAX families have solved the performance and range issues.

Across the board, US airlines are upgauging, switching to larger aircraft for short-haul flights. In the past, another reason why airlines would buy smaller aircraft is to right-size capacity, but the US legacy carriers have strongly employed fare segmentation as a core commercial strategy.

This has reduced the need to operate smaller narrowbodies, since releasing various numbers of differently priced tickets can help fill planes on slower days. This is something that United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby has publicly commented on.

Fare segmentation and basic economy fares mean that his airline no longer requires a small narrowbody to meet demand, allowing United to standardize on larger, more economical aircraft. Tellingly, United ordered 45 737-700s in 2016, added another 20 units, then converted all orders to the 737-800 and 737 MAX 9 later the same year.

American Airlines ordered 32 A319-100s new from Airbus, while also acquiring a handful of used examples. United Airlines converted all of its later 737-700 orders to larger variants, while also acquiring a handful of used A319-100s. Delta, on the other hand, ordered 145 A220s while also acquiring 88 717s. Of course, the capital costs play a huge role in this.

Specifically, the 717s were essentially a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity due to Southwest's acquisition of AirTran, which originally owned the planes, while the A220s were sold at very low prices. However, another benefit of the small narrowbodies to Delta comes from its pilot agreement.

The agreement stipulates scope clauses, which place limits and restrictions on regional jet flying contracted out to other airlines under the Delta Connection brand. The largest planes that may be flown for Delta Connection are 76-seaters, and there are hard limits on how many of these planes Delta may operate under the Delta Connection, as they are more economical than 70-seaters or 50-seaters.

Delta's scope agreement, however, allows the airline to add additional 76-seaters if it adds a new small mainline narrowbody. The 717s, in addition to being cheap to acquire, unlocked additional 76-seaters for the Delta Connection brand. The A220 order did the same thing, and this is a significant benefit given the scale of the regional operations run by the US airlines. However, this was also a very specific set of circumstances that, combined, made the two purchases work for Delta.

These airlines are the world's three largest operators of the type.

An opportunity like the 88 717s that Southwest was looking to offload rapidly was only going to occur once, as is also the case for the pricing on Delta's initial A220 order. Beyond this, American Airlines specifically does not have a trigger in its scope clauses for additional 76-seaters if it acquires a new small narrowbody type. Rather, the size of the 76-seater fleet is tied directly to the airline's overall mainline fleet size.

For American, the aircraft has to have merit on its own, and that's difficult to justify. United Airlines does have the same trigger clause as Delta, which means that acquiring an aircraft type sized like the A319-100 would unlock additional 76-seaters. However, the carrier is currently focused on substantial network-wide growth through frequency increases and upgauging.

Buying 100+ A220s does not fit its general strategy today, especially considering United's current order book, which is dominated by larger aircraft variants. For both airlines, there is less benefit to acquiring the A220 or a similar small narrowbody aircraft type like Delta has.

Apart from the unique circumstances that made the 717s and A220s attractive to Delta, however, the Atlanta-based carrier is also practicing upgauging and is noticeably doing so throughout the network. The carrier has also shied away from the 737 MAX 8, and there's a distinct possibility that it may simply not order this variant at all.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Definitely would be cool to see an A220-300 in UA colors, but I honestly wonder if they won’t order a replacement due to their preference for larger aircraft.

Customers can expect savings of up to 30% off bikes and a whopping 50% off camping gear on REI’s deals page. For those interested in dipping their toe into the camping lifestyle, expect savings on plenty of the gear you’ll need to get started, including tents, sleeping bags, and camping essentials, like a whopping 50% off the REI Co-op Campwell 6 tent. Head out on your next big trip through Yellowstone National Park or Glacier in style, and without the worry that you’ll be underprepared once you arrive. From camping chairs to keep you comfortable around the firepit to video cameras that always capture that perfect shot for your Instagram (or your memories), there are plenty of ways to save on all your necessities—and a few extras just in case.

No longer do you need to head to a store in person and battle it out for the last jacket on the rack: REI’s online outlet has tons of great gear to save on, all shoppable from the comfort of your own home. From shoes and socks to helmets, boots, and bags, expect huge savings on something for everyone. One of my favorites includes 27% off Smartwool Active Fleece Wind pants. There’s also plenty of other deals on travel gear worth calling out, like 30% off the CamelBak All Around travel tumbler and 41% off the Osprey Arcane small crossbody bag. On REI’s outlet page, shop top brands like Arc’teryx, Hoka, Keen, Osprey, Patagonia, Salomon, and Columbia, all in one spot.

For something a bit more consistent, sign up for an REI lifetime membership to score an estimated 10% off every year on all eligible purchases. Memberships are a one-time payment of $30, and last the rest of your life, so you’ll be able to score benefits for years to come. To get your rewards, simply shop as you usually would, and earn back an estimated 10% Co-op Member Reward annually on eligible full-price co-op purchases. Your reward will automatically be uploaded to your account in the following month.

Members get more benefits, like free standard shipping on every order (5–7 business days)—a convenience that non-members can only reap the reward of when they hit the $60 minimum spend. Members also save 20% off on bike and snow shop services, have extended return windows of up to a year rather than the usual 90 days, get free ski and board wax and a flat tire tube with repair, and up to 33% off gear rentals. All of these benefits more than make up for the $30 fee.

As an added bonus, those who sign up by November 12, 2026, will also receive a $30 gift card, which they can use on whatever they please for 30 days after they sign up. To be eligible to receive this gift card, all you have to do is make a $50 purchase at REI and buy your membership in the same order. This means your $30 one-time membership fee is basically free once you take advantage of the gift card.

Give your gear and clothing a second life when you trade in gently used products to REI’s Re/Supply platform—and receive a gift card for eligible items. Simply fill out the trade-in form to get an estimate on your product’s eligibility and credit value. Then drop your products off at your nearest REI store. Once your trade-in is complete and your product has been evaluated, you’ll receive an email with an REI e-gift card that you’ll be able to use to purchase more of your favorite gear.

Your used products will head to REI’s Re/Supply shop. Not only is this a great way to keep textiles and other items out of landfills, but you’ll get money back to spend on something else. These gently used secondhand products are shoppable as well, and at great discounts, so if you’re open to taking home a pre-loved item rather than springing for a new piece, expect to find some excellent savings. The brand is closing its online version of the shop, but customers can still purchase gently used items in its brick-and-mortar stores.

One final way to keep to your budget and still get some great deals is by signing up for the REI credit card. Customers who open an REI Co-op Mastercard get a total of 15% in REI rewards (5% card rewards on all REI purchases and 10% Co-op member rewards). Cardholders also earn 1.5% in rewards on all other purchases when not shopping at REI. As a bonus, there is no annual fee, and the rewards no longer expire.

REI credit cards are only available to members, so you’ll have to complete the one-time sign-up and $30 membership fee, but once you do so, you’ll be able to sign in online and validate your Co-op membership to join and start racking up rewards. All rewards are ready to be redeemed online and in stores at REI as soon as they pop up in your account. As a bonus, customers can expect a $100 REI gift card after their very first purchase outside of REI, but use it quickly, as the gift card expires 60 days after your account is opened.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6191. Is It True That The Airbus A321XLR Flies With Its Nose Pitched Up At Cruising Altitude?

Did you feel like your plane was a little nose-up on your last long flight? Well, you're not wrong. In fact, nearly every single commercial jetliner cruises with a noticeable nose-high pitch for most of the journey. The physics of flight dictate that an aircraft on a steady level cruise rarely maintains a perfectly parallel relationship with the horizon. It's especially remarkable on Airbus' newest long-haul narrowbody, the A321XLR.

While a nose-up attitude is basic physics, a couple of factors make it highly noticeable on the A321XLR. An aircraft wing does not generate lift when aligned perfectly flat with the oncoming air mass. It requires a pitch of two to three degrees above the horizon to force the air under the wings and produce efficient lift. The A321 is a very long narrowbody aircraft, and its silhouette creates a clear visual profile compared to shorter aircraft like the A319.

This is not an abnormality of the A321XLR design. It is the standard operating condition for the entire commercial fleet, ranging from the small Airbus A220 to the massive Boeing 777. As a flight progresses and the engines burn through fuel, the plane becomes lighter. When it needs less lift, the fly-by-wire system gradually lowers the nose. The cabin floor is rarely level, though the tilt is subtle enough that most passengers won't notice it while seated.

Despite carrying far more weight than other planes in its class, the XLR retains the Airbus A321's baseline wingspan of 117 feet (35.8 meters). Given the restricted wing area compared to a widebody jet that flies similar routes as the XLR, it must fly at a higher angle of attack than many commercial jets. Raising the nose one to two degrees above most other airliners allows the XLR to generate more lift at a similar altitude and airspeed.

It must take off with a far greater payload than the standard A321neo, which is often configured with a higher seating capacity, because of the fuel it carries to make long journeys. That requires gradual step climbs with the XLR slowly raising and lowering its altitude relative to the fuel in its tanks as the route progresses.

Pilots on simulator forums online cite pitch ranges between one and three degrees for cruise flight. These values fluctuate depending on the precise fuel load, passenger count, and chosen speed schedule. Weight is the primary driver of these fluctuations. For the Airbus A321XLR, this calculation is pushed to the absolute extreme of the single-aisle category. The jet stands out as the heaviest iteration of the A321 family, boasting a maximum takeoff weight reaching 223,000 pounds (101,100 kg).

When heavily loaded with fuel at takeoff, the thin air at high altitudes cannot provide enough density to support an XLR efficiently. To avoid an unfavorable flight profile, the XLR is heavily reliant on step climbs. It will initially level off at a lower altitude where the air is denser. Even at this lower altitude, the engines must operate at high thrust to maintain cruise speed while holding a high nose pitch.

United’s first Airbus A321XLR begins a new premium narrowbody era for long-haul flying.

Walking toward the front of the A321XLR cabin on a transatlantic flight might make a passenger feel as though they are moving up a shallow ramp. While the plane behaves flawlessly from an engineering standpoint, its high nose-up posture changes how passengers experience the flight. That is most noticeable during the initial hours of a transcontinental mission when the aircraft is heaviest.

In the early phase of such a trip, flight attendants must manage heavy galley carts on a tilted floor. Service typically starts from the front of the cabin and moves backward, allowing the crew to push the heavy carts downhill rather than fighting gravity to push them forward. To guarantee a pleasant ride for a full passenger payload, the aircraft relies on a highly optimized, non-emergency 'comfort envelope.'

To prevent passengers from feeling any sudden jerks or wallowing motions, the autopilot performs continuous micro-trimming. The computers maintain a specific cruise speed, typically Mach 0.78, at an altitude where the air density allows the plane to ride smoothly. By keeping the XLR in the 'buffet margin' performance band, the system ensures a rock-solid, vibration-free ride for the customers in the back.

The story behind Delta's reluctance to invest in long-haul narrowbodies.

Inside the advanced cockpit of the A321XLR, a suite of flight computers handles most of the workload required to balance the jet's pitch. The flight computers eliminate the need for pilots to manually adjust the plane's controls as the trip progresses. These avionics let the flight crew spend more time focused on navigation rather than constantly correcting the aircraft's attitude.

Flying at a nose-up angle naturally creates extra aerodynamic drag. To combat this, the computer systems linking the navigation data and the engine throttles work together seamlessly. The autopilot uses a continuous feedback loop that monitors how the aircraft is interacting with the thin air. As the plane burns off fuel and changes mass, the computer automatically commands the tail stabilizers to pivot by microdegrees.

This smooth, automated adjustment gently lowers the nose to a flatter angle without requiring any input from the flight crew. The system calculates the exact engine thrust needed to glide efficiently at the ideal angle. It maintains a steady cruise speed without burning excess fuel, keeping the plane at the mathematically perfect intersection of pitch, speed, and fuel efficiency.

Analyzing the real world performance of the world's longest range narrowbody.

The A321XLR navigation computer removes all the guesswork from changing altitudes during long-haul flights. The plane cannot safely cruise at its final high altitude right after takeoff because the air is too thin to support it. The automation constantly runs real-time calculations to find the optimal moments to climb. Simultaneously, flying a long-range narrowbody like the XLR near its performance margins also requires strict safety boundaries.

When the plane reaches an ideal state, the system notifies the crew, executes the climb smoothly, and automatically recalibrates the nose position for the new altitude. The flight control software also includes hard-coded safety protections that act as an invisible safety net. If severe turbulence or a sudden wind shift tries to force the nose into a dangerously high angle, the computer automatically intervenes. It overrides unsafe tendencies and stabilizes the plane well before it approaches an aerodynamic stall.

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

The automation on the A321XLR acts as both an active stabilizer during rough weather and an immediate backup to the autopilot. The flight computers do not just wait for the plane to get bounced around. Instead, they use a real-time response system. The throttle computer continuously tracks wind shear to detect if a sudden draft causes a drop in speed. Then, the engines instantly spool up to add energy, and if a gust spikes the speed, the throttles dial back.

Accelerometers and sensors throughout the fuselage detect sudden pockets of rising or sinking air instantly. By minutely deflecting these wing surfaces in direct opposition to the bumpy air, the plane counteracts the turbulent forces. Even if the autopilot is hand-flying or navigating severe weather, the computer software enforces strict performance limits. If an extreme event exceeds the autopilot's limits, the XLR will drop offline to hand control back to the pilots.

Because an unexpected disconnection is highly critical, the cockpit is designed to make the handover impossible to miss. The plane will not allow the nose to point higher than 30 degrees up or lower than 15 degrees down, and the system limits the maximum roll angle to 67 degrees. If the autopilot projects that intervention is needed to stay within tolerances, red flashing warning lights illuminate directly in front of both pilots on the main dashboard panels.

The evolving industry, and climbing price, of extra-large turbofan engine repairs.

Although the A321XLR looks identical to a standard variant of the family, the jet has some subtle differences inside and out to match the flight efficiency of its light, shorter-haul peers. Lighter, standard A321neo jets are optimized for high-capacity, short-haul routes where low-speed lift during frequent takeoffs and landings is a major priority. To achieve this, standard A321s have featured complex, heavy double-slotted inboard flaps. For the A321XLR, Airbus deleted the double-slotted configuration in favor of a single-slotted inboard flap.

The simpler control surface slashes the wing's physical weight and provides an optimized profile that reduces drag in high-altitude cruise. During an 11-hour long-haul cruise, a double-slotted mechanism creates excessive, unnecessary weight and parasitic aerodynamic drag. To ensure the plane doesn't lose low-speed lift during takeoff at maximum weight, Airbus pairs this single-slotted flap with advanced software that introduces automated flap programming.

Looking at the internal components, the XLR once again differs from older long-range models like the A321LR. On the legacy jets, extra fuel is carried in up to three separate additional center tanks which resemble large cargo containers bolted into the luggage hold. These add weight and eat up cargo space that would otherwise be used for bags and shipments. The XLR solves this by replacing separate cargo-bay tanks with a single, permanent rear center tank.

Concentrating thousands of liters of fuel entirely behind the wings completely shifts the aircraft’s weight and balance. As the flight progresses and the aft tank drains, the center of gravity dynamically sweeps forward. The XLR's flight computers use automated fuel management to precisely monitor fuel burn across the outer wings, forward tanks, and rear tank, keeping the plane perfectly balanced in its optimal cruise pitch from takeoff to touchdown.

#6190. End Of An Era: Hong Kong’s Iconic “Symphony Of Lights” Show Ending

Hong Kong is one of my favorite cities in the world. When I think of Hong Kong, the beautiful waterfront and skyline on both sides of Victoria Harbour come to mind. Along those lines, a nightly staple of the waterfront is coming to an end, and I’m sad about it…

Since 2004, Hong Kong has had the “Symphony of Lights” show every single night at 8PM, lasting for around 10 minutes. It holds the Guinness World Record for being the world’s largest permanent light and sound show, as it involves dozens of buildings.

It’s one of the things that contributes to Hong Kong’s electric energy, as you have a sea of people lining up on the waterfront (typically on the Tsim Sha Tsui side, though sometimes also on the Central side) every night to watch it.

Well, after 22 years, the Symphony of Lights will be coming to an end. The last show is expected to take place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. To mark the end of the era, the final show will feature special pyrotechnics and fireworks.

Why has Hong Kong decided to end the nightly Symphony of Lights show? Officially, it’s a strategic shift in the city’s tourism and event strategy, described as being driven by shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions. We’re told that we can expect “something new” in the future, but it doesn’t sound like it’ll be a full replacement for the Symphony of Lights.

I must admit, I’m sad to see this change in Hong Kong. No matter how often I visited Hong Kong, I always made a point of watching the Symphony of Lights, and always found it to be so enjoyable. Hong Kong has one of the world’s most gorgeous skylines, and the nightly show just took that to the next level.

I am curious what the backstory here is. Was the cost of operating this really so high, in the scheme of things? While I can in theory appreciate the concept of diminishing appeal, the nightly show always had a crowd in the thousands waiting to enjoy it — that was true 20 years ago when I first visited Hong Kong, and it was also true when I visited earlier this year.

Hong Kongers will soon have to bid farewell to the Symphony of Lights, the iconic nightly show that has been lighting up the city’s skyline since 2004. Officially, this change is described as being due to shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions.

I’ve enjoyed this show every time I visited Hong Kong, so I’m sad to see this development. The skyline is still incredible and leaves me in awe every time, but there’s no denying that the nightly show added just a little bit of extra sparkle.

What do you make of Hong Kong’s nightly Symphony of Lights ending?

#6189. Buy Wyndham Rewards Points With Best-Ever 100% Bonus (0.65 Cents Each): Worth It?

Wyndham Rewards has launched its latest promotion on purchased points, which is potentially in line with the best-ever offers that we’ve seen from the program. This could be a great value for unlocking discounted award stays, as the program is offering up to a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.65 cents each.

Link: Buy Wyndham Rewards points with a bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM on December 31, 2026, Wyndham Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. The best offer appears to be for up to a 100% bonus, though you’ll have to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for.

With this offer, you can unlock the highest bonus if you purchase at least 3,000 points in one transaction. If you purchase 1,000 or 2,000 points, you don’t receive any bonus. If you purchase points, they’ll post to your account within 72 hours, and purchases are non-refundable. Purchased points don’t count toward Wyndham Rewards elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy Wyndham Rewards points for 1.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses, and that includes all taxes and fees.

If you maxed out the promotion and were eligible for a 100% bonus, you could purchase 400,000 points (including 200,000 bonus points) for $2,600, which is a rate of 0.65 cents per point.

This is the best bonus offer I ever recall seeing from Wyndham Rewards, so if there has ever been a time to buy points, this is it.

Wyndham Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 100,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been doubled, to 200,000 points.

When Wyndham offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s most commonly an 80-100% bonus. So this 100% bonus is at the very top end of that scale. However, personally I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Wyndham Rewards on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Wyndham Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

Generally speaking, I only recommend buying points when you have a specific, short-term use in mind. In the case of Wyndham Rewards points:

More generally, there are definitely some properties where there’s value in outright buying points for the purposes of a redemption. Let me actually give a direct example, as I recently purchased some Wyndham points for a hotel stay, rather than booking with cash. I needed to be in Colorado Springs, and I booked The Mining Exchange Hotel, part of Wyndham Registry Collection (the hotel even has a Michelin key!)

The cash rate for a base room at the hotel would’ve been $307.57, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Meanwhile the hotel was charging just 30,000 points. At a rate of 0.65 cents per point, that’s like paying $195 for the stay, inclusive of taxes & fees. Not bad, eh?

Well, it gets better than that. Wyndham Rewards often lets you book premium rooms at no extra cost when redeeming points, so I was able to book a club room for the same 30,000 points.

If paying cash, that would’ve cost $438.54, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Now, the club rooms absolutely aren’t worth it, since you just get access to a pantry with some packaged snacks. But hey, if the cost is the same, I’ll take it. 😉

Wyndham Rewards has a four tier award chart, so free night redemptions will cost one of the following amounts:

While I wouldn’t say there’s widespread appeal to buying Wyndham Rewards points for these kinds of redemptions, there are some situations where the numbers will work out. Perhaps the best value would come in situations where you just need to buy a few thousand points to have enough for an award stay.

Wyndham Rewards has more than 9,000 hotels across 20 brands in 80+ countries. Some of the most popular Wyndham Rewards brands include Registry Collection, Wyndham Grand, Dolce, Wyndham, La Quinta, Wingate, Wyndham Garden, Ramada, Days Inn, Super 8, Howard Johnson, and Travelodge.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Wyndham Rewards points to be worth 0.6 cents each. Admittedly that’s a very conservative valuation, and there should be opportunities to get way more value than that.

Wyndham Rewards has one of the most complicated points expiration policies of any hotel loyalty program:

Wyndham Rewards partners with a variety of transferable points currencies, including Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou. The catch is that transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, so I wouldn’t at all consider that to be a good redemption value.

That’s because you could be getting way more value from your transferable points than moving them to a program where points can be purchased for well under a penny each.

Wyndham Rewards also has a portfolio of credit cards issued in the United States, which are potentially quite lucrative if you frequent the brand.

Wyndham Rewards is offering up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.65 cents each. While I most definitely wouldn’t speculatively buy Wyndham Rewards points at this cost, there are some situations where the math works out, so everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves.

To those who are Wyndham Rewards fans, are there any properties you can get outsized value at with this promotion?

#6187. FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop

Flights were grounded across the U.S. Friday afternoon over suspected air traffic control communications issues.

The FAA issued a highly unusual mass ground stop shortly after 3 p.m.

“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped,” the agency said in an advisory. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”

In a separate statement, the FAA said a communications issue affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers is to blame. Agency technicians are now investigating the issue.

According to ABC News, this is only the second time since the 9/11 attacks that departures across the country have been stopped. Flights currently in the air are believed to still be in contact with ATC.

National media outlets showed footage of commercial airplanes queued up but not moving at numerous major airports, including Los Angeles, Boston, Reagan National, New York-LaGuardia, Houston Bush, Dallas/Fort Worth, and Raleigh–Durham.

The ground stop will almost certainly cause a cascade of cancellations and delays lasting into the weekend.

The first Cabinet-level official to comment in person on the incident was Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who spoke to reporters outside the White House. Mullin said there is no indication that the outage is a cyberattack, or connected to the recent Microsoft outage.

The situation is close to “unprecedented,” the secretary added, but there is no threat to public safety or reason to panic. Mullin said it is still too early to say when the problem will be resolved.

It was not immediately clear if the outage is connected to ongoing upgrades on ATC systems and infrastructure. The FAA has been moving rapidly to replace outdated equipment, such as old radios and floppy disks, and install more automated technology. The agency is also ripping out old copper wiring and replacing it with fiber optic cables.
