#6172. Airbus' Clever Engineering Tricks That Made The A330 Become The "Butter Machine"

The Airbus A330 has earned an unusual nickname among aviation enthusiasts: the “Butter Machine.” The name comes from its reputation for exceptionally smooth landings, often marked by a gentle first contact between the rear wheels and the runway before the rest of the landing gear settles.

So what exactly is Airbus doing under the wings? Which parts are true engineering tricks, and which are folk wisdom repeated on aviation forums for twenty years? Even the experts disagree about why the gear sits at an angle, and the answer changes how you should read every “smoothest landing ever” video. Stay with us, because the most surprising answer sits in the middle of the article, and it comes from pilots who say the landings that look smoothest from the fence are not always the ones passengers feel as smooth. Let’s start with the part everyone can see.

The first clue is the tilt. According to Flightradar24, the A330 is often called ‘The Butter Machine’ because of its smooth landings, and it names the main landing gear as the jet’s easiest identifier: two sets of four wheels, tilted backward. Canada’s Transportation Safety Board (TSB) describes the same arrangement in an A330 investigation report: each bogie carries four wheels in a twin-tandem layout, and the bogies are inclined so the rear tires touch the runway first. Flightradar24 adds a useful contrast: the four-engine A340 carries an extra center landing gear, while the A330 relies on its two main bogies alone, which puts even more attention on how those two units behave.

That arrangement becomes more interesting once the wheels actually meet the runway. According to the same report, forces are transferred gradually when the wheels touch down, instead of arriving through all eight main tires at once. Simple Flying’s explainer on why the A330 lands so smoothly adds the supporting cast: oleo-pneumatic shock absorbers, a balanced bogie design, titanium and corrosion-resistant steel, and two landing gear control units that alternate for reliability.

The wheels, however, cannot simply remain tilted on their own. Something has to position the bogie before touchdown and control its movement as the aircraft transitions from flight to the runway.

That job belongs to a hydraulic ram called a pitch trimmer. Pilots and engineers on the PPRuNe forum describe it as the part that sets the bogie nose-up when the gear is selected down, and a research paper on tire heat at touchdown says it lifts the front wheels of the bogie and lets the rear wheels descend around the bogie beam. The same paper adds that the pitch trimmer can act like a shock absorber.

That damping role is not just forum talk. A patent for a variable-damping pitch trimmer explains that the actuator positions the wheels before touchdown, helps stow the gear, and also damps the motion of the bogie beam relative to the leg. Meanwhile, a shortening mechanism pulls the shock absorber up inside the leg during retraction, which shrinks the gear so it fits into a compact bay. Simple Flying notes that Airbus had not used such a feature on many earlier models. The TSB report adds that the bogie beam pivots at its center on the shock strut, and that the beam position is always the same when the gear is selected.

That last point is important because it separates two jobs that are often blended together when the A330’s landing gear is discussed. The pitch trimmer clearly helps position and damp the bogie, while the shortening mechanism helps package the landing gear inside the aircraft. That raises a bigger question about the original purpose of the backward tilt itself.

Delta is currently the world's largest A330-900 operator, while Cathay Pacific has the most on order.

The reason for the angle is less settled than the nickname might suggest. In a PPRuNe thread on landing gear lean, a contributor insists that simple geometry points to storage, noting that the tilt exists so the bogie fits the bay. Another poster counters that the A330 and A340 are a special case, claiming the nose-up tilt is intentional and works a bit like the semi-levered gear on the Boeing 777-300ER, improving clearance under the aft fuselage.

Enthusiasts keep a dedicated Airliners.net thread on A330 main gear bogie tilt, while The Points Guy reports that wheel orientation is mostly a space-saving choice, even though pilots generally agree that trailing-link gear produces the most flattering landings. In other words, the tilt may exist for storage, yet it still shapes the touchdown. Designers rarely mind when a packaging solution doubles as a comfort feature.

The landing gear explains why the A330 touches down in stages, but it does not explain everything passengers see or feel during the final seconds of a landing. Once the aircraft is close to the runway, the flight-control system and the wing become just as important.

The A330 was designed to give pilots familiar handling near the runway even though it uses fly-by-wire controls. According to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ASB), flare mode replaces the normal load-factor law with a flare law, letting crews use the same landing technique as on non-fly-by-wire aircraft. Airbus’ own Safety First magazine says the flare should begin around 40 feet (12 meters) above the runway on the A330, A340, A350 and A380, compared with 30 feet (nine meters) on smaller Airbus jets. The same article warns that a steeper approach slope than the nominal three degrees may call for an earlier flare, reminding pilots that the software supports them rather than replacing their timing.

Handling plays a part too. Many pilots describe the A330 as stable and predictable, with an older-generation wing that gives a slightly heavier control feel than the A350. Members of the Infinite Flight Community go further, crediting a wing size and strong ground effect, though that is speculation rather than confirmed engineering. A pilot on a PPRuNe flare-height thread offers a more practical view, saying the A330 and A340 settle nicely with a 40-foot (12-meter) retard and a smooth rotation.

With the gear tilted, the bogie damped, and the flare law handling the final phase, the ingredients for a smooth touchdown are certainly there. There is still one catch, though: the first contact with the runway is not necessarily the end of the landing sensation.

From mass to mechanics: why the A380 needs more wheels than a semi-truck.

On a PPRuNe thread about hard A330 landings, pilots describe how the aircraft can touch down beautifully on the rear wheels, then float along the runway before the front wheels come down heavily. Their advice is to touch down on the rear wheels, then pitch down firmly enough to bring the front wheels gently onto the runway while speed remains, which is exactly what they say the autopilot does on an autoland. That distinction changes how the A330's landing should be judged from the ground. A long, graceful hold-off can look almost perfect to somebody watching from the fence while producing a noticeably firmer second contact for people inside the aircraft. The sequence is therefore less about eliminating every bump than about controlling when each part of the landing gear takes the load.

Timing matters for another reason. A separate thread about A340 touchdowns explains that applying reverse thrust as the rear axle lands can make the aircraft drop onto the front axle once the ground spoilers kill the lift, and that a higher pitch attitude at the flare makes the thump worse. A pilot in the same thread says the A330 behaves similarly, and that the cure is to flare for the rear axle, derotate smoothly until the front axle is down, and only then use reverse. Ground spoiler logic, according to an ATSB investigation of an A330 landing, depends on weight on both main gears plus either a radio altitude below 6 feet (1.8 meters) or a wheel speed above 72 knots (133 kilometers per hour). One Airliners.net user also lists three distinct bumps: rear wheels, front wheels, then the nose wheel.

The sequence also explains why the A330's landing gear remains interesting beyond the aircraft itself. Airbus did not stop developing large-aircraft landing gear after the A330, and some of the same principles appear on later widebodies.

The A330's basic approach clearly survived into later Airbus designs. As Simple Flying previously explored, the A350-1000’s six-wheel bogie is built, so the rear wheels typically touch down first, stabilizing the aircraft before the forward wheels settle, which reduces pitching forces and improves comfort. The A380 needs 20 tires on its main gear, which shows how far the same weight-spreading problem can be pushed. Both aircraft inherit the same basic logic: share the load, sequence the contact, and let the shock absorbers do the rest.

Airbus also launched the A330neo with new engines and winglets that improved per-seat fuel economy by 14 percent, but the family's touchdown personality barely figures in that story.

That is what makes the landing gear such an interesting part of the A330's legacy. The aircraft has evolved through new engines and winglets, but the gear that helped create the Butter Machine reputation remains fundamentally part of the family. As the NEO version continues to fly across more route networks, pilots, passengers, and spotters still get the same butter landings.

#6171. Singapore Airlines Reconsiders New Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-new cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change…

On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the new business class seat design.

In response to this, he reportedly said “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin said this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the new design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”

To state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a new business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

Is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a new business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#6170. Richard Avedon, Fashion Guru, Does Old Age

A moving, incisive photography exhibition in Toronto and Montreal explores the way of all flesh.

Left: Richard Avedon, Gloria Swanson, actor, New York, September 4, 1980, gelatin silver print. Right: Richard Avedon, The Duke and Duchess of Windsor, Waldorf Astoria, suite 28A, New York, April 16, 1957, gelatin silver print.

© The Richard Avedon Foundation, courtesy of the Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund

Old faces — some seem to crease and crumble as we watch — were a specialty for Richard Avedon (1923–2004), the photographer famous for his fashion work for Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Revlon, and Elle, magazines not known for plugging geezers. I didn’t know this, so I learned something new in my first minutes in Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging, 1951–2004, finishing its tour next month, when it goes to The Image Center in Toronto and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts. Avedon was a pioneer in presenting cool, stark, tough beauty — he gave us a nude Nastassja Kinski with a boa constrictor licking her earlobe, Brooke Shields in jeans, and lots of movie stars and potentates at their peaks. But old age? Shades of decadence are one thing, but decrepitude?

The Image Center is Canada’s premiere photography museum and part of Toronto Metropolitan University. The exhibition there is similar to Montreal’s edition and displays 100 Avedon portraits. Avedon died more than 20 years ago, and the show spans 50 years, so the subjects are from another era. That said, old age is timeless as well as time-limited. On view are superstars such as Gloria Swanson, Ronald Reagan, the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, and the Dalai Lama. Then there are the period pieces like Dorothy Parker, Oscar Levant, Ezra Pound, and Coco Chanel.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

My husband and I have always dreamed of visiting London, but we knew we wanted to do it the right way: comfortable flights and a chic hotel stay, with room left in our budget for things like afternoon tea, souvenirs and even a day trip.

All of that can sometimes require some pretty deep pockets, which is why we spent the past year allocating our spending strategically, using my to earn points toward both our flights and our hotel stay.

But like anyone on a budget, we wanted to get the most bang for our “point.” So when American Express last offered a 30% transfer bonus to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers, I knew I had to jump on the opportunity and book our trip asap. The good news? Amex is offering this same transfer bonus to Virgin again, now through Nov. 30, 2026.

Here’s how I made the most of the transfer bonus, including the redemptions I made and how you can do the same with the current offer.

First, let’s break down how the bonus works:

The American Express Membership Rewards® program is offering a 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers until Nov. 30, 2026. That means every 1,000 Membership Rewards points you transfer becomes 1,300 Virgin Points®. Terms apply. Note that Amex points must be transferred in multiples of 1,000, with a minimum of 1,000 points.

Now I’m no math whiz, but I do know that means 100,000 Membership Rewards points would convert to 130,000 Virgin Points, instead of the standard 1:1 ratio. That's one of the best transfer rates Amex offers.

Several Amex cards earn transferable Membership Rewards points, including:

Editor tip: If you’re new to transferring Membership Rewards, like I was, I highly recommend checking out our beginner-friendly guide that breaks down how to transfer Membership Rewards points to partners like Virgin step by step, along with any restrictions you need to be aware of.

The best part about Virgin as a transfer partner is its surprising breadth. You can redeem your points for flights on Virgin Atlantic, as well as stays at Virgin Hotels and cruise sailings with Virgin Voyages.

I had built up a solid balance of Membership Rewards points through a combination of the Gold Card's welcome offer and my everyday spending, but the limited-time window of that bonus meant I couldn't afford to think about it for too long.

I live in Central Florida, and luckily for me, Virgin Atlantic offers nonstop flights from Orlando

International Airport (MCO) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR). However, Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop to LHR from airports across the U.S., including:

Personally, I’ve always been curious about Virgin’s premium economy cabin after hearing so many great things about it from my fellow TPG colleagues. So for our outbound flight, we booked premium economy, which comes with perks like extra legroom and an elevated meal service.

It cost me 35,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. With the 30% bonus, I only needed to transfer 54,000 Amex points for the two of us, which means I saved 16,000 Amex points on the outbound leg alone.

Note that taxes, fees and charges apply in addition to the points price for reward flights in all classes. These vary depending on factors such as your destination and travel dates, and the applicable amount is shown at the time of booking.

From check-in to landing, the premium economy cabin proved to be the perfect balance of value and comfort. Extra touches like a dedicated check-in desk, a glass of bubbly after boarding, upgraded dining and amenity kits made the experience feel so special. The wide leather seats with extra legroom meant we arrived in London well-rested and ready to explore. I could see why so many people rave about it; it was the perfect middle ground between budget-friendly and comfortable.

The real splurge was our return flight, which turned out to hardly be a splurge at all because I found a nonstop Upper Class flight home from LHR to MCO for just 29,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. Thanks to the bonus, I only needed to transfer 46,000 Amex points total for two people. That's 12,000 Membership Reward points saved on an already incredible redemption. Needless to say, I felt like I’d won the lottery.

I’ll be the first to tell you that it doesn’t get any better than Virgin’s Upper Class for R&R on a nine-hour flight across the Atlantic. The direct-aisle-access seats converted into lie-flat beds, and the amenity kits were well curated. Not to mention that the dining and inflight service made me feel like, well, royalty.

By the time we touched down in Orlando, I had slept through most of the flight, which is a rarity for me as a nervous flyer. We arrived home feeling restored rather than depleted.

Combined, our flights cost us 128,000 Virgin Points plus taxes and fees, which took 100,000 Amex points to cover. The transfer bonus saved my husband and me 28,000 Membership Rewards points across both flights, and we used them to redeem on Virgin Red for a rewards stay at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch.

Once I had committed to the Virgin Atlantic booking, staying at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch was a no-brainer with that 30% transfer bonus. And yes, when you transfer Membership Rewards points to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you can use them toward a stay at a Virgin Hotels property.

Editor tip: Once you’ve transferred your Membership Reward points to Virgin,  check out our easy-to-follow guide to booking Virgin Hotels with Virgin Points.

On our dates, the stay came out to about 60,000 Virgin Points per night. For our four-night stay, I was looking at 240,000 points in total, which felt like a lot to give up. With the 30% transfer bonus, though, I only needed to transfer 185,000 Membership Rewards points, which was much easier to wrap my head around.

When I booked the hotel, I had a feeling using my points would be well worth it, and from the moment we arrived at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch, my suspicions were confirmed. The hotel sits in trendy East London, far enough from the crowds and tourist traps, but close to the Old Street Tube station for easy access to activities and dining across the city. It’s also a convenient 10-minute walk from Liverpool Street Station, which has direct access to LHR.

The hotel has quintessential Virgin design, with red accents everywhere, from the lobby carpets to the Smeg fridges in the guest rooms. Beyond the rooms, the property has a rooftop pool for the warmer months and a retro hi-fi listening bar called Hidden Grooves, which serves creative cocktails that are perfect after a long day exploring London.

As for how it compares to cash pricing, a comparable room size runs around $450-$550 per night. Our four-night stay on Virgin Points was equivalent to saving roughly $2,000 in cash, which suddenly made the Amex transfer bonus feel like money in the bank.

With our flights and hotels covered by points, we had cash to spend on our most anticipated experiences in London. Here are a few of my favorite trip highlights:

My Membership Rewards transfer to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club covered nearly every big-ticket item on our London trip: flights in both directions, including a lie-flat Upper Class seat home, and four nights at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch. With the 30% transfer bonus stretching every point further, we were able to spend our cash on experiences, dining and souvenirs.

If you've been sitting on a stash of Membership Rewards points, this is one of the best ways to use them right now, and you don’t need to go to London. Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop from the U.S. to Manchester and Edinburgh and connecting through Heathrow opens up destinations like Barbados, Cape Town, Dubai, Mumbai and the Maldives.

Your points aren't limited to flights, either. You can put them toward a stay at Virgin Hotels or even a Virgin Voyages cruise. Just keep in mind that the 30% transfer bonus, available to eligible U.S. cardmembers, ends Nov. 30, 2026, so whether you're dreaming of a lie-flat seat across the Atlantic or days in the sun at sea, now is the time to book your next trip.

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express is one of the most perks-rich business cards out there, and is useful if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 300,000 points are worth a staggering $5,100. As I see it, that’s basically the best welcome offer you’ll find on any card.

Let me emphasize that Amex uses a variety of factors when deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Platinum Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible Amex Business Platinum bonus through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there.

That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method. However, it can always be worth checking back every so often, because the promotions people are targeted for can change over time.

The Amex Business Platinum bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to nearly $6,700 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners. Also keep in mind that having this card lets you unlock the full value of Amex Pay With Points, potentially allowing you to get up to 1.54 cents of value per point toward the cost of airfare on a designated airline (this comes in the form of a 35% Pay with Points rebate, up to one million points per year). You could then use that redemption rate for all your linked Amex Membership Rewards cards.

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find the Amex Business Platinum to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Platinum, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). While this isn’t the most rewarding card in terms of the return on spending, it does have a huge number of valuable perks, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the Amex Business Platinum annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

#6167. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

Every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only showed up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):

So this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

It’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

American had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

What do you make of this American pilot being arrested?

#6166. White House Urges Congress To Approve $30 Billion In Upgrades To US Aviation Infrastructure

The White House is urging Congress to approve an additional $30.1 billion for US aviation infrastructure upgrades. Reuters reports that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and budget director Russell Vought are pushing for action before Democrats take control of Congress in January. The request follows the Republicans' defeat in November's midterm elections, leaving the administration with a narrowing window to secure funding.

The appeal comes as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has reportedly ordered a nationwide ground stop on November 13, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns. The administration first requested approximately $30 billion in additional funding in September, on top of the $12.5 billion previously approved by Congress.

Duffy and White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought have written to congressional leaders requesting swift approval of the additional investment. With Democrats preparing to assume control of Congress on January 3, 2027, the administration is seeking to advance the proposal during the remaining weeks of Republican control. However, the legislation's prospects remain uncertain, and a change in congressional leadership does not necessarily mean the funding would be rejected.

The administration argues that the funding is essential to replacing outdated air traffic control equipment, improving airport capacity, and strengthening the safety of the national airspace system. The latest proposal builds on a modernization program announced in 2025, following years of concern about aging communications infrastructure, controller shortages and operational disruptions. The investment is intended to accelerate upgrades that officials say cannot be completed with existing appropriations.

In their November 13 letter to Congress, Duffy and Vought said:

"This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace"

$12.5 billion in initial funding approved

Duffy requests approximately $30 billion more

The funding campaign began well before this week's political developments. Duffy called for additional investment on September 22, shortly after a major Northeast air traffic control disruption. Senator Eric Schmitt subsequently introduced the Modern Skies Act on September 28, supported by major airlines and aviation industry organizations. The latest White House intervention represents a renewed effort to secure congressional approval rather than an entirely new funding initiative.

The proposed investment would bring federal aviation modernization funding to approximately $42.6 billion, including the $12.5 billion originally approved in 2025. Unlike the earlier allocation, which concentrated on ATC improvements and controller recruitment, the latest request includes substantial funding for airports. Of the $30.1 billion, $18 billion would support airport infrastructure, including $10 billion to modernize or replace aging terminals.

ATC modernization, automation and cloud computing

Replacement and improvement of ATC towers

Airport infrastructure, including terminal modernization

The FAA's infrastructure problems have accumulated over decades. Some facilities still depend on aging computers, with replacement components reportedly purchased through auction websites. The agency recently announced plans to eliminate floppy disks used to distribute weather and other critical information at more than 400 ATC facilities by the end of 2028. These technological limitations have compounded existing concerns about staffing shortages, congestion and delays.

Nevertheless, modernization is already underway. According to Duffy, 68% of the FAA's legacy copper telecommunications network has been replaced with high-speed fiber infrastructure. The additional funding would accelerate upgrades to controller workstations, automation platforms and telecommunications, while expanding airport capacity. The challenge is implementing these improvements across one of the world's busiest aviation networks without creating further operational disruption.

A severed backup fiber line triggered ATC Zero conditions, grounding major Northeast airports and sending disruption toward Boston.

The funding appeal coincides with an extraordinary disruption to US aviation. Earlier on Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, instructing departing aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice. According to Axios, the advisory cited "extraordinary circumstances and safety reasons," with international arrivals to be handled individually, although at the time of writing, the cause of the disruption had not been officially established.

The incident follows September's major Northeast ATC meltdown, when simultaneous telecommunications failures disrupted thousands of flights. A circuit failed at an air traffic facility in Philadelphia, while an Amtrak construction crew accidentally severed a fiber-optic cable in New Jersey. Ground stops affected several major airports, including Newark, Philadelphia and New York's airports, with knock-on delays extending to Boston.

Although the causes of today's nationwide ground stop still need to be established, the September incident demonstrated how communications failures can spread disruption across multiple airports. The FAA's modernization program aims to reduce these vulnerabilities through more resilient telecommunications, upgraded technology and improved infrastructure. With billions of dollars awaiting congressional approval, the latest disruption provides a timely backdrop to the administration's argument that further investment cannot wait.

#6165. Buy Etihad Guest Miles With 60% Bonus (2.0 Cents Each): Worth It?

Etihad Guest has just launched its latest promotion on buying miles, which is being marketed as the biggest offer of the year. With this, members can buy Etihad miles with a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire them for as little as two cents each.

Is that offer worth it? Let’s cover all the details, but I’ll say right away that I think this offer has fairly limited appeal, and you should only take advantage of this with a specific use in mind.

Link: Buy Etihad Guest miles with a bonus

Between 12:01AM GST on November 12 and 11:59PM GST on November 22, 2026, Etihad Guest is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger bonus the more miles you buy, as follows:

Note that purchased Etihad Guest miles post within 72 hours of completing the purchase (typically faster than that), and that purchased miles don’t count toward Etihad Guest elite status.

Etihad Guest ordinarily charges 3.2 cents per purchased mile, and there are no further taxes and fees. That’s before any bonuses or discount. With the 60% bonus, if you maxed out this promotion you’d receive a total of 320,000 Etihad Guest miles at a cost of $6,400, which is a rate of two cents per Etihad Guest mile.

Etihad Guest limits members to purchasing 200,000 miles per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. The exception is Etihad Guest Platinum members, who can purchase up to 300,000 miles per year, before any bonuses.

The current Etihad Guest buy miles promotion is described as the biggest offer of the year. To compare this to other offers we’ve seen so far this year, we’ve seen bonuses of 25-50% (2.56 cents to 2.13 cents per mile), as well as discounts of up to 35% (2.08 cents per mile).

As you can see, Etihad Guest’s current offer gives you the best cost per mile so far this year. However, Etihad isn’t exactly aggressive with selling miles, so it’s hard to get too excited about any of these amounts.

Etihad Guest mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There are lots of ways to redeem Etihad Guest miles. While the airline doesn’t belong to one of the major alliances, there are many ways to redeem the miles on both Etihad and on partner airlines.

Below you can find the award chart for travel exclusively on Etihad. The pricing is based on the one-way distance of travel. Note that these redemption rates are specifically for situations where there’s GuestSeat availability, which is Etihad’s capacity controlled, saver award space.

If you see higher award pricing than what’s listed below, that generally means there’s not saver award space, and redemptions won’t be a very good deal. Furthermore, in some situations you’ll find higher saver level award costs, including for travel in the carrier’s A380 first class.

Etihad Guest has a separate award chart for travel on partner airlines, which is also distance based, and you can find that below. This is based on the one-way distance, and you can’t mix airline partners on a single award.

The main reason to consider collecting Etihad Guest miles is because the program has access to a lot more Etihad award space than partner programs do. Partner programs, like American AAdvantage and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, typically only have access to a subset of premium cabin Etihad availability. Furthermore, if you want to fly in Etihad’s The Residence, your ticket needs to be issued by Etihad, so an Etihad Guest award redemption would qualify.

There are two major catches when it comes to Etihad Guest, in addition to not really having slam dunk redemption values:

I’d really only recommend buying Etihad Guest miles with a very specific use in mind, if you know what you’re doing.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Etihad Guest miles to be worth 1.1 cents each. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Etihad Guest miles than that.

Etihad Guest miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Note that you can only reset the expiration of your miles by crediting a flight to the program every 18 months, so other activity wouldn’t help in that regard.

Keep in mind that there are many ways to earn Etihad Guest miles, so outright buying miles isn’t the only option. Etihad Guest also partners with select transferable points currencies. In the United States, you can move points to Etihad Guest at a 1:1 ratio from Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so that gives you quite a bit of flexibility.

Admittedly not everyone has access to credit cards in the United States, and some people may also prefer to just buy miles if they can acquire them at a reasonable cost.

Etihad Guest is selling miles with up to a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy miles for as little as two cents each. This could be worth it if you have a specific use in mind, but Etihad Guest just seems rather unserious with its buy miles promotions, since the program isn’t that lucrative, in terms of redemption rates, and the policies for changing and canceling awards is also incredibly frustrating.

So for a vast majority of people, I’d recommend giving this offer a pass, unless you’ve done the math, and it checks out.

#6164. Elizabeth Warren’s Plan to Abolish Credit Cards

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.) host a roundtable on housing affordability and accessibility on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., January 7, 2026.

Elizabeth Warren, never short on annoyances, thinks that interest on consumer credit cards is too high.

The average rate currently hovers around 21 percent. Her solution: Pass a law to cap interest rates at 10 percent. She says she has a bill ready to go, and like-minded lawmakers have signaled their support for controlling rates.

Like any other price ceiling, an interest cap would create a shortage of the product it attempts to make more affordable. With only a tiny fraction of credit cards now offering interest at 10 percent or less, capping rates at that level would force lenders to dramatically restrict accounts — requiring borrowers to put up collateral or limiting access to people with exceptionally good credit — or eliminate them outright.

To progressives, interest on credit cards is nothing but usury — the exploitation of poor borrowers who can’t afford to pay their bills on time. Warren’s sales pitch implies that, under her bill, people would enjoy the same credit just at a lower cost. In reality, almost everyone would see their current credit cards disappear.

Regrettably, Warren may also find allies for her proposal among Republicans. She claims she is open to working with President Trump, who called in 2024 for a temporary cap on credit card interest of “around 10 percent.” Senator Josh Hawley (R., Mo.), a right-wing progressive of sorts, recently joined hands with Bernie Sanders to translate that thoughtless musing into legislation.

Interest rates are not some arbitrary number. They are the price for lenders to provide liquidity on the promise, but never the certainty, that it will be repaid. To issue loans through a credit card, banks must first obtain the money by borrowing it themselves, either from depositors or other financial institutions. Interest must be paid on that debt and passed through to cardholders.

It’s true that rates on credit cards, as well as other consumer loans, are typically much higher than those for mortgages and businesses. That is because personal credit is one of the riskiest kinds to extend. Unlike secured loans, repayment depends wholly on borrowers’ creditworthiness. That often fails to hold up: 13 percent of credit-card balances are seriously past due, and approximately 5 percent of debt is never repaid. Higher interest rates exist to compensate for these losses.

Rates also vary based on individual creditworthiness. Borrowers with poor credit history, or people just starting to build their history after leaving childhood or moving to the country, have the most to lose from interest caps. They must accept costlier rates to obtain any credit whatsoever, and if lenders can’t adjust for their added risk, they will simply be cut off. Those in need of funds will instead have to turn to pawnshops or illegal loan sharks.

The credit card industry could always use more competition to keep interest rates at their fair market level. Ironically, the Dodd-Frank Act that Elizabeth Warren championed likely reduced the availability of consumer credit by increasing lenders’ regulatory burden. She also despises credit reporting agencies for tracking borrowers’ repayment histories, even though they replaced a far more discretionary and intrusive system in which bankers evaluated applicants’ personal reputations. For someone so appalled by alleged discrimination in finance, Warren should love objective credit reports.

By and large, Americans like their credit cards and wish to keep them. In trying to rescue consumers from their own financial decisions, Warren would deprive them of their plastic and consign them to infinitely more treacherous alternatives.

Those points transfer to a variety of airline and hotel programs, now even including American AAdvantage. Many of the card’s annual benefits are on a calendar year basis so you have the opportunity to take advantage of them twice in your first cardmember year: the $300 hotel benefit for 2+ night stays booked through Citi Travel; the $200 Splurge credit (take it for American Airlines travel!), and $100 in Blacklane credits twice each year. #6162. World Of Hyatt Brand Explorer: Free Night Awards For Staying At New Brands

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night award awards. In this post, I’d like to talk about one of the often overlooked ways to earn Hyatt free nights, which is with World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion.

This offers World of Hyatt members the opportunity to earn free night awards for exploring Hyatt’s portfolio. Given the huge brand inflation that Hyatt has seen in recent years, this can potentially offer up to seven free night awards, and counting.

With World of Hyatt’s Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a Category 1-4 free night certificate for every five unique Hyatt brands you stay at. When it comes to earning Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

If you want to see how many Hyatt brands you’ve stayed at, you can do so either through the World of Hyatt website or mobile app. Just go to the “Brand Explorer” section, and there will be a display showing how many unique brands you’ve stayed at (including which ones), and also how many free night certificates you’ve earned.

When it comes to redeeming Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

Of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt currently has 38 brands, which are as follows:

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

With World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a free Category 1-4 free night awards for every five Hyatt brands you stay at. This is a way to earn up to seven free nights over time, based on Hyatt’s current portfolio of 38 brands. As Hyatt’s portfolio continues to grow, the opportunities to earn free nights continues to increase.

However, staying at Hyatt’s all-inclusive properties requires some effort, given that they’re not typically places you just drop into for a night.

Given how easy Hyatt makes it to track this, I’m curious — how many Hyatt brands have you stayed at? Which OMAAT reader has the record for the most brands?

#6161. Ken Paxton Spotted Fleeing Texas With Girlfriend After Voters Reject His Senate Bid—Flying Coach To Fiji

Eight days after losing his U.S. Senate race, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was photographed at San Francisco airport with his girlfriend, Tracy Duhon, wearing a straw hat and carrying a Republican Attorneys General Association backpack. They were apparently headed to Fiji. And photos show them in coach. They departed Wednesday night, November 11. A witness says they worried about their bags making it to Fiji. Michael Board shares the photo of Ken Paxton and Tracy Duhon at San Francisco airport Another photo shows them standing in the aisle of coach. TMZ: Ken Paxton spotted in San Francisco International Airport, witness says he was traveling to Fiji https://t.co/GNFXuDuPvY — Kalshi Politics (@KalshiPolitics) November 12, 2026 Meanwhile, Paxton’s divorce finalized Thursday. State Senator Angela Paxton filed to end their 38-year marriage last year “on biblical grounds.” I’ve covered the travels of Ted Cruz, Elizabeth Warren, AOC, Bernie Sanders and others, and the credit card spend habits of former Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker. This choice isn’t partisan. Paxton Has A History Of Getting Out Of Town A Texas politician fleeing the state for warmer climes brings to mind Ted Cruz flying to Cancún during the February 2021 winter storm while millions of Texans were without power. This time the disaster was electoral. But Paxton has his own winter storm escape story. He and his then-wife went to Utah during that same freeze, saying he had meetings with Utah’s attorney general about the state Google antitrust case. This summer, I wrote about Paxton spending America’s 250th birthday in London with Duhon. He marked the anniversary of separating from Britain by going to Britain. The pair had been spotted traveling through Washington Dulles on their way to Iceland in late June. Then came the London video, with Marriott County Hall in the background. They apparently flew economy on that trip. Video of Ken Paxton and Tracy Duhon in London over the Fourth of July weekend In October, the Wall Street Journal reported on video of Paxton and Duhon celebrating New Year’s Eve 2024 overlooking the Burj Khalifa fireworks with fugitives indicted in a federal healthcare fraud case who had contributed $190,000 to Paxton’s campaign. James Talarico’s campaign shares footage of Ken Paxton at the Dubai gathering Republicans Knew Who They Were Nominating The Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Attorney General Paxton. Paxton’s own senior staff reported him to the FBI. House investigators alleged that an Austin real estate developer provided home renovations and helped conceal Paxton’s activities, including through an Uber account under the name “Dave P.” He also employed a woman Paxton previously had an affair with. The Uber account apparently let Paxton carry on his affair and visit his donor without his security detail or using his identifiable state vehicle. In return, Paxton allegedly used his office to help the developer. One example was a rushed legal opinion invoking pandemic restrictions to stop foreclosure auctions. The Texas Senate, under pressure large donors and the Lieutenant Governor, acquitted him in 2023. He’d also spent years under state felony securities fraud charges. That case ended through an agreement requiring restitution, community service and ethics training. The federal corruption investigation ended without charges. President Trump endorsed Paxton against incumbent Senator John Cornyn a week before their May runoff. Republicans then had to spend heavily defending a seat they’d held for decades, with a candidate that may have been one of the worst campaigners I’ve seen in 30 years even apart from his past challenges. Here he is wearing a reported-$40,000 watch and a Four Seasons golf shirt. And this clip of him was promoted by his campaign: .@KenPaxtonTX: The future of our state and the future of our country ride on this race. https://t.co/2ZvVWdhwzp — Paxton War Room (@PaxtonsPatriots) August 29, 2026 That choice cost Republicans dearly. Cornyn would’ve been far better-positioned in the general election. Counterfactuals are hard, but the rest of his party’s nominees at the state level were clearly brought down by his place on the ticket. Republicans even appeared in advertising against him. Former Republican state Representative Glenn Rogers, who’d voted to impeach Paxton, appeared in a pro-Talarico ad saying he’d never trust or support Paxton. The most revealing ad may have been the one Angela Paxton made because polls showed over 10% of Republicans staying home. While divorcing him, she urged Republicans to vote without mentioning her husband by name: “It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line.” Paxton wasn’t the only Republican with problems. Governor Greg Abbott had helped defeat Republican legislators who opposed school choice in the 2024 primaries. That left resentment in rural communities where public schools are major employers, and there are fewer private school options where the vouchers could be used. Republicans also faced a terrible national election environment, with an unpopular President and high gas prices. I Even Agree With Him On Some Of His Lawsuits Just this morning, I wrote about Austin’s airport rail plans and the financing arrangement Paxton’s office challenged. The city raised property taxes, then routed the money through a separate corporation to issue the debt, allowing the city to claim that it isn’t borrowing. Economically, property taxes support the bonds, while the city claims its not running afoul on state borrowing rules. The arrangement is probably illegal, but the state’s new attorney general may not be as inclined to continue the litigation. Credit: Gage Skidmore via Wikimedia Commons Even where they might agree with Paxton on an issue, plenty of Texans would’ve been happy for him to leave much earlier, even without a ticket to Fiji. #6160. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

I had a similar experience flying them from Algiers to Constantine. Biz class is just a coach seat (window or aisle) with the middle seat blocked off. Fairly mediocre experience but still miles ahead of Royal Air HardasaRoc, I mean, Maroc. Now that was a craptacular experience.

The tray arrangement does seem to confirm my suspicion they are round-trip catering their TATL flights…!

#6159. The Fight Over Obamacare’s Phantom Enrollees

The Trump administration is right to take on the problem of improper enrollment.

Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks during a press conference on anti-fraud initiatives at the White House campus in Washington, D.C., September 22, 2026.

More than a dozen Democratic senators are criticizing the Trump administration’s efforts to address the problem of phantom enrollments in Obamacare. In a letter to insurers, the senators accuse the companies of “colluding” with the administration to terminate coverage for more than 760,000 enrollees. Their criticism gets insurers’ financial incentives backward and overlooks the extensive safeguards the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) employed before terminating these highly suspicious enrollments.

Insurers have little incentive to drop phantom enrollees. For years, insurers have been the biggest beneficiaries of the expanded Obamacare subsidies — reaping tens of billions of dollars in higher subsidies. By making millions of plans free to consumers, Democrats created powerful incentives for improper and phantom enrollment. Given these incentives, the administration was right to scrutinize suspicious enrollments.

#6158. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?
