#6157. The US Navy Retired A 10,000-Lb Cargo Workhorse For A Tiltrotor That Carries 4,000 Lbs Fewer

On the surface level, it seems like the US Navy committed a strategic folly when it decided to replace the venerable Grumman C-2A Greyhound carrier-onboard delivery plane with a Bell Boeing tiltrotor. The newer and totally different rotary-wing aircraft has 40% less total payload than the 1960s vintage fixed-wing tail-hook plane it succeeded.

However, there is a crucial caveat that made all the difference when America's Navy decided to trade in for a new cargo plane. Unlike the Greyhound, the Osprey can carry the engine of the Lockheed Martin F-35C Lightning II. This is a vital mission in supporting the new USN Carrier Air Wing, which is now deploying the world's first carrier-capable stealth fighters in combat missions.

Fitting the colossal jet engine into the Greyhound would have required a ground-up redesign of the plane's fuselage, which would have been a massive investment in a nearly obsolete platform. Although the Navy did lose some raw payload capacity, it gained a massive amount of mission flexibility and the benefit of operational commonality with the US Marines.

The USMC has a very large number of V-22 Ospreys, which are deployed daily aboard US Navy vessels. That makes maintenance and logistics much simpler, but also taps into a skill pool of technicians and aircrew that has been refined for two decades to make the Navy's transition smooth.

Beyond the Marine Corps connection, the Osprey fundamentally changed how a Carrier Strike Group handles logistics, moving the Navy away from rigid, predictable Operations. The C-2 Greyhound was bound to the aircraft carrier's Flight Deck and airfields on the shore for every mission. If a C-2 Greyhound needed to pick up supplies near a conflict zone, it required a long, secure, paved military runway ashore.

The CMV-22B eliminates the middleperson. It can fly parts, mail, or personnel from a shore base directly to a destroyer, cruiser, or amphibious assault ship. It can also land on dirt fields, beaches, open drop zones, or small helicopter pads ashore to retrieve critical supplies or evacuate wounded personnel.

Additionally, the Osprey has a refueling probe that allows it to perform air-to-air refueling and extend its mission radius, which the Greyhound was never upgraded to receive. Another game-changing advantage is night operations. The Navy considered the aging C-2 Greyhound too risky for routine night landings on carriers. The CMV-22B, equipped with modern night-vision systems and avionics, can land vertically on a carrier's pitch-black deck at midnight, giving the fleet a true round-the-clock supply chain.

Superior night ops capability significantly improves the operational flexibility of not only Air Wing but also the entire Carrier Strike Group. More than that, the new ability is a force enhancement to the entire coalition as the US Armed Forces pivot to the Pacific with a focus on joint domain operations in a distributed battle space.

Likewise, the ability to resupply forces on remote islands without an airstrip is crucial in the Indo-Pacific. And the ability to perform aerial refueling will make the aircraft not only more practical but also enhance the safety of flight operating over vast expanses of open ocean.

Refocusing on the core capability that spurred the decision to make the transition to the COD mission, the capability to receive replacement engines for the Air Wing aircraft is crucial in a conflict. The Navy does not usually ship the entire, fully assembled engine at once. Instead, they transport the core F135 Power Module. This is the heaviest and most critical component of the engine.

It is, in fact, so heavy that the Osprey cannot perform a pure vertical lift but must execute a short rolling takeoff to get airborne. The C-2’s cabin is too narrow and awkwardly shaped to clear the engine's widest components. The Osprey's cargo bay can physically encompass these dimensions, but it leaves absolutely zero margin for error.

The engine module is mounted to a low-profile, heavy-duty wheeled metal frame that is compatible with a custom-designed skin rail system. The cargo crew pushes the module up the rear ramp, and it locks directly with the cargo floor's locking points to ensure the massive 3,750-lb (1,701 kg) powerplant cannot move during flight. While the engine technically fits, the tight clearance forces the Navy to accept unique operational compromises.

Because the module takes up nearly every cubic inch of the cargo bay, loading and unloading are a slow, meticulous process. Additionally, the F135 engine inside its standard shipping container will not fit inside the Osprey. Consequently, the engine must be flown 'naked,' or loosely wrapped. Ultimately, although it may not be the perfect transport option, it is the best available for the US Navy to sustain its fifth-generation Air Wing in the 21st century.

The legacy behind the latest and greatest Army helo.

The absolute cornerstone of the fifth-generation air wing is the F-35C Lightning II, which has just one powerplant. If an F-35C suffers an engine failure out at sea, that multi-million-dollar stealth fighter is completely useless until a replacement arrives. This is especially critical as the aircraft is a single-engine airframe.

While the F135 is the most powerful fighter jet engine ever made, the fact that the F-35C only has one is a major departure from the recent portfolio of carrier-capable aircraft flown by the USN and USMC. The F-35C is vastly more maintenance-intensive than the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.

The Legacy 4.5-generation Strike Fighter will be the support platform that continues to be the workhorse of the Air Wing, while the Joint Strike Fighter takes over the highest-risk missions like penetrating integrated enemy air defenses. To achieve supersonic speeds without a twin-engine layout, the F135 engine operates under extreme temperatures and pressures.

It generates massive electrical power to feed the jet's advanced radar, jamming systems, and electronic warfare sensors. In fact, the entire F-35 fleet of all variants around the world has suffered a critical readiness issue, and the latest upgrade package under Technology Refresh Three, Block Four, has been significantly delayed.

Despite the US Navy pumping nearly 1 billion dollars into a Lockheed Martin contract for advanced electronic warfare equipment, it doesn't solve the problem that these aircraft are more delicate, and working on them on the ship is far more burdensome as well.

The dynamic duo of America's carrier air wings.

The F-35C is built to strike targets deep inside enemy territory while the aircraft carrier stays positioned safely outside the range of land-based anti-ship missiles. This means the carrier operates much farther out to sea than it did in previous decades. The Osprey will liberate the logistical chain of the carrier strike group from airfields ashore and also improve the efficiency of operations to smaller vessels in the CSG.

This is thanks to the fact that the CMV-22B can perform vertical resupply to smaller vessels as well. The Navy variant of the Osprey features massive fuel bladders bulged into the sides of the fuselage. It can fly over 1,150 nautical miles (2,130 km) on a single internal tank of fuel.

Unlike the old Greyhound, the Osprey features an aerial refueling probe. It can take fuel directly from F/A-18 'Buddy tankers' or the upcoming Boeing MQ-25 Stingray drones, which will take over air-to-air refueling for the Air Wing. Aerial refueling gives the Osprey virtually unlimited range, allowing it to fetch an urgent F-35C engine core from a distant shore base and sprint back to a fast-moving strike group without stopping.

Even more importantly, with the entire US Armed Forces concentrating their strategic disposition in the Pacific, the Osprey supports Joint Forces as a whole because it is engineered for the theater, and it can carry the engine of the most important fighter jet for virtually every operator in the region.

Out with old, in with the new for the USMC, but what's the catch?

The Indo-Pacific is an F-35 theater. The Air Force flies the F-35A from mainland bases, the Marines fly the short-takeoff/vertical-landing F-35B from amphibious ships and austere islands, and the Navy flies the carrier-borne F-35C. Crucially, all three variants of the F-35 use the same foundational Pratt & Whitney F135 engine core.

Because the Navy’s CMV-22B can haul this engine, it doesn't just service aircraft carriers. A Navy Osprey can fly an engine from a remote Air Force base in Guam, land on an amphibious assault ship, or drop it off at a rugged island outpost. In the vast Pacific, the Navy doesn’t have to build its own dedicated maintenance hubs on every island.

The military knows that in a conflict, large, centralized bases like Kadena Air Base in Japan will be targeted by enemy ballistic missiles. To survive, the branches have developed decentralized strategies. Under modern Pacific strategy, a 100,000-ton Nimitz- or Ford-class aircraft carrier does not just exist to launch its own planes. It acts as a massive, floating logistical mothership for the entire joint force.

In a shooting war, if a Marine or Air Force F-35 engine fails on a forward island outpost, the Navy's CMV-22B can lift a spare engine directly off the supercarrier's deck or from any depot in the first or second island chain operated by the US or its regional allies. It can then fly it directly to that carrier, 'Big Deck' assault ship, or tiny island airstrip.

Then the Osprey can land right in the dirt next to the stranded jet. It allows all of the US Armed Forces, Japanese, Australian, South Korean, Singaporean, and other regional military allies to pool their resources dynamically, thanks to the universal platform of the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter.

#6156. New York Times Blames Trump For Air Safety Risks—Gets Blasted By The Independent NTSB

The National Transportation Safety Board says the New York Times distorted its comments to attack President Trump. The paper’s aviation safety story has bigger problems than just politics. It gets a major crash wrong and credits a pilot hours rule for a safety record that began years before the rule took effect. James Fallows’s “Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?” describes real issues of overworked air traffic controllers, military aircraft operating around passenger flights, and safety recommendations that haven’t been adequately addressed. Then it tries to turn them into a story about Trump dismantling the institutions that keep us safe, even though the issues he cites have been going on far longer than the current administration. I’ve written predominantly critically about Trump since he first ran for president 11 years ago. I rejected his effort to blame diversity hiring for the American Airlines 5342 tragedy before investigators had established what happened. That doesn’t make every argument against him a good one. The Times introduces Fallows as an instrument-rated private pilot with more than 2,000 hours. That’s true but while he’s written extensively about aviation it’s an odd way to frame him as author of this story. He’s also Jimmy Carter’s former chief speechwriter, a longtime Atlantic writer and editor, and a familiar voice on NPR. His career has been about politics and public policy. His own introduction to the article frames the piece as meant to connect aviation under Trump with public health, international aid, diplomacy, higher education and the rule of law. Aviation is the vehicle for a larger political point. The piece isn’t really about aviation, it’s using aviation. The Independent NTSB Attacks The Piece The NTSB says the article: Distorts the agency’s responses with political statements intended to attack the current administration. Mischaracterizes the NTSB’s role in the 1,500 hour pilot requirement. Incorrectly implies negligence by the Black Hawk pilots involved in the Washington National Airport collision. The statement also thanks the administration for supporting the agency and providing resources. That last part is political messaging too. (Gratitude for a budget doesn’t answer address aviation safety, but is probably necessary as a defensive measure.) “We are disappointed that this article sensationalizes and politicizes tragedies.” The NTSB’s response to the New York Times Magazine. — NTSB Newsroom (@NTSB_Newsroom) November 12, 2026 Fallows interviewed NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy. The agency argues she’s being mischaracterized, but they don’t actually say how. In the article she says, “Recommendations alone don’t save lives. Action does.” Her own July statement about the Washington crash warned that delays implementing the board’s recommendations represented a continuing, unacceptable risk. The Article Gets The Colgan Air Crash Wrong Fallows spends considerable space describing the 2009 Colgan Air crash near Buffalo – as the last U.S. airline crash with loss of life before American 5342. In fact, PenAir flight 3296 overran the runway at Unalaska in October 2019, killing a passenger. His account has the Colgan Air plane accumulating ice until it becomes a “frigid brick.” He writes that by the time the captain recognized the problem, it “might already have become unflyable.” But that isn’t what the investigation found. The FAA’s accident analysis says icing wasn’t a cause. When the stall warning activated, the airplane wasn’t yet stalled. The captain pulled back on the controls and put it into a stall. The crew had failed to monitor their airspeed and mishandled the approach. And both Colgan pilots already had more than 1,500 hours: The captain had 3,379 hours. The captain had a history of training failures despite the hours. The first officer had 2,244 hours, including 1,470 hours as a light airplane flight instructor and 774 hours in turbine aircraft. The 1,500 Hour Rule For Co-Pilots Isn’t The Reason For The Safety Improvements After Colgan, Congress and regulators made several changes. Pilot rest rules improved. Training changed. Pilot qualification requirements changed. Sharing pilot records improved. Evidence that safety has performed well after a package of changes doesn’t establish that (1) every element of those changes (2) caused the improvements. And there’s strong reason to believe the the 1,500 hour rule has the opposite effect. It makes becoming a pilot take far longer and become far more costly, which keeps talented people from becoming pilots. Those with a higher opportunity cost, or lacking access to resources needed, get excluded from the pool of potential pilots. You’re then drawing from a smaller group. The NTSB didn’t recommend the 1,500 hour number. In 2010 Senate testimony, then-chair Deborah Hersman explained that the board had investigated accidents involving both high-time and low-time pilots. It found a relationship between failed practical tests and subsequent accidents, but there wasn’t evidence that number of hours actually mattered. The higher minimum took effect in 2013. Fallows’s safety streak begins in February 2009. The first four and a half years of that streak can’t be credited to a requirement that wasn’t yet in effect. Making pilots chase hours can allow relevant skills to deteriorate and bad habits to develop before an airline has to train those habits out of them. Repeated flights in clear weather, making takeoffs and landings at the same familiar airports, aren’t equivalent to structured training for instrument flying in a jet with another pilot, airline procedures, and complex air traffic control instructions. Hours in a hot air balloon count. The hot air balloon can be tethered. European co-pilots don’t face the same restriction, but their safety record is equivalent. Sub-1,500 hour European pilots fly in the United States every day without concern (and American pilots fly in Europe without elevated risk). The argument for the rule is that experience can build judgment, and that the higher threshold was part of a successful improvement in regional airline standards. But that’s an argument for useful experience and rigorous standards. That’s not what we got. An hour spent building time isn’t as valuable as an hour spent in a supervised airline training program. And there’s zero evidence that 1,500 is the right metric. It was chosen because it’s expensive and time-consuming, restricts entry into the pilot profession and drives up wages, and was supported by the major pilots union. The Black Hawk Crew Bears Responsibility The NTSB objected to Fallows implying negligence by the helicopter pilots. But its own probable cause finding identifies the helicopter crew’s failure to maintain effective visual separation as a cause of the collision. The crew accepted responsibility for avoiding the airliner and failed to do so. The existence of systemic failures don’t eliminate pilot error. In Homendy’s testimony explaining the findings, the board concluded that the helicopter’s altimeter probably understated its altitude by about 100 feet. The crew likely believed it was below the route’s ceiling. Fallows also describes the crew flying through civilian traffic without monitoring its traffic avoidance systems. The helicopter had no integrated cockpit traffic display. The pilots had tablets capable of showing traffic, but looking down at them while flying low at night with night vision goggles was problematic. Their audio alerts weren’t integrated into the pilots’ helmets. There were failures of FAA route design, and the FAA failed to act in the face of repeated warnings. But it’s genuinely weird to pin the blame for that on the first nine days of the Trump administration before the crash. I’ve criticized efforts to preserve military exceptions around Washington National. Civilian aviation shouldn’t have to accommodate unnecessary military risks. The Pentagon needs to change, and the current administration is responsible for making that happen. But it didn’t invent the culture that allowed these risks to exist in the first place. The Article’s Own Incident Data Doesn’t Support A Partisan Cause Fallows combines airline accidents, rocket debris, military encounters, airshow incidents and presidential flyovers which generally have different causes. And a list that attributes incidents while a given President is in office to that President doesn’t do a good job of evaluating what decisions caused those incidents. But more simply, even the article’s own figures for the most serious runway incursions are problematic for the Fallows narrative: 2023: 22 incidents. 2024: 7 incidents. 2025: 14 incidents. 2026 through October: 9 incidents. The increase from 2024 to 2025 looks dramatic – a doubling! But it’s still far lower than under Biden in 2023! These are relatively small numbers, and they don’t show a steadily worsening trend. (And there are more aircraft operations than in 2023.) Air Traffic Control Was Broken Before Trump Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand. The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election. Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal. And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue. And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place. I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider. Pilot qualification requirements changed. Sharing pilot records improved. Evidence that safety has performed well after a package of changes doesn’t establish that (1) every element of those changes (2) caused the improvements. And there’s strong reason to believe the the 1,500 hour rule has the opposite effect. It makes becoming a pilot take far longer and become far more costly, which keeps talented people from becoming pilots. Those with a higher opportunity cost, or lacking access to resources needed, get excluded from the pool of potential pilots. You’re then drawing from a smaller group. The NTSB didn’t recommend the 1,500 hour number. In 2010 Senate testimony, then-chair Deborah Hersman explained that the board had investigated accidents involving both high-time and low-time pilots. It found a relationship between failed practical tests and subsequent accidents, but there wasn’t evidence that number of hours actually mattered. The higher minimum took effect in 2013. Fallows’s safety streak begins in February 2009. The first four and a half years of that streak can’t be credited to a requirement that wasn’t yet in effect. Making pilots chase hours can allow relevant skills to deteriorate and bad habits to develop before an airline has to train those habits out of them. Repeated flights in clear weather, making takeoffs and landings at the same familiar airports, aren’t equivalent to structured training for instrument flying in a jet with another pilot, airline procedures, and complex air traffic control instructions. Hours in a hot air balloon count. The hot air balloon can be tethered. European co-pilots don’t face the same restriction, but their safety record is equivalent. Sub-1,500 hour European pilots fly in the United States every day without concern (and American pilots fly in Europe without elevated risk). The argument for the rule is that experience can build judgment, and that the higher threshold was part of a successful improvement in regional airline standards. But that’s an argument for useful experience and rigorous standards. That’s not what we got. An hour spent building time isn’t as valuable as an hour spent in a supervised airline training program. And there’s zero evidence that 1,500 is the right metric. It was chosen because it’s expensive and time-consuming, restricts entry into the pilot profession and drives up wages, and was supported by the major pilots union. The Black Hawk Crew Bears Responsibility The NTSB objected to Fallows implying negligence by the helicopter pilots. But its own probable cause finding identifies the helicopter crew’s failure to maintain effective visual separation as a cause of the collision. The crew accepted responsibility for avoiding the airliner and failed to do so. The existence of systemic failures don’t eliminate pilot error. In Homendy’s testimony explaining the findings, the board concluded that the helicopter’s altimeter probably understated its altitude by about 100 feet. The crew likely believed it was below the route’s ceiling. Fallows also describes the crew flying through civilian traffic without monitoring its traffic avoidance systems. The helicopter had no integrated cockpit traffic display. The pilots had tablets capable of showing traffic, but looking down at them while flying low at night with night vision goggles was problematic. Their audio alerts weren’t integrated into the pilots’ helmets. There were failures of FAA route design, and the FAA failed to act in the face of repeated warnings. But it’s genuinely weird to pin the blame for that on the first nine days of the Trump administration before the crash. I’ve criticized efforts to preserve military exceptions around Washington National. Civilian aviation shouldn’t have to accommodate unnecessary military risks. The Pentagon needs to change, and the current administration is responsible for making that happen. But it didn’t invent the culture that allowed these risks to exist in the first place. The Article’s Own Incident Data Doesn’t Support A Partisan Cause Fallows combines airline accidents, rocket debris, military encounters, airshow incidents and presidential flyovers which generally have different causes. And a list that attributes incidents while a given President is in office to that President doesn’t do a good job of evaluating what decisions caused those incidents. But more simply, even the article’s own figures for the most serious runway incursions are problematic for the Fallows narrative: 2023: 22 incidents. 2024: 7 incidents. 2025: 14 incidents. 2026 through October: 9 incidents. The increase from 2024 to 2025 looks dramatic – a doubling! But it’s still far lower than under Biden in 2023! These are relatively small numbers, and they don’t show a steadily worsening trend. (And there are more aircraft operations than in 2023.) Air Traffic Control Was Broken Before Trump Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand. The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election. Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal. And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue. And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place. I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider. Fallows spends considerable space describing the 2009 Colgan Air crash near Buffalo – as the last U.S. airline crash with loss of life before American 5342. In fact, PenAir flight 3296 overran the runway at Unalaska in October 2019, killing a passenger.

His account has the Colgan Air plane accumulating ice until it becomes a “frigid brick.” He writes that by the time the captain recognized the problem, it “might already have become unflyable.” But that isn’t what the investigation found.

The FAA’s accident analysis says icing wasn’t a cause. When the stall warning activated, the airplane wasn’t yet stalled. The captain pulled back on the controls and put it into a stall. The crew had failed to monitor their airspeed and mishandled the approach.

Fallows points to deregulation and falling fares as sources of overcrowding. More people being able to afford to fly is a good thing, and flying is still safer than driving. The failure is an FAA air traffic organization system that hasn’t kept up with demand.

The Times has done excellent reporting on this subject. In August 2023, I covered its investigation into 46 close calls in one month and roughly 300 near collisions in a year. Staffing shortages, fatigue, outdated equipment and a culture that tolerated recurring warnings weren’t the result of the 2024 election.

Fallows discusses 132 union-represented FAA employees fired during the DOGE purge. Their union announced their reinstatement in March 2025. Firing them was disruptive, but he leaves out the reversal.

And recruiting gamers doesn’t establish that the FAA is lowering controller standards. The FAA has been growing the top of the funnel but there’s no indication that unqualified people are being advanced in training to a greater degree. I’ve criticized Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for counting initial trainee hires as progress, that strikes me as juking the stats but hasn’t been a safety issue.

And the Trump administration is doing modernization work that’s valuable and that’s been ignored for decades even if I’m skeptical that it’s close to enough because they don’t seem to be addressing the management problems at the FAA that created failed technology investment and decades-long controller shortages in the first place.

I’ve been critical of pouring money into the existing organization. We need to address how air traffic control is managed, how it buys equipment, how it finances long projects and how it’s held accountable for performance. We’d be far better off separating the air traffic control operator from its regulator, with stable funding and professional management, as Canada has done with its nonprofit provider.

Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. American Airlines is planning to add more flights from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), as part of a “gradual build” at its West Coast hub.

The Fort Worth-based carrier said it's about to add more LAX service to its schedule, with a focus on places executives describe as “important markets.”

It’s not clear whether that means entirely new routes or more frequent service on existing ones.

But either way, it comes after a long stretch where American seemed to focus far more of its attention on other parts of the country.

After the pandemic, the airline doubled down on its Sun Belt hubs, fortifying its strongholds in Dallas, Charlotte and Miami.

More recently, American reignited a longstanding Chicago turf war with United Airlines when it rapidly reinstated flying at O’Hare International Airport (ORD).

It looks like LAX will be its next project.

“We’re going to grow," American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said, speaking this week at an industry conference. "We’re going to tailor a schedule to the local market."

American has a smaller presence today in Southern California than it did several years ago.

This year, the carrier will operate about 32% fewer flights than it did in 2019, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

That’s a significant drop-off at LAX, which is one of the nation’s most competitive airports — and the only where each of the “big three” legacy carriers operates a hub.

By contrast, top L.A. rival Delta Air Lines has solidified its place as the airport’s top carrier, and plans operate its largest-ever schedule there next year.

United Airlines has also signaled it has future growth aspirations at LAX.

Speaking earlier this year, United’s top network planner, Patrick Quayle, lamented the fact that the airport is United’s only hub where there’s another airline with a larger presence.

“I don’t like being No. 2,” Quayle said during a company event at LAX in March. “And so I will, today, put Delta on notice here in L.A. — we will be No. 1, as well.”'

Pieper said the carrier needs to start by catering more to local Los Angeles customers — not just using the airport as a hub to route connecting traffic.

Doing that, he acknowledged, will likely require AA to offer a longer list of unique destinations.

Today, for instance, the carrier only serves four long-haul cities from LAX: London, Tokyo, Sydney and Auckland.

“People don’t only want to fly domestically. They want to go to Latin America. They want to go to Europe. They want to go to Asia,” Pieper said on stage this week at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York. “We need to be able to serve that with our own airplanes.”

United is clearly following that formula. The carrier already serves more than a half-dozen transpacific destinations from Southern California — and will expand next year with a new route to Osaka.

Delta, for its part, is also pointing to LAX as a linchpin of its Pacific growth aspirations, having launched nonstops to Hong Kong and Melbourne within the past year. New flights to Manila will begin in 2027.

Delta’s Los Angeles growth is also thanks, in part, to massive infrastructure investments the carrier has made at the hub which, among other things, is the only airport that's home to two Delta One Lounges.

American’s LAX digs, meanwhile, are still a construction zone.

The carrier had to consolidate its presence at the airport last year to make way for a rebuild of the airport's Terminal 5.

American will grow at a "gradual" pace, Pieper said, until its LAX facilities are "ready to roll." That's expected to happen in late 2028, at which point the carrier will have access to 30 gates.

“Our facility will be as good as anybody’s,” he said.

That, along with more flights — plus connectivity to American's Pacific partners like Qantas and Japan Airlines— have the airline more bullish about its hub that's grabbed far fewer headlines in recent years.

“You combine all those things together,” Pieper added, “I think we’re going to have a compelling offering there.”

#6154. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

#6153. Boeing Admits Its 737 Was Unsafe In Construction—Tells Door Plug Passengers Tough Luck On Punitive Damages

Boeing admits the 737 MAX 9 whose door plug blew out on Alaska Airlines flight 1282 “was not reasonably safe in construction” when it left the factory. But the planemaker is still fighting to keep passengers from collecting punitive damages. Its argument amounts to tough luck: the airplane was built in Washington, and Washington law generally doesn’t allow those damages. Boeing already won that argument against a mother and her son who was nearly sucked out of the opening in the fuselage. Another group of passengers is trying to show that the misconduct reaches back to decisions made at the company’s former Chicago headquarters – in order to access Illinois law. Boeing has formally acknowledged the defective construction that resulted in the blowout. On January 5, 2024, the Alaska Airlines jet was climbing out of Portland for Ontario, California when the plug departed the airplane at nearly 15,000 feet. The cabin rapidly depressurized. Oxygen masks dropped, belongings flew out, and the pilots brought the aircraft safely back to Portland. Spirit AeroSystems had built the fuselage. At Boeing’s Renton factory, the plug was opened for rivet repairs, then closed without reinstalling the four bolts that kept it from moving. I covered the whistleblower’s account of those missing bolts before investigators eventually confirmed them. The National Transportation Safety Board identified Boeing’s inadequate training, guidance and oversight as the probable cause. “Not reasonably safe in construction” is the language of Washington’s product liability law. A manufacturer can be strictly liable for injuries caused by a product that materially departed from its specifications when it left the manufacturer’s control. That leaves the fight to focus on the value of passenger injuries and whether Boeing can be punished beyond paying compensation. Last month, I wrote about Cynthia Tisher and her son, whose shirt was sucked off his body. According to their lawsuit, his seat pitched toward the opening. His mother held onto him, afraid he’d be pulled out, too. Other passengers helped them move away. Their federal lawsuit sought punitive damages against Boeing and Spirit AeroSystems. The judge ruled that Washington law governed and threw that request out. The blowout happened over Oregon, but the manufacturing failure occurred in Washington. The judge refused to reconsider. The current admission comes in litigation by a 47 plaintiff group suing Boeing, Spirit AeroSystems and Alaska Airlines, which claims Boeing management promised safety improvements to regulators and the public while failing to deliver them. They say decisions at the former Chicago headquarters helped produce the failures that sent this airplane out without its bolts. Boeing’s admission makes sense as litigation strategy. Boeing can argue testimony over how badly it acted is unnecessary to decide how much compensation each passenger deserves. And its strategy turns on getting punitive damages thrown out. #6152. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights Again: Will They Resume In December?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. Is that actually happening now, or what exactly is going on?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Interestingly, the airline has promised to provide a schedule update by November 12, 2026, but that date has now come and gone, and there was no update.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of December, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. The company does have a section on its travel updates page with FAQs, and one of the questions is “will the dates change again?” The answer is “we chose dates we are confident in,” but also notes that “if anything changes, you will hear from us first.”

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in December.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. That timeline has come and gone, and now the airline claims it’ll resume operations as of December 2026. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#6151. What Pilots Actually Do Hour-By-Hour On An 18-Hour Flight To New York JFK

SQ23/SQ24, Singapore Airlines' Airbus A350-900ULR flights between Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) and New York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), are a technological and logistical marvel. They cover an average of 9,537 miles (15,348 km), requiring the aircraft to remain in the sky for 18 to 19 hours. The world's longest flight also requires the personnel crewing it to remain sharp throughout.

Unsurprisingly, such a long flight time well exceeds the legal limits for a two-person flight crew. The flight crew is bolstered to four members, allowing each crew member to use the crew bunk for a four-hour-long and a 2.5-hour-long rest period. These crew members aren't just sticking the A350-900ULR on autopilot and relaxing. It is essential that they are well rested because they have essential duties to carry out while the aircraft is in flight.

In response to the rapidly approaching launch of Project Sunrise, Qantas' Airbus A350-1000ULR flights from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Sydney (SYD), Pilot Nick from Lessons from the Flight Deck gave his reflections on what it's like to fly for such extended periods. He said that:

"The metabolic cost is the constant vigilance. You’re monitoring six fuel tanks, four engine indicators, weather radar, traffic radar, ATC frequencies in three regions, oceanic crossing procedures, alternate airport availability over the next 1,500 miles, and the dozen subtle ways the airplane talks to you."

The table below is an impression of what pilots will do hour-by-hour on the Singapore to New York flight based on each crew member having a four-hour and a 2.5-hour rest allowance. This is an estimation based on an 18.5-hour flight time. It is clear that ultra-long-haul crew do far more than put the autopilot on and watch the world go by. They also do all of these duties in an environment where the air is thinner, and they are steadily dehydrated.

Departure from Singapore. This is a high-workload period, with potential assistance from the reserve crew. It is standard ultra-long-haul procedure to have all four crew members in the cockpit for takeoff and landing.

Initial cruising period with regular route, fuel, and weather checks, along with communication with air traffic control. The reserve crew may rest during this period.

Reserve crew returns from rest and takes over for the middle cruise. They'll receive a briefing from the primary crew on anything that they need to be made aware of. The primary captain and first officer may take a rest period.

The first crew returns, allowing the reserve crew to go for their long rest. This is a period of deep cruise, where remote Pacific airspace is crossed.

The reserve crew returns from rest, allowing the primary flight crew to go for their long period of rest. The reserve crew begins to prepare for arrival, with frequent air traffic control communications as they approach and enter US airspace.

The primary crew returns and receives a handover. The approach to New York begins. This is another high-workload period, with the crew having to navigate New York's exceptionally busy airspace before landing and taxiing to the gate.

One of the main activities that a pilot will be doing aboard Singapore Airlines' flight from Singapore to New York is resting, with each getting almost seven hours away from the flight deck. According to Executive Traveller, A350s come with two upstairs rest areas for pilots and cabin crew members.

The forward rest area, located above the foremost passenger cabin, is for pilots, while the rear rest area is for cabin crew. You can usually tell where these rest areas are because of the lack of central overhead luggage bins. The pilot rest area has two beds, while the cabin crew's space has six bunks. Pilots and crew stay safe in these rest areas because each is concealed behind a steadfast security door with a combination lock.

Singapore Airlines' flights from Singapore to New York don't just need pilots who are talented and well-rested. It also requires a plane, which is an undeniable engineering marvel. While the standard A350-900 can fly 8,500 nautical miles (15,742 km), the A350-900ULR, built bespoke for Singapore Airlines, can fly 9,700 nautical miles (17,964 km), with a maximum flight time of 20 hours.

The table below shows specifications for the A350-900ULR according to data from Aircraft Investigation. It shows a high maximum takeoff weight and fuel capacity and a substantially lower passenger capacity than is standard.

2 x Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-84 producing 84,190 lbf (374.5 kN)

The A350-900ULR will soon no longer be the longest-flying operational A350 variant. That is because of Qantas' Project Sunrise flights from SYD to LHR, which will make use of the upcoming A350-1000ULR. It will be able to fly commercially for up to 22 hours, with test flights exceeding this duration. That will require a reduced seating capacity of just 238 passengers to facilitate a new 4,400-gallon (20,000-liter) rear-center fuel tank.

The Project Sunrise philosophy for a better mechanical range is much like the A350-900ULR: more fuel and a higher maximum takeoff weight to sustain it. Airbus engineers have also been hard at work to show that the fuel system can operate safely, particularly in scenarios where large quantities of fuel have to be suddenly diverted.

This aircraft also makes use of the advantages that come as standard with all A350s, such as the 25% fuel efficiency improvement compared with jets of the previous generation. The Rolls-Royce Trent XWB, which exclusively powers this aircraft family, is also known for being among the world's most efficient widebody engines. The jet achieves all of this while having a 50% lower noise footprint than the A330.

As with Singapore Airlines' ultra-long-haul A350 flights, Project Sunrise trips will be crewed by four pilots, with long and short rest periods built into the schedule. All four pilots will usually make their way to the flight deck during the busiest periods, such as takeoff and landing. These systems have been standardized by ultra-long-haul carriers such as Singapore Airlines, Qantas, Emirates, and Cathay Pacific over the past 20 years.

Project Sunrise flights will cross between nine and eleven time zones, depending on the exact time of year that they will be flying. Qantas' circadian rhythm research will help pilots to recover more quickly from jet lag. Meal times, lighting, and rest cycles will need to be carefully choreographed with this need in mind.

Anticipation is growing for Project Sunrise, which is set to launch in 2027.

It isn't just the flight from Singapore to New York that is long enough for pilots to need plenty of rest. After all, Singapore Airlines also has plenty of other long routes that originate at Singapore Changi Airport (SIN). Away from New York, the North American destinations are Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) on the West Coast.

Singapore Airlines also flies its A350-900ULRs to five European airports. These are Manchester Airport (MAN), London Heathrow Airport (LHR), London Gatwick Airport (LGW), Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD), and Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat Airport (BCN). The final destination is Cape Town International (CPT).

The shortest of these routes is the 14-hour-and-ten-minute flight to Cape Town, which is operated via Johannesburg (JNB). This route is operated daily. The most frequent route is to San Francisco, which operates twice daily. The flights to LGW are less regular but peak at twice daily. Finally, the longest routes are to the two New York airports, both of which have a block time exceeding 19 hours.

The A350-900ULR deviates from Singapore Airlines' standard A350 layout of 253 seats across three classes. This features 42 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, 24 premium economy seats in a 2-4-2 layout, and 187 economy seats in a 3-3-3 configuration.

Singapore Airlines' A350-900ULR configuration has space for just 161 passengers, with 67 business class seats and room for 94 premium economy passengers. Meanwhile, there is no economy cabin, and the jets will soon be reconfigured with an even more exclusive 132-seat layout.

#6150. American Airlines Tells Flight Attendants To “Speak Up”—So Nearby Passengers Hear The Credit Card Pitch

American Airlines is teaching flight attendants to answer credit card questions loudly enough that nearby passengers hear the pitch, and to use stories about family, friends and other cardmembers to sell the benefits. A slide from recent flight attendant sales training lays out six tips. The most revealing one is “Speak up.” When one passenger asks about the card, American wants the answer to attract the attention of everyone around them. You may have declined the brochure, but the next row’s question is another chance to sell you. The slide presents these as best practices from fellow flight attendants: Share specific examples or stories. Use anecdotes from cardmembers, family or friends to explain how the card can help. Know your facts. Review the brochure and become comfortable discussing the benefits. Speak up. Answer questions at a volume that lets neighboring passengers hear. The slide says projecting your voice will attract their interest and curiosity. Take initiative. Coordinate with the other flight attendants about who makes the announcement and who walks the aisle. The cabin lights must remain on. Consider the timing of the flight and avoid making the announcement when the lights are off. Treat customer information confidentially. Never share, copy, photograph or retain personal information encountered on an application or screen. Knowing the product and protecting personal information are basic requirements. Coordinating the crew’s efforts means one announcement and brochures for passengers who want them. The stories, volume and lights are where this gets interesting. American Has More Riding On Its Citi Partnership Onboard credit card sales have been around for years. Under American’s old arrangement, Barclays had the inflight acquisition channel while Citi had other ways to acquire customers. The expanded Citi agreement brings those channels together under an exclusive U.S. card issuer. I’ve reported that the new relationship has been described to me as a joint venture. American’s stake goes beyond supplying miles and benefits to a bank. They’re more closely tied to the performance of the card business itself. A bank collects interchange, annual fees and interest, and pays for funding, credit losses, rewards and acquiring customers. Sharing in the economics of that business gives American more reason to care about who applies, who keeps the card, and who actually uses it. Getting another application on a flight is the beginning of that relationship. American also needs passengers to like the airline enough to keep it in their wallets. The sales push has been building. In May, I covered top inflight card sellers receiving a Clearwater, Florida getaway. Card approvals have also become accelerators in American’s flight attendant performance scoring. In August, I wrote about the push to get flight attendants more excited about selling. American was emphasizing both how much crew could earn and how providing better service would make passengers more receptive. The airline has a good audience for its card: people already buying its flights. Scott Kirby brought onboard pitches to United, which made them mandatory in 2018. These pitches work. Whether making them longer, louder or more frequent works well enough to justify annoying everyone else is a different calculation. Flight Attendants Object To Being Required To Train For Voluntary Sales On October 15, the Association of Professional Flight Attendants objected to American putting a 15-minute card sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. According to the union, management first tried to include it in third quarter training, backed off after objections, then inserted it in the fourth quarter package. Completing the module qualifies flight attendants for the program and makes them eligible for a $25 qualification reward. Selling remains voluntary. The union’s objection is that employees who haven’t chosen to sell are being required to take the sales training anyway, and that required training should focus on safety, security and performing their jobs. Some flight attendants welcome commissions on approved applications. Others resent being drawn into selling financial products. Read The Script, Tell Stories, And Make Sure Other Rows Hear American’s announcement guidance requires the approved script to be read verbatim. It should take about a minute and be delivered once per flight segment. That’s in tension with telling flight attendants to share cardmember stories. Adding an anecdote to the announcement would depart from the script. And then there’s the direction to speak loudly enough that neighboring passengers hear. An individual conversation becomes an unscripted sales pitch to several rows. I’ve criticized onboard claims about bonuses covering two roundtrips to Hawaii when that wasn’t generally realistic. “Know your facts” is good advice. But familiarity with a brochure doesn’t necessarily equip someone to explain award availability or the restrictions on a benefit. Encouraging personal stories, delivered so that other passengers overhear, brings regulatory risk into the sales process. Lights On Shouldn’t Become A Reason To Keep Passengers Awake The slide says, “The cabin lights must remain on,” followed by an instruction to consider flight timing and avoid announcements when the lights are off. Read together, that means choosing an already illuminated part of the flight. It doesn’t tell flight attendants to turn on the lights and wake everyone for a pitch. American’s separate guidance says to make the announcement at cruise, before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. It excludes late night and redeye flights and tells crew to refrain during delays, diversions and other disruptions. Having the lights on doesn’t erase those restrictions. I covered similar limits in 2019, when American told me they were existing training rather than new rules. One of the most annoying moments on a flight is the credit card pitch over the loudspeaker, being forced to hear the 1,000th monotonous message. The airplane environment is already stressful enough from noise and crowding. It even pieces through my noise-canceling headphones.

Crews should not have to do this. They don’t want to. We, the passengers, don’t want them to. This is just management and banks forcing unnecessary things on all of us. Block spam.

This is just another reason I hate unions.

The last American flight I took was later October out of Phoenix. I don’t remember where the crew was based, but we were not subjected to the credit card spiel. I was going to thank them when disembarking but then thought that could cause problems for them. The lack of the sales push was enjoyable.

They don’t “have” to do it. Numerous other jobs don’t have this requirement. Update that resume.

To strengthen branding and passenger participation for the Citi®/AAdvantage® Executive card, I recommend putting the American Airlines and Citi logos on every sheet of aircraft lavatory toilet paper. Because nothing says “premium travel experience” quite like a captive audience using premium two-ply corporate messaging.

Of course crews should have to do this. The credit cards are the profit center of the airlines. You can’t complain about things like AA’s profitability on the one hand and then not play a role in pitching the profit center on the other.

And – spoiler alert – this is why having screens at every seat is essential. You can put your phone down for 30-60 seconds when the wifi ads play. But screens that cannot be turned off that are directly in front of your face…

What you really want is a 45 second celebrity video pitching the card first, and then the FAs come back over the loudspeaker with the current offer and then walk down the aisle smiling with the applications.

And gamify it! Everyone can apply while they are in flight with free wifi. First one on the plane that applies gets an extra 10k miles on top of the already generous SUB. Second person gets an extra 5k. Something like that.

It’s only a matter of time before FAs that sell the most get to jump up the seniority ladder. I’d be pushing for that hard if I was negotiating the next union contract on the airline side.

@Peter — The excessive and needless financialization of everything is leading us to another totally avoidable 1929, lest we forget. Airlines do not need to be credit cards with wings (and many around the world simply are not).

@Johnny — The flight attendants unions don’t want any of this; they represent their members who don’t either.

@Mike P — Take down your silly Civil Peace flag, Ayn Rand.

From the merger of an airline that at one point, couldn’t give us a beverage without opening an advert for the card (that would be the tray table), or god forbid, let us walk through the middle of any corridor at PHL without tripping over about 10 carts hawking the card…

“The excessive and needless financialization of everything is leading us to another totally avoidable 1929,…”

“Take down your silly Civil Peace flag, Ayn Rand.” He can’t refute the argument, so he resorts to a mindless insult. Typical

I fly a lot. I have yet to see a single person take interest in credit cards being hawked or even ask a question.

Get over it people. David says he has never seen someone take an application. LOL. Many FAs for AA make over 2k per month in sales commissions. (Verified) 24k extra salary per year for doing something voluntary and momentarily is nothing to sneeze about. The 15 minute training is great as it gives the hardest workers more I kwowledge to make more money.

@1990 – I mean, that’s a bit of a leap. Ads are pervasive in our society. You want to go see a movie – you’re going to see some ads before that movie, including for other movies. You want to watch a sporting event? Ads, ads, ads. Riding on the subway? Ads everywhere – including on video ad screens. The idea that we should have some cultural expectation that an airline tube is some “sacred space” where folks can’t be subjected to an ad for 1-2 minutes… I don’t buy it.

Flight attendants are the fire safety not for marketing nor salesman.. terrible that the company exposed them to do sales like a market.. unacceptable…

@Peter — Bit of a false equivalency, but I’m not saying ‘no advertising at all,’ just saying, the crew shouldn’t need to do this; before free WiFi? On the screen? SkyMall? Ok, I get those. Why AA does this but Delta and United doesn’t (or at least not as overtly, lately.)

@Mike P — I expected you to say, “I do not recognize your jurisdiction.” Regardless, doubling-down on your strawmen doesn’t make them real… I accept your surrender.

I would like to see data on how many card applications are submitted on board.

@1990 – why shouldn’t the crew have to do this? One may wish the profit center of the airline was elsewhere, but the idea that employees should not even try to contribute to the profit center of the airline seems anathema to me. I realize that the crew is of course primarily there for safety reasons, but this is literally an extra 2 minutes of work, during a time that they are getting paid to work. It’s ok to pass out drinks but not sign up bonuses? It’s ok to sell buy on board cheese plates but not credit cards? Why?

Now, one can make a judgment as to whether their performance should be evaluated on pitching a credit card. Lots of factors as to why someone might sign up for a card. But in an over-saturated market, having more ‘touches’ with respect to a product helps to sell that product. And companies, in general, are in the business of making money, and therefore want to promote their products. And FAs are, you know, representatives of their company.

Personally I’m shocked that the airlines have not tried to better monetize the FAs they have working for them that do YouTube/tiktok or whatever on the side. You’d think those FAs would naturally want to pitch cards for their respective airlines.

I’ve always felt that if the credit card pitches were more bespoke, perhaps they would get more sign-ups?

#6149. Chase Sapphire Reserve Business Bonus: 200K Points Welcome Offer

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. Initially the offer for 200,000 points was supposed to end in September 2026, but it was extended, though we don’t know the official end date.

When it comes to applying for the Chase Sapphire Reserve Business, eligibility is unrelated to that of any other Chase Sapphire or Chase Ink card. That means if you’re eligible for business credit cards, you should be eligible for the welcome offer on this card, making this offer pretty widely available.

Keep in mind the general rules of applying for Chase cards, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though select business cards don’t count toward that total).

If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

The $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve Business is a pretty compelling business card. As is the case with many premium cards, the idea is that the annual fee can be justified based on a combination of the rewards structure, benefits, and airport lounge access, among other things.

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its plans. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier plans to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

It will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

Starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

Denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives said the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.
