#6147. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

I was a CK for 10 years thanks to my former employer (we did a lot of long haul international travel in business class). The automatic domestic upgrades were nice, the Flagship Lounge access impressed friends and family (said one experienced traveler when we were handed champagne at the FL in ORD, "Wow, I heard stories about this but assumed it was an urban legend"), the expediters at certain international airports were helpful, and getting to the front of the lines during storms and chaotic days like today was reassuring. The most important benefit, though, was the elimination of hassles -- the tight connection, the missed flight and, in one memorable case, helping my daughter get out of Paris in the midst of a nationwide transportation strike when she wasn't even flying AA. My colleagues and I referred to the CK team as "the angels" because they could perform miracles. We often joked (sort of) that our employer could cancel our health insurance, seize our retirement benefits, but that they would have to pry our CK card out of our cold, dead hands. When I left for a new position at a much smaller company, I was able to keep my CK status for the remainder of the program year (about six months). Watching it flip to "Executive Platinum" at 12:01 am on March 1 -- yes, I stayed up to mourn -- was unnerving, but somehow I survived...

#6146. An Intellectual History of California’s Proposition 40

How a French academic research project and an elite public university nearly took down the Golden State’s venture capital economy with a wealth tax

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

On November 3, California voters narrowly rejected Proposition 40, a 5 percent tax on the net worth of the state’s billionaires. That outcome was not assured. In September, the measure led 52 percent to 46 percent in the Public Policy Institute of California’s survey of likely voters. Had it passed, the state that received 62 percent of all U.S. venture capital dollars in 2025 would have begun taxing founders on the paper value of companies, potentially driving them elsewhere.

The union that sponsored Proposition 40, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, supplied the signatures and most of the campaign money. The idea came from an intellectual movement that began with the French economist Thomas Piketty, found an institutional home at the University of California, Berkeley, and received financing from the foundation of a Boston insurance executive.

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

#6145. Why Your Airline Credit Card Is Worth Keeping—But Rarely Useful For Spending

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

An airline credit card can save you enough in checked bag fees to justify keeping it, but cost you hundreds of dollars in rewards if you use it for your spending.

In this week’s episode of Airlines Confidential, Ed Pizzarello favored flexible bank points while former American AAdvantage President Maya Leibman preferred the simplicity of airline and hotel cards. Later, she recalled something an unnamed former loyalty program president had told her:

“people will pay anything for a free flight.”

For at least the last decade and a half I’ve been arguing that getting an airline card for benefits doesn’t mean it should become your default payment method, and that there are different distinct reasons to get a card besides payment processing (and bundled financing): An initial bonus. Spending enough to earn a large bonus can make sense even when the card’s normal earning rate isn’t attractive. And the bonus can be a reason to apply for the card, but you still need to decide if it’s worth using for ongoing spend. Benefits that come with keeping it. Checked bags, boarding benefits, lounge access or an anniversary certificate can justify the annual fee. The card may belong in the sock drawer, not your wallet, if actual rewards for spend aren’t great enough. Rewards for actual spending. This is where the return on the next dollar matters, including any status credit or spending threshold you’re working towards. Some benefits require paying with the card. Make the purchases needed to use those benefits. That still doesn’t make the card the best choice for the rest of your spending. Holding a UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) is great if you fly United because you earn more miles, and then you spend fewer miles on your redemptions. That doesn’t require spending on the card itself. What Your Free Flight Actually Costs Put $30,000 of spending on a card earning one airline mile per dollar, and you earn 30,000 miles. Put the same spending on a 2% cash back card and you earn $600. You wouldn’t pay 2 cents per mile to buy miles, but that’s what you’re doing at 1 mile per dollar of spend, leaving aside other benefits from that spending (such as credit towards airline status). If you use those 30,000 miles for a flight you could have bought for $300. You’ve given up $600 to avoid paying $300. That’s just dumb. If the same miles buy a trip you’d actually pay $900 for (not just one that’s priced at $900 but where you’re unlikely to spend that), it’s anothe matter. That’s why airline miles make more sense for premium cabin international awards than domestic coach ones – because there’s generally more leverage when redeeming the points. And if the spending also earns credit towards status or another useful benefit, it can make sense also. Scott McCartney compared cash back with the value of individual hotel points and airline miles. But you have to multiply the value of each point by how many you earn. A half-cent point earned twice per dollar is a 1% return. The same point earned six times per dollar is 3%. You Can Earn Airline Miles Without An Airline Card Leibman’s preference for simplicity is fine as far as it goes, but bank points don’t require abandoning airline awards. You can keep points flexible – such as on a Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) or a Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) – and transfer them when you find the award you want. Even American, which was long unusually difficult to access through transferable bank points, is now a Citi transfer partner. The same bank sells you American’s credit card and a competing currency that can become American miles or points in other programs. Spend on a Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) or a Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) and transfer to AAdvantage. That flexibility lets you choose where to redeem instead of committing all your earnings before you know which program has the best deal. American’s cards earn Loyalty Points towards status and it’s uncapped. And, as I recently explained about the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard®, eligible employee-card spending can earn status credit for both the employee and the primary cardmember at the same time. That’s a reason I’d consider moving spending: earning status for my wife as well as myself. For at least the last decade and a half I’ve been arguing that getting an airline card for benefits doesn’t mean it should become your default payment method, and that there are different distinct reasons to get a card besides payment processing (and bundled financing):

An initial bonus. Spending enough to earn a large bonus can make sense even when the card’s normal earning rate isn’t attractive. And the bonus can be a reason to apply for the card, but you still need to decide if it’s worth using for ongoing spend. Benefits that come with keeping it. Checked bags, boarding benefits, lounge access or an anniversary certificate can justify the annual fee. The card may belong in the sock drawer, not your wallet, if actual rewards for spend aren’t great enough. Rewards for actual spending. This is where the return on the next dollar matters, including any status credit or spending threshold you’re working towards.

Some benefits require paying with the card. Make the purchases needed to use those benefits. That still doesn’t make the card the best choice for the rest of your spending. Holding a UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) is great if you fly United because you earn more miles, and then you spend fewer miles on your redemptions. That doesn’t require spending on the card itself.

Put $30,000 of spending on a card earning one airline mile per dollar, and you earn 30,000 miles. Put the same spending on a 2% cash back card and you earn $600. You wouldn’t pay 2 cents per mile to buy miles, but that’s what you’re doing at 1 mile per dollar of spend, leaving aside other benefits from that spending (such as credit towards airline status). If you use those 30,000 miles for a flight you could have bought for $300. You’ve given up $600 to avoid paying $300. That’s just dumb. If the same miles buy a trip you’d actually pay $900 for (not just one that’s priced at $900 but where you’re unlikely to spend that), it’s anothe matter. That’s why airline miles make more sense for premium cabin international awards than domestic coach ones – because there’s generally more leverage when redeeming the points. And if the spending also earns credit towards status or another useful benefit, it can make sense also. Scott McCartney compared cash back with the value of individual hotel points and airline miles. But you have to multiply the value of each point by how many you earn. A half-cent point earned twice per dollar is a 1% return. The same point earned six times per dollar is 3%. You Can Earn Airline Miles Without An Airline Card Leibman’s preference for simplicity is fine as far as it goes, but bank points don’t require abandoning airline awards. You can keep points flexible – such as on a Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) or a Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) – and transfer them when you find the award you want. Even American, which was long unusually difficult to access through transferable bank points, is now a Citi transfer partner. The same bank sells you American’s credit card and a competing currency that can become American miles or points in other programs. Spend on a Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) or a Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) and transfer to AAdvantage. That flexibility lets you choose where to redeem instead of committing all your earnings before you know which program has the best deal. American’s cards earn Loyalty Points towards status and it’s uncapped. And, as I recently explained about the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard®, eligible employee-card spending can earn status credit for both the employee and the primary cardmember at the same time. That’s a reason I’d consider moving spending: earning status for my wife as well as myself. #6144. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#6143. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

Lockers for my stuff so I can nap in peace or better yet locker usage without being in the lounge so that I can roam the airport/city to walk, stretch out and buy useless stuff. I'm willing to bet if food was minimal, traffic will die down a lot.

#6142. Chase’s New $350 IHG Card Offers 200,000 Points—Plus $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (See rates and fees)

Chase’s new $350 annual fee IHG credit card can return $400 in flight credits before your first renewal, on top of a 200,000-point initial bonus. It also gives you enough elite nights to choose a confirmable suite upgrade without first earning those nights through hotel stays.

I covered the changes to Chase’s IHG card portfolio earlier, but the new IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card deserves a good look. I’ve generally thought of IHG cards as something to get for the bonus and keep for the benefits. This one gives me a reason to consider putting some spending on it, too.

And Chase confirmed to me that its elite nights stack with those from other IHG cards. For someone who already has both the Premier and Business cards, adding Premier Select means 50 annual elite nights total starting with the existing cards’ January 2027 deposits which is enough to choose hotel lounge membership without stays or spending.

The launch offer lets you earn 200,000 IHG points after $5,000 in purchases within three months of account opening. At my half-cent valuation, the 200,000-point bonus is worth $1,000. Having another IHG personal or business card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The published restriction applies to current holders of this particular card, and previous holders who received its new cardmember bonus offer within the past 24 months. Chase told me that 5/24 applies. How To Get $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal The card offers a $200 airline statement credit per calendar year through December 31, 2027. It takes a single purchase of at least $250 in flight tickets booked directly with an airline. Open the card this fall, make a qualifying purchase in 2026, and make another in 2027 before your first anniversary. That’s $400 back against airfare you’d otherwise buy, compared with a $350 first-year fee. The spending has to land in the appropriate calendar year, so I wouldn’t leave the December purchase until the last minute. That’s a particularly good first year deal. For ongoing value, one $200 airline credit leaves $150 of annual fee to justify. The currently published benefit ends in 2027, so we’ll see if it continues after that. But $150 should not be hard. The Free Night And Hotel Dining Benefits Additional key benefits include: A free night after each account anniversary, capped at 60,000 points. You can add your own points for a more expensive redemption. A 90,000-point night would take the certificate plus 30,000 points. The stay must be completed within 12 months of issuance. This starts at your first anniversary. Up to $300 a year in IHG Food & Beverage Rewards. You get one $75 voucher each quarter. It expires at the end of the quarter, must be applied to eligible charges on your room folio during a participating stay, and any unused balance disappears when you redeem it (e.g. use just $45 and you lose the other $30). Every fourth night free on qualifying points stays. This applies to consecutive standard room award nights at the same hotel. Certificates don’t substitute for the points nights needed to trigger it. Automatic Platinum status. That brings benefits including upgrades subject to availability, but it doesn’t include Diamond’s breakfast welcome amenity choice. Up to $50 in United TravelBank cash. Register to receive $25 in each half of the year. The first-half deposit expires July 15 and the second-half deposit expires January 15 of the following year. I wouldn’t value the dining vouchers at $300 unless I already expected eligible hotel dining in every quarter. And while a 60,000 point certificate can replace $300 worth of points at my valuation, it’s less flexible than 60,000 points in an account since you have to use it for one night before it expires. There are smaller benefits as well like an application fee credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or NEXUS; no foreign transaction fees; and a 30% points-purchase discount that doesn’t stack with other purchase promotions. There’s also a year of DoorDash DashPass and three months of Instacart+, with enrollment by December 31, 2027, plus monthly $10 non-restaurant DoorDash and $10 Instacart offers through that date while the relevant membership is active. A Suite Upgrade Choice Without 20 Hotel Nights The card comes with 20 elite night credits on opening and annually thereafter. Chase allows six to eight weeks for the initial credits, with subsequent annual deposits due by February 1. They count toward both elite status and Milestone Rewards. At the 20-night milestone you can choose 5,000 points, two $20 Food & Beverage Rewards, or one confirmable suite upgrade. I’d take the upgrade. That upgrade can cover an eligible stay of up to five nights, including a points stay. You call IHG between 14 days and 24 hours before arrival to confirm an available entry-level suite. It isn’t a promise that every hotel will have a suite for your dates, and the rules exclude free night certificates and certain brands and rates. The award expires 12 months after selection. At 40 nights you get two milestone choices, which can include both annual hotel lounge membership and another confirmable suite upgrade. The lounge membership covers the member and one guest on eligible stays at hotels with a participating lounge. It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year. Elite Nights Stack Across Cards Chase confirmed to me: Cardmembers who hold multiple IHG One Rewards Credit Cards will receive the applicable Elite Night Credits each card provides. For existing cardmembers, annual ENCs will first be deposited in January 2027. New accounts opened on or after October 1, 2026, will receive their applicable ENCs upon card opening. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. For existing cardholders adding Premier Select, the January 2027 deposits mean: Premier Select plus either Premier or Business: 35 annual elite nights. That leaves just five qualifying hotel nights to reach the 40-night lounge-membership choice. Premier Select plus both Premier and Business: 50 annual elite nights. That gets you the 40-night choices, including lounge membership and a suite upgrade, plus the 50-night reward choice, without hotel stays or card spending. The timing is different for new accounts: cards opened on or after October 1 qualify for their opening credits now. Existing accounts receive their first annual deposits in January. And the spending counters stay separate—$3,000 on one card and $2,000 on another won’t combine into a $5,000 block that earns two nights. $15,000 In Spending Is More Interesting Than It First Looks The card earns 12 points per dollar at participating IHG hotels, 6 on dining and other travel, and 3 on other purchases. At half a cent per point, those are returns of 6%, 3% and 1.5%. Chase’s advertised “up to 28X” at IHG includes base hotel program earnings and the Platinum bonus not just the rewards for credit card spend. But there are spending rewards that change the calculation. You earn two elite nights per $5,000 in purchases, plus five additional nights and 20,000 bonus points at $15,000 in calendar-year spending. Here’s what the card alone produces, assuming the nights credit in the same calendar year. The spending thresholds are cumulative so actual qualifying hotel nights would add to these totals. Calendar-Year Spending   Total Card Elite Nights   Additional Spending Benefits Earned $0   20   20-night milestone choice $15,000   31: 20 + 6 + 5   20,000 bonus points; also reaches the 30-night milestone $25,000   35: 20 + 10 + 5   Diamond status through the following calendar year $40,000   41: 20 + 16 + 5   Additional free night capped at 60,000 points, with points top-up allowed; also reaches the 40-night milestone On $15,000 of purchases earning 3 points per dollar, you’d receive 45,000 points plus the 20,000-point spending bonus. That’s 65,000 points worth $325 at my valuation, compared with $300 from a 2% cash back card, before assigning anything to the eleven additional elite nights or the 30-night milestone choice. That’s better than just a basic return of just 3 points per dollar which I view as about 1.5%. At $40,000, you’d have 140,000 points from those same unbonused purchases and the spending bonus, worth $700 versus $800 in cash back. You’d also have Diamond status, the additional free night, and enough nights to select lounge membership and another suite upgrade. The launch offer lets you earn 200,000 IHG points after $5,000 in purchases within three months of account opening. At my half-cent valuation, the 200,000-point bonus is worth $1,000.

Having another IHG personal or business card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The published restriction applies to current holders of this particular card, and previous holders who received its new cardmember bonus offer within the past 24 months. Chase told me that 5/24 applies.

The card offers a $200 airline statement credit per calendar year through December 31, 2027. It takes a single purchase of at least $250 in flight tickets booked directly with an airline. Open the card this fall, make a qualifying purchase in 2026, and make another in 2027 before your first anniversary. That’s $400 back against airfare you’d otherwise buy, compared with a $350 first-year fee. The spending has to land in the appropriate calendar year, so I wouldn’t leave the December purchase until the last minute. That’s a particularly good first year deal. For ongoing value, one $200 airline credit leaves $150 of annual fee to justify. The currently published benefit ends in 2027, so we’ll see if it continues after that. But $150 should not be hard. The Free Night And Hotel Dining Benefits Additional key benefits include: A free night after each account anniversary, capped at 60,000 points. You can add your own points for a more expensive redemption. A 90,000-point night would take the certificate plus 30,000 points. The stay must be completed within 12 months of issuance. This starts at your first anniversary. Up to $300 a year in IHG Food & Beverage Rewards. You get one $75 voucher each quarter. It expires at the end of the quarter, must be applied to eligible charges on your room folio during a participating stay, and any unused balance disappears when you redeem it (e.g. use just $45 and you lose the other $30). Every fourth night free on qualifying points stays. This applies to consecutive standard room award nights at the same hotel. Certificates don’t substitute for the points nights needed to trigger it. Automatic Platinum status. That brings benefits including upgrades subject to availability, but it doesn’t include Diamond’s breakfast welcome amenity choice. Up to $50 in United TravelBank cash. Register to receive $25 in each half of the year. The first-half deposit expires July 15 and the second-half deposit expires January 15 of the following year. I wouldn’t value the dining vouchers at $300 unless I already expected eligible hotel dining in every quarter. And while a 60,000 point certificate can replace $300 worth of points at my valuation, it’s less flexible than 60,000 points in an account since you have to use it for one night before it expires. There are smaller benefits as well like an application fee credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or NEXUS; no foreign transaction fees; and a 30% points-purchase discount that doesn’t stack with other purchase promotions. There’s also a year of DoorDash DashPass and three months of Instacart+, with enrollment by December 31, 2027, plus monthly $10 non-restaurant DoorDash and $10 Instacart offers through that date while the relevant membership is active. A Suite Upgrade Choice Without 20 Hotel Nights The card comes with 20 elite night credits on opening and annually thereafter. Chase allows six to eight weeks for the initial credits, with subsequent annual deposits due by February 1. They count toward both elite status and Milestone Rewards. At the 20-night milestone you can choose 5,000 points, two $20 Food & Beverage Rewards, or one confirmable suite upgrade. I’d take the upgrade. That upgrade can cover an eligible stay of up to five nights, including a points stay. You call IHG between 14 days and 24 hours before arrival to confirm an available entry-level suite. It isn’t a promise that every hotel will have a suite for your dates, and the rules exclude free night certificates and certain brands and rates. The award expires 12 months after selection. At 40 nights you get two milestone choices, which can include both annual hotel lounge membership and another confirmable suite upgrade. The lounge membership covers the member and one guest on eligible stays at hotels with a participating lounge. It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. Some nuance here – the lounge membership lasts the year you redeem the award, which may be up to 90 days after “you earn the milestone”. That is, if one earns the milestone today, it may be redeemed up though about mid February 2027. Redeeming today would provide lounge membership for the remainder of 2026 plus 2027. Deferring until January 1, 2027, would provide lounge membership for all of 2027 and 2028.

#6141. Hilton Honors Amex Card Bonus: Points + Free Night Award Welcome Offers

For applications through January 13, 2027, American Express and Hilton are offering increased welcome offers on their four co-branded credit cards, and these are among the best deals we’ve seen on the cards. With these lucrative welcome offers, you can earn both points and an uncapped free night award (valid at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, which is Hilton’s highest award cost for standard room redemptions).

Not only are these great welcome offers, but these cards offer valuable benefits for those who stay at Hiltons with any frequency, so if you travel often, it’s worth having (at least) one of these cards in your wallet. In particular, I love the free night awards, given that they can even be redeemed at top Waldorf Astoria or Conrad hotels, or even Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties.

Link: Learn more about the Hilton Honors American Express Card, Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card, Hilton Honors American Express Business Card, and Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card

For applications through January 13, 2027, Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards are offering limited time welcome offers, which are among the best that we’ve ever seen on these cards.

In addition to offering bonus points, three of the cards also include a free night award as part of the bonus (and the fourth card offers a free night award as an annual benefit, including the first year). For the purposes of framing the value of the points, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each.

These are standard Hilton Honors free night awards, which can be redeemed at a vast majority of Hilton Honors properties around the world for a standard room, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I’d consider this to be the single most valuable hotel credit card free night award out there, given that it can be redeemed at a property costing up to 250,000 points per night.

Let’s go over the details of the Hilton card bonuses, from least premium to most premium. First, below is a quick chart comparing the Hilton Honors Amex welcome offers (let me emphasize that the welcome offer value doesn’t factor in the free night awards, which arguably make up a majority of the value with these offers).

The Hilton Honors American Express Card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 70,000 Hilton Honors bonus points plus a free night award after spending $2,000 within the first six months.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Honors Amex Card features the following perks in the long run:

Read a full review of the Hilton Honors Amex Card.

The Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card has a $150 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 130,000 Hilton Honors bonus points plus a free night award after spending $3,000 within the first six months.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Honors Surpass Card features the following ongoing benefits:

Read a full review of the Hilton Honors Surpass Card.

The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card has a $195 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 150,000 Hilton Honors bonus points plus a free night award after spending $8,000 within the first six months.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Honors Business Card features the following perks in the long run:

Read a full review of the Hilton Honors Business Card.

The Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card has a $550 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and for applications through January 13, 2027, the card has a limited time welcome offer of 200,000 Hilton Honors bonus points after spending $6,000 within the first six months.

While not explicitly being marketed as part of the welcome offer, keep in mind the card always offers a free night award on an annual basis, including the year in which you open the card. So for all practical purposes, think of the welcome offer as being 200,000 points plus a free night award.

Beyond the welcome offer, the Hilton Aspire Card features the following ongoing benefits:

Read a full review of the Hilton Aspire Card.

Anecdotally Hilton Honors Amex cards are pretty easy to be approved for:

If you’re trying to decide which of these offers makes the most sense, here are a few considerations:

For applications through January 13, 2027, Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards are offering limited time welcome offers. Three of the four cards are offering points plus a free night award, while the most premium card is offering a best-ever offer in terms of the number of points you can earn.

If you’re looking for a no annual fee card, then the Hilton Honors American Express Card is for you. Meanwhile, if you’re looking for a card with stronger perks and an even better bonus, I recommend the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card or Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card. The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card is also a good option for small businesses.

#6140. Three Cheers for Gridlock

Democrats are about to get a stern lesson in the separation of powers.

Senator Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.), President Donald Trump, and Senator Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.)

Alex Wong/Getty Images, Jonathan Ernst, Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

The ballots from last week’s midterms haven’t even all been counted and congressional Democrats are already all over your money like Jensen Huang on a sexy Chinese spy.

Senator Bernie Sanders wasted no time in renewing his call for Congress to pass Medicare for All, citing various polls showing that the public favors socialized health care dressed up as a modest Medicare expansion. According to a recent White House Council of Economic Advisers estimate, Sanders’s plan would increase federal spending by $32 trillion over the next decade.

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

Cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The route originally launched in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

It was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun new ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

The Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

It was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are currently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.)

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

Not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced new service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Related: 9 flight award booking hacks every traveler should know

Of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Award search tools are increasingly a big part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

Flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly launched (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.

#6138. Former Hyatt Renovation Halted After Inspectors Find Families Living Inside—And Rooms Chained From The Outside

Inspectors entered the closed former Hyatt Regency Dearborn and found families living upstairs. Hotel room doors on the property were chained and padlocked from the outside. Two days later, police searched. The families were gone. Officers closed the case after about a two hour search. On September 22, inspectors found, On the 12th floor: Dozens of people, including young children, with groceries, suitcases, puppies and dog feces. On the 10th floor: Doors chained and padlocked from outside, apparently impossible to unlock from within. In a hallway: Packaging for a large machete (though no machete was seen). A project manager initially suggested a worker’s family was visiting for lunch. A guard said up to 100 people had lived there over the previous year, and his bosses told him to ignore residents. The hotel’s owner denied knowing families were living there. Police said the locked rooms secured workers’ equipment and their search found no criminal activity, such as human trafficking. This is the Edward Hotel and Convention Center which once had a revolving restaurant and a monorail connection to Fairlane Town Center. It left Hyatt in 2012, and the city shut it down in 2018. The property was acquired in 2016 for $20 million. That owner faced criminal charges in Canada that were ultimately withdrawn. It was sold in 2021 in a forfeiture sale for $18.25 million. The buyer defaulted on the mortgage and in 2024 it was auctioned by the sheriff for $9.85 million, but apparently an auction of the distressed note and sheriff’s deed ended at $5.925 million. According to Dearborn City Council materials from October 2024, Hyatt had expressed interest in returning if sufficient capital investment could be secured. This exterior photo is from September 2024, by Warren LeMay via Wikipedia. But Wait, It Gets Worse According to a local activist a supposed immigration agent had thrown someone to the floor and killed a dog by throwing it through glass. She later reached an injured woman inside, who told her: “I don’t know how to get out.” The activist also said workers reported wages withheld because employers supposedly used the money to bribe immigration agents and being told: “Look, we’re keeping ICE away from you. Now you have to work for free.” Immigration and Customs Enforcement denies conducting enforcement at the hotel. A Detroit councilwoman’s office says Mayor Abdullah Hammoud was alerted September 18, four days before the inspection. Reportedly police failed to review the hotel’s surveillance video before closing the investigation. The Hotel Was Supposed To Make A Comeback Dearborn has sunk subsidies into the hotel’s redevelopment plans. In December 2025, the city approved a 12-year property tax exemption and a 30-year brownfield plan for a redevelopment involving a $45 million rehabilitation, plus acquisition costs. The project would combine hotel rooms, apartments and convention space. In January, the mayor said the hotel would return as a Hilton, with a hoped-for opening by the end of 2026. Here’s a walk-through of the property from before the current state of affairs: I don’t think the former Hyatt Regency Dearborn is re-opening as a Hilton in 2026. It strikes me that the city isn’t adequately investigating issues at a redevelopment site that it’s subsidizing.
