#6137. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

#6134. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

#6133. Bitter Christmas: A Bah Humbug to Moviemaking

Almodóvar’s loss of creativity and camp is cause for alarm.

Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas explores his own recent creative crisis. Using a prismatic structure, Almodóvar tells three stories that reflect one another with diminishing returns. These interwoven tales never blend due to the blockage suffered by gay male Spanish filmmaker Raul (Leonardo Sbaraglia, styled with a storm of gray-white hair to resemble Almodóvar himself). Viewers must do a meta reading about the nature and purpose of filmmaking and artistic expression.

Almodóvar makes the mistake of introducing Raul’s imaginary stories before revealing their real-life source. As Bitter Christmas becomes more and more convoluted and uninvolving, it undeniably reflects a peculiar Millennial crisis: the internalized post-Covid repression that has paralyzed many filmmakers. Once the most exciting filmmaker of the late 1980s, Almodóvar now suffers the same malaise that has also befallen comparable colleagues Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. You don’t have to be a cinephile to realize that most contemporary filmmakers are bereft of fresh ideas and genuine inspiration.

Before getting to that core Raul/Almodóvar narrative, Bitter Christmas first presents stories in which a female filmmaker Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) imagines the drama of a woman, Patrizia (Victoria Luengo), who feels her same maladies and longs to escape an unhappy marriage, and then another woman, Natalia (Milena Smit), who is deep in mourning. This narrative contraption is the worst example of a gay male’s feminine empathy that Almodóvar has ever contrived. Unlike Law of Desire and Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, this film lacks the camp buoyancy that made Almodóvar a comic hybrid of Jean Cocteau and Luis Buñuel, putting him at the vanguard of the world’s evolving sexual sophistication.

Now foregrounding his identification with female experience, Almodóvar seems to cater to political correctness rather than flout it. That a once-major pop artist can no longer make irresistible movies but instead succumbs to patronizing political trends is a cause for alarm more significant than any particular misbegotten film.

In one subplot, Raul is told, “You can lie in your life but not in your fiction,” referring to how he mistreats his partner Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) while also exploiting his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) as fodder for his newest script.

This contorted set-up suggests that Almodóvar feels pressure to join the global progressivism that a former bad boy of the Spanish underground is now obliged to endorse. That’s why the ultra-bourgeois Bitter Christmas lacks comedy and eroticism. Raul’s sex life is transferred to the shallow, quasi-porn of Elsa’s relationship with boytoy Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a firefighter and part-time stripper (probably an homage to the superior João Pedro Rodrigues satire Will-O’-the-Wisp.

Almodóvar has lost audacity. Sadness pervades the movie. Its title comes from “Amarga Navidad” (“Bitter Christmas”), a ranchera (folk torch song) performed by Chavela Vargas. But this is the least impassioned film Almodóvar has made; its emotions are distanced by artifice — in imagination, storytelling, and performance. The projection of Raul/Almodóvar’s true feelings into fakery distances real life so much that the melodrama is drab. It’s not fabulous or funny (despite ornamental design and another urgent Alberto Iglesias score), but arid like Lanzarote, the black-sand volcanic island where make-believe characters Elsa and Victoria retreat into a dull version of Ingmar Bergman’s Persona — another go at Almodóvar’s insipid The Room Next Door. None of these meta-antics result in moral summation like Fellini’s masterpieces La Dolce Vita and Otto e mezzo.

Although Almodóvar avoids obvious political pronouncement like those that ruined Killers of the Flower Moon, West Side Story, and Disclosure Day, the twisted autobiographical aspects of Bitter Christmas still indicate that he suffers a similar personal liberal panic. (Unlike Spielberg and Scorsese, Almodóvar has made foolish partisan comments on American politics.) Almodóvar can’t escape the private anxiety that Scorsese and Spielberg experience along with the rest of us. Almodóvar’s inability to disentangle primal emotional need from political confusion is evident on screen in Bitter Christmas and ultimately unsatisfying.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6132. FAA Ground Stop: Every U.S. Airport Departure Halted As Air Traffic Control Communications Fail

The FAA has ordered departures stopped at every U.S. airport after a communications failure hit air traffic control centers across the country. Planes are being held on the ground as Friday afternoon travelers head into the weekend, with no announced time for flights to resume. Aircraft already in the air are being allowed to continue and land. There isn’t a general order to put every plane down at the nearest airport, like 9/11. The FAA says inbound international flights will be handled individually. The agency’s national ground stop advisory, issued at 3:54 p.m. Eastern on November 13: DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS. The FAA’s status board lists the reason as “EQUIPMENT / OUTAGE.” This is in place “until further notice.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirms a communications issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, with FAA technicians investigating. These are the facilities that handle aircraft flying between airport areas. Secretary Sean Duffy’s statement — November 13, 2026 Aviation watchdog JonNYC reported widespread frequency failures before the nationwide order. His initial reports named Boston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center and New York Approach, with Boston Approach also experiencing problems. Some New York Center sectors reportedly couldn’t accept traffic. Then things spread. Chicago O’Hare and Midway were placed under ground stops before the nationwide halt. JonNYC’s reports of air traffic control frequency failures — November 13, 2026 A cockpit message shared by JonNYC tells crews: ATTENTION ALL CREWS- PER FAA GUIDANCE, ALL DEPARTURES ARE STOPPED NATIONWIDE. PLEASE STANDBY FOR FURTHER INFORMATION. UPDATE IN 15 https://t.co/XQvj5neLF2 — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 13, 2026 A Software Upgrade Issue Has Been Reported The New York Post reports that an unnamed source points to a possible software upgrade behind the disruption. The FAA hasn’t identified the failed system or what triggered the outage. However, controller and pilot message boards have several more specific accounts. In Reddit’s air traffic control forum, one commenter writes, “Allegedly all [backup emergency communications] sites on the east coast went out at the same time. They’re trying to figure out why.” Another commenter describes those backups as a third radio system, with separate radios, antennas, power and communications links. If the reported simultaneous failures are accurate, the behavior of those backups becomes a particularly important part of the investigation. In a second controller forum, a poster reports, “A lot of the frequencies and landlines in the Houston area started going hot on their own randomly over the past hour.” That adds a report of unexpected activity on both radio and telephone connections. In the flying forum, a commenter says the word they’re hearing is a communications problem between en route facilities. Others report hearing controllers announce the nationwide stop in Seattle and Redmond. JonNYC reports facilities preparing for “ATC Zero,” the status used when a facility can’t provide air traffic services. The FAA Has A Long History Of Technology Failures The closest recent comparison is the January 11, 2023 nationwide ground stop, when the system that provides safety notices to pilots failed. The FAA later traced that outage to contractors accidentally deleting files while trying to correct synchronization between the primary database and a backup. That was only the second nationwide ground stop, after 9/11. In March I covered an overheated circuit board that disrupted five Washington area airports. Transportation researcher Bob Poole reported that the board was part of a 25 year old voice switch, describing an FAA maintenance policy that allowed equipment to run until it failed, with fewer technicians and inadequate training to keep old systems going. The FAA’s own equipment photos illustrate what they’ve been working with: When I reviewed the administration’s air traffic control overhaul, the plan called for replacing 25,000 analog radios and 800 voice switches, along with moving thousands of sites off legacy telecommunications connections. My criticism was that the same organization that spent decades failing to deliver upgrades would be asked to deliver another one. The FAA regulates itself, both running the system and regulating its safety, while long term capital projects depend on annual congressional appropriations. Buying equipment doesn’t fix bad incentives or project management. Earlier today, the administration asked Congress for another $30.1 billion in aviation funding, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. The new request also includes money for control towers and airport projects. They want taxpayers bailing out the system, rather than airlines and passengers. Even a quick repair won’t immediately put the airlines back on schedule. Planes held now will be late for their next flights, connecting passengers will miss departures, and crews can run out of permitted duty time. Then with planes out of position, disruptions continue. The FAA’s own equipment photos illustrate what they’ve been working with:

When I reviewed the administration’s air traffic control overhaul, the plan called for replacing 25,000 analog radios and 800 voice switches, along with moving thousands of sites off legacy telecommunications connections.

My criticism was that the same organization that spent decades failing to deliver upgrades would be asked to deliver another one. The FAA regulates itself, both running the system and regulating its safety, while long term capital projects depend on annual congressional appropriations. Buying equipment doesn’t fix bad incentives or project management.

Earlier today, the administration asked Congress for another $30.1 billion in aviation funding, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. The new request also includes money for control towers and airport projects. Even a quick repair won’t immediately put the airlines back on schedule. Planes held now will be late for their next flights, connecting passengers will miss departures, and crews can run out of permitted duty time. Then with planes out of position, disruptions continue.

The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing flights across the U.S. to resume after halting takeoffs for several hours Friday evening.

But travelers will face significant disruptions through the weekend as airlines unwind one of the most significant disruptions to air travel in decades.

At 8:15pm EST, the FAA began allowing flights to operate, the Trump administration said. It came after a four-hour ground stop that stranded flyers at airports across the country.

Most departing flights in the U.S.were grounded indefinitely late Friday afternoon after the FAA reported communication issues impacting air traffic control centers.

The fallout for travelers was severe, affecting thousands of flights — a meltdown that was likely to cascade across multiple days.

More than 6,000 departures had been canceled as of 8:45 p.m. Friday evening, according to FlightAware. At least 1,400 departures for Saturday had been scrapped.

That number is likely to rise sharply as airlines work to get operations back on track.

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a news conference Friday evening.

Friday's communications outage occurred during an upgrade to FAA technology, officials said.

The disruption marked only the second time since 9/11 that a ground stop affecting the entire nation had been issued

Airlines issued travel advisories in the midst of the travel chaos. These waivers typically allow passengers with flights booked more flexibility to change their itineraries:

Some departures continued, despite the wide-ranging ground stop.

In a social media post, United Airlines said international departures were being managed on a case-by-case basis, the carrier reported.

Alaska Air Group, which owns Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, said flights within the state of Alaska were still cleared to operate. Neighbor island service in Hawaii was also unaffected. Departures from the West Coast to Hawaii were also continuing, a spokesperson said.

Passengers whose flights are canceled or significantly delayed are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel or accept a rebooked flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption.

Under Department of Transportation rules, a significant delay generally means arriving at your final destination at least three hours late on a domestic itinerary or six hours late on an international itinerary. For passengers who decide to not travel on those flights, airlines must provide refunds to the original form of payment, not just travel credits.

In large-scale travel disruptions like this, rental cars and hotel rooms at or near airports can book up quickly, so it can make sense to act fast if you want to secure a backup option.

If you have airline miles you can use to book a flight for tomorrow, that can also be a good self-insurance policy in case the disruption isn't resolved quickly. Just make sure you understand the cancellation and refund rules before booking a backup ticket.

And while many rewards credit cards offer built-in trip delay or cancellation protection if you used them to book your original airline tickets, it's not guaranteed that those benefits will cover FAA groundings of this nature. Still, save your receipts for any unexpected expenses in case you're eligible for reimbursement.

#6128. How the Electoral College Dies

Blue-state activists are about to be perfectly positioned to execute an end run around the constitutional system.

In the wake of the 2026 midterms, we are on the cusp of a total transformation of the U.S. election system. After decades of Republican dominance in state legislatures, Democrats now control enough state governments to push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past its 270-vote activation threshold and dismantle the Electoral College from below.

But it seems like the right has barely realized the importance of the fight that’s about to begin.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

#6123. Combat Took on America’s Socialism Fever

The National Review newsletter captured a time in which revolutionary violence tried to join the mainstream.

Young men raise their fists and chant slogans during the “Days of Rage” demonstrations organized by the Weatherman to protest the Chicago Seven trial and “to bring the war home” in Chicago, Ill., in 1969.

Socialism looks in 2026 a lot like bell bottoms: tried on, worn out, and out of fashion.

Decades ago, Germany, Russia, Cambodia, Ethiopia, and points beyond tried socialism to disastrous results. Many American leftists, as judged by the election returns, believe in an American exceptionalism of sorts, too. They think that socialism in the United States will be different. We won’t need a world war, societal collapse, or the obligatory charitable single and accompanying global benefit show to save us from its consequences. Socialism, for its true believers, amounts to salvation and not that from which people living under it require deliverance.

#6122. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6120. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6119. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.
